Decisions and the questions waiting for the product owner are in [11 Decisions: engine](11-decisions-engine.md) and [11 Decisions: frontend](11-decisions-frontend.md). How this set of documents is organised, and every planned diagram, is in [About this document set](00-doc-plan.md).

## What exists today, and how to see it

Document 10 (Build plan and status), which the two leads will write, says what runs today and how to run it. Until it exists:

- **The editor's design** is a set of clickable mockups, outside this repository, in the `workflow` folder beside it: `../workflow/mockups/index.html` (relative to this repo's root). Its rules and words are in `../workflow/spec/editor-model.md`.
- **The contract** is in `contract/`: the authored format with sample workflows in `contract/fixtures/`, the core, authoring and runtime APIs, and the catalogue of connections. Document 6 ([The contract](06-the-contract.md)) explains it.
- **The engine** follows kernel spec v2.20, kept in the `workflow-platform` repository, with a copy in `engine/spec/`. Its core package, which decides everything a request does, is built: 1899 tests pass. The server's store and its authoring and runtime APIs are built too, with 237 tests passing; its workers, its endpoints for other systems, the mock systems and its development host are not yet, so nothing can run against the server.
- **The frontend** is built: every screen of the editor and of the pages people use. It runs on the engine's core in the browser, and a stand-in plays the server until the real one can be run. Document 8 ([Frontend design](08-frontend-design.md)) says what is not built yet.

**To see it running:** in `frontend/`, run `npm install` once, then `npm run dev`, and open `http://localhost:5173`. Pages have hash addresses, such as `#/tasks`. It opens on the workflows list, with three sample workflows, Change request among them. The footer has "Reset sample data", which starts the samples again.
## Ten words to know first

The editor's word is what people see on screen. The engine's word is what engineers and the engine's documents use. Document 4 has the full list.

| Editor word | What it means | Engine word |
|---|---|---|
| **Workflow** | What an author builds. Edited as a **draft**; each publish makes a new **version** that never changes. | Definition (one per published version) |
| **Request** | One use of a workflow, from the start form to an ending. | Request, with its history of events |
| **Stage** | A box on the diagram: where a request sits, with a status people see. | Stage. One authored stage becomes a short chain of engine stages. |
| **Task** | The part of a stage that asks people: who is asked, a form, buttons. | Person wait |
| **Button** | How a person finishes a task: Submit, Approve, Reject. | Outcome |
| **Arrow** | "When ... go to ...": where a request goes next, and when. | Transition |
| **Value** | A named piece of data the workflow remembers, such as an answer. | Data path in the request's data |
| **Action** | Something the workflow does by itself: save a value, notify, tell other systems, create a Jira issue, look something up. | Set, notification or event rule, or call wait, by type |
| **Connection** | Another system the platform is linked to, set up by an administrator. | Connection (a configured connector) and its catalogue entries |
| **Stuck** | A request that cannot move until someone acts, always shown with its reason: an action failed; nobody is there to ask (nobody was asked, or the group's recorded members include nobody able to answer); no arrow fits; or an error. The people who look after stuck requests are told. They can close it; where running again can help (a failed action, nobody to ask) they can also retry it. | `stuck { reason, at }`; inside the kernel, a fault or a person wait with nobody asked |
===\ndocs/01-context.md\n===
# Context

Owner: Frontend owner (draws); the Engine owner supplies the facts.

Answers: Who and what does the platform touch?

The platform touches two kinds of thing: **people**, who only ever use its screens, and **other systems**, which it reaches only through a fixed set of doors. This document names every person by role and every other system in the first build, and says what crosses between them and the platform, in which direction, and who starts it.

Two terms first. A **door** is one of the seven ways data or control can cross the platform's edge (decision E-9 in [Decisions: engine](11-decisions-engine.md)); nothing crosses any other way. A **connection** is another system the platform is linked to, set up once by an administrator; a workflow uses what a connection offers but never sees how it is set up.

## The platform and the systems around it

Things that come in are on the left; things that go out are on the right. A solid line is control: it starts a request, answers one, or makes something happen in another system. A dotted line is data. Data that comes in is recorded and can still decide what happens next: a looked-up value is read by arrows, and the read of a group's members decides whether anybody can answer a task. The numbers are the doors.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  people["People<br/>fill in forms and press buttons<br/>in the platform's pages"]
  hd["Helpdesk<br/><i>can start a request</i>"]
  dir["Directory<br/><i>gives data</i><br/>people and groups"]
  sc["Service catalog<br/><i>gives data</i>"]
  signin["Sign-in<br/>existing application"]

  platform["<b>The platform</b><br/>editor and pages<br/>engine<br/>connections"]

  jira["Jira<br/><i>does something</i>"]
  deploy["Deploy pipeline<br/><i>does something and waits</i>"]
  mail["Email and Slack<br/><i>carries messages</i>"]
  rep["Reporting<br/><i>is told what happened</i>"]

  people ==>|"1 start a request<br/>2 answer a task"| platform
  hd ==>|"1 a ticket is created"| platform
  dir -.->|"3, 4 who is in a group"| platform
  sc -.->|"5 choices for a question<br/>3 look up a service"| platform
  signin -.->|"who is signed in"| platform

  platform ==>|"3 create an issue,<br/>issue key back"| jira
  platform <==>|"3 run the pipeline,<br/>it reports back later"| deploy
  platform -.->|"6 messages"| mail
  platform -.->|"7 what happened"| rep

  classDef ours fill:#e4e6fc,stroke:#4f46e5,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#1c2030
  classDef existing fill:#f4f5f7,stroke:#a0a6b1,color:#1c2030
  classDef other fill:#ffffff,stroke:#a0a6b1,color:#1c2030
  class platform ours
  class signin,dir,mail existing
  class hd,sc,jira,deploy,rep,people other
```

*D1. The platform and everything around it, with the door each line uses*

In a real deployment, sign-in, the directory, and email and Slack come from the existing application the platform lives in. The first build has real connectors for the directory, Jira, and email and Slack. On the development and test hosts, every system on this picture except sign-in is a small mock server with real HTTP in and out, so the wiring is real and each can be inspected (E-12). Document 5 ([Integrations](05-integrations.md)) gives each door's rules: what is recorded, what is retried, and what failure does.

## Who does what

Six roles use the platform. One person can hold several; for example, the author of a workflow usually also looks after its stuck requests. Every signed-in person can open any request's page in the first build, and sees there whether it is stuck and why; the Stuck requests list, the technical detail, and Retry and Close are only for the people who look after stuck requests and for platform admins.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  author["Workflow author"]
  requester["Requester"]
  asked["Person asked"]
  keeper["People who look after<br/>stuck requests"]
  padmin["Platform admin"]
  builder["Connection builder<br/>(an engineer)"]

  editor["Editor<br/>Diagram, In words, Values, forms,<br/>To do, Try it, Publish, Settings"]
  connlist["Connections list<br/>read-only"]
  start["Start a request"]
  tasks["My tasks"]
  page["Request page"]
  stuckview["Stuck requests,<br/>with Retry and Close"]
  setup["Connection configuration<br/><i>no screen in the first build</i>"]
  code["Connector code and<br/>catalogue entries"]

  author --> editor
  author --> connlist
  requester --> start
  requester --> page
  asked --> tasks
  keeper --> stuckview
  padmin -->|"any request"| stuckview
  padmin --> setup
  builder --> code

  classDef role fill:#ffffff,stroke:#a0a6b1,color:#1c2030
  classDef screen fill:#e4e6fc,stroke:#4f46e5,color:#1c2030
  classDef none fill:#f4f5f7,stroke:#c9cdd4,stroke-dasharray:4 3,color:#464d5e
  class author,requester,asked,keeper,padmin,builder role
  class editor,connlist,start,tasks,page,stuckview screen
  class setup,code none
```

*D2. Who does what: each role and the screens it uses*

| Role | What they do | On which screen | What they can never do |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Workflow author** | Builds a workflow, tries it with test requests, and publishes it. Chooses who looks after its stuck requests. | The editor; the read-only Connections list. | Set up a connection or see how one is reached. Change a published version: publishing always makes a new one. Send anything real from Try it: every connection is pretended there. |
| **Requester** | Starts a request by filling in the start form, and answers again if the request is sent back. | Start a request; the request page; My tasks after a send-back. | Answer their own request where the author turned on "The requester can't answer their own request". Move a request except by pressing a button. |
| **Person asked** | Answers a task: fills in its form and presses a button. | My tasks; the task on the request page. | Press a button before the questions it needs are answered. Act on a task not asked of them: whether they are in the group is checked when they act. |
| **People who look after stuck requests** | Are told when a request is stuck. Close it, or retry it where running again can help: a failed action, or nobody to ask. Close any open request, stuck or not. Pause or resume a "Starts when" of the live version, see the starts that were refused, and run a refused start again. The editor's setting is "Stuck requests go to"; the engine calls them the workflow's admins. | Stuck requests; the request page. | Skip a task, send a request to another stage, change its values or reopen it: none of these is in the first build. Act without their name and reason being recorded. |
| **Platform admin** | Holds the existing application's platform-admin entitlement. Sets up connections and chooses which systems are told what happened. In the first build this is configuration, not a screen: an entry for the connection plus its secret in the secret store. Can retry or close any request, under the same rules. | No screen for connections in the first build; Stuck requests; the request page. | Change what a connection offers: that is code. Change a workflow's behaviour from outside the editor. |
| **Connection builder** | An engineer who writes a connector (the code that talks to one kind of system) and the catalogue entries that describe what it offers. The connector ships with a deployment of the platform. In the first build, that is us. | None: code and data in the repository. | Name a connector in the editor or the engine: both read the catalogue as data (E-10). Name a customer's workflow in platform code. |

Document 9 ([People and permissions](09-people-and-permissions.md)) says where each of these rules is enforced.

## Every outside system in the first build

One line each: what crosses, in which direction, and who starts it. "Engine" means the engine starts the exchange; it always records what comes back before it acts on it.

| System | What crosses | Direction | Who starts it | Door |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Sign-in** (existing application) | Who the signed-in person is, with every call from a page. | In | The application, on each call | none: it is not a door, the engine just records who acted |
| **Directory** | Who is in a group. The engine adds this recorded read to every task that may ask a group, so it can tell from the history when nobody is able to answer; "members" steps and "is in group" tests read it too. | In | Engine, when the request enters the stage | 3 (look up) |
| **Directory** | The people in a group, as choices for a question: read live while the form is shown, and the chosen person looked up again when the person presses. | In | The page asks; the engine reads the directory | 5 |
| **Directory** | Which groups a person is in, at the moment they press a button. Recorded as evidence. | In | Engine, when the person acts | 4 |
| **Directory** | People and groups for pickers and samples in the editor. Not recorded. | In | The page | none: a page concern |
| **Email and Slack** | Messages: "Your change request was rejected", a new task, a stuck request. | Out | Engine, after each step it records | 6 |
| **Helpdesk** | "A ticket is created", with the ticket's fields. It starts a request only if it fits the workflow's "Starts when", which may name the Requester from a person field of the ticket. Helpdesk is told at once what became of what it sent: started, did not fit, paused, refused and why, or already started. | In, reply out | Helpdesk | 1 |
| **Service catalog** | The list of services, as choices for a question, read while the form is shown and not recorded. When the person presses, the chosen service is looked up again and recorded with the catalog's label at that moment, together with the lookup. From the author's side, only the answer is kept: a later change in the catalog does not change a request's answer. | In | The page asks; the engine reads the source | 5 |
| **Service catalog** | One service's owner and tier ("Look up a service"), saved as values. | Out, result in | Engine | 3 (look up) |
| **Jira** | "Create an issue" with the request's values; the issue's key and link (`key`, `url`) come back. In the integrated sample this happens only after a failed deploy. The sample's create is a plain create: if Jira's answer is lost, sending again can create a second issue, which an admin closes by hand. | Out, result in | Engine | 3 (does something) |
| **Deploy pipeline** | "Run the pipeline" with the service and the Helpdesk ticket reference. The result comes back later, minutes or days after: the engine asks for the run's status, and a callback from the pipeline only makes it ask sooner. | Out, result in later | Engine asks; the pipeline reports | 3 (does something and waits) |
| **Reporting** | What happened to each request: started, status changed, stuck, ended, and anything a workflow chooses to tell. | Out | Engine, after each step it records | 7 |

Two rules hold for all of them. **Nothing outside moves a request unless the workflow asked it to**: another system can start a request, or answer a request that asked it something, and nothing else. **A message, or telling other systems what happened, never holds a request up**: of everything that crosses the edge, only two things can leave a request stuck: an action that uses a connection and fails where its author chose "stuck", and a read of a group's members that finds nobody able to answer a task, or that fails.

## We build the platform; customers build workflows

The platform is the editor and pages, the engine and the connections. A customer's workflow is data: an author builds it in the editor and publishes it without anyone deploying code. So:

- **"Change request" is sample data.** It is the example in every mockup and diagram, and it lives in `contract/fixtures/` as a test workflow. Platform code never names it, nor any of its stages, values or buttons.
- **The sample systems are sample data too.** Helpdesk, Service catalog, Jira, Deploy pipeline and Reporting appear to the editor and the engine only as catalogue entries such as `jira.createIssue@1`. The editor lists whatever the catalogue offers and hard-codes no system (E-10).
- **What is ours, and what is the customer's.** Ours: the editor, the pages, the engine, the connectors and the catalogue. The customer's: their workflows, their Domains-list-style tables inside those workflows, and the choice of who looks after stuck requests.

===\ndocs/02-the-parts.md\n===
# The parts

Owner: Engine owner.

Answers: What runs where, and who owns it?

Two teams build the platform. The **frontend team** owns the editor and the pages people use in the browser. The **engine team** owns everything on the server, plus one package of engine code, **core**, that also runs in the browser. The **existing application** the platform will live in supplies three things: sign-in, the directory of people and groups, and the message service that sends email and Slack. This document shows where each part runs, who owns it, what it depends on, and where state is kept. Core and the server are built: they run in the engine packages' own tests and on the development host, against in-memory mock systems, and the frontend runs on core. Nothing runs yet inside the existing application.

Terms used below. A **turn** is how the engine handles one input (a start, a button pressed, a connection's result, an admin's retry or close): one database transaction that records the input and everything that follows from it. A **job** is background work a turn queues in its own transaction and a worker runs after the turn commits. A **connector** is code that talks to one kind of outside system; a **connection** is one configured instance of it, written in the deployment's configuration by a platform admin.

## What runs where

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph browser["Browser"]
    ui["Editor and pages<br/>[frontend]"]
    bcore["core package<br/>check, facts, form state, Try it<br/>[engine]"]
  end
  signin["Sign-in<br/>[existing application]"]
  subgraph serverside["Server side [engine]"]
    app["Application server<br/>authoring API, runtime API,<br/>inbound hook"]
    score["core package<br/>compile, check, decide, evolve"]
    workers["Job workers<br/>a job per call, a notify job<br/>and a publish job per turn"]
    pg[("Postgres")]
    conn["Connectors"]
  end
  dir["Directory<br/>[existing application]"]
  msg["Message service<br/>email and Slack<br/>[existing application]"]
  out["Outside systems<br/>Helpdesk, Service catalog, Jira,<br/>Deploy pipeline, Reporting"]

  ui -->|"in process"| bcore
  ui -->|"HTTP"| app
  signin -.->|"who is signed in"| app
  app -->|"each turn"| score
  workers -->|"rules"| score
  app -->|"one transaction per turn"| pg
  workers <-->|"jobs"| pg
  app -->|"memberships, choices"| conn
  workers -->|"calls, messages, events"| conn
  conn --> dir
  conn --> msg
  conn <--> out
  out -.->|"events that start requests"| app

  classDef fe fill:#e7f5ec,stroke:#15803d,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#1c2030
  classDef eng fill:#e4e6fc,stroke:#4f46e5,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#1c2030
  classDef existing fill:#f4f5f7,stroke:#a0a6b1,stroke-dasharray:4 3,color:#1c2030
  classDef other fill:#ffffff,stroke:#a0a6b1,color:#1c2030
  class ui fe
  class bcore,app,score,workers,pg,conn eng
  class signin,dir,msg existing
  class out other
```

*D3. What runs where, who owns each part, and what does the existing application supply?*

The owner is written in each box as well as shown by colour: green is the frontend's, blue the engine's, grey and dashed the existing application's, white the outside systems. The outside systems shown are the mock systems of the first build (E-12); a real deployment connects whatever its platform admins set up.

The pages never reach Postgres, a job or an outside system: they call the two APIs over HTTP and core in the browser. The engine never reaches an outside system except through a connector, the directory and the message service included. How the server side is split into processes, and where the job workers run, is not designed. The APIs are plain functions with thin web-standard `Request -> Response` handlers, so they can be mounted in the existing Next.js application later (E-11); where they are mounted is unknown: depends on the existing application.

## Each part

"First build*" marks a part built, in its thinnest form, beyond the MVP's requirements, at the product owner's request (E-9, E-33).

| Part | What it does | Owner | Depends on | Build |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Editor | The diagram, "In words", forms, values, To do, Try it, Publish, settings | Frontend | core, authoring API, the catalogue | First build |
| Pages | Start a request, My tasks, a task, the request page, request lists, Stuck requests with Retry and Close | Frontend | Runtime API; core (`formState`); the published source of each version; the words files | First build |
| core package | The authored-format types, `parse`, `check`, `facts`, `formState`, `evaluate`, `compile`, `story`, `diff`, the turn function with `decide` and `evolve`, the expression environment, the Try it host (E-3, E-15) | Engine | The expression library, `@marcbachmann/cel-js` 8.0.0, and nothing else | First build. Built, with tests, except `diff` and `upgrade` (E-27). |
| Authoring API | The workflows list, drafts, publish, versions, workflow settings, the catalogue, the server's core version (`contract/authoring-api.md`) | Engine | core, Postgres, the directory (authors listed as groups) | First build |
| Runtime API | Start, choices, My tasks, act, retry, close, pausing a binding, listing and retrying refused starts, reads for lists and the request page, sign-in and directory reads for pages (`contract/runtime-api.md`) | Engine | core, Postgres, the directory (memberships when a person acts, looked up before the request is locked), data sources (choices and their look-up, likewise) | First build |
| Inbound hook | `POST {hooks}/hooks/v1/events/{connection}`: an outside event starts a request through a "Starts when" binding, answered at once; every event is one row of the inbound log | Engine | Connectors (`verify`, `parse`), core, Postgres | First build* |
| Call job | One per call: sends it with its recorded key; runs again later while there is no clear answer; asks a "Wait for" job for its status every poll interval; turns an answer into a result turn | Engine | The jobs table, connectors, Postgres, the workers' clock | First build |
| Notifier | One job per turn whose events could match a notification rule: applies the version's notification rules to the turn's events and sends each message with the values as they were at that event | Engine | core's rule matching, the directory (groups expanded when sending), the message service, the words file `contract/words/notifications.json` | First build |
| Publisher | One job per turn: works out the turn's public events and posts each, in the request's order, to every address in the configuration, at least once | Engine | core, Postgres | First build* |
| Connectors and connections | Code for one kind of system, and its configured connections with their settings and the names of their secrets, read from the deployment's configuration at start-up and held in memory with the catalogue. A snapshot test fails the build when an entry's shape changes under its version | Engine builds; a platform admin writes the configuration | The outside system | First build: connectors for the directory, Jira, and email and Slack, and the mock connectors for development and tests. The interfaces of the existing application's directory and message service: unknown: depends on the existing application. |
| Postgres store | Every table in [Where state lives](#where-state-lives) | Engine | A Postgres server | First build; PGlite on the development and test hosts (E-11). Which server, schema name and migration naming: unknown: depends on the existing application. |
| Jobs | The engine's own table, written inside the turn's transaction and taken by polling workers (E-30) | Engine | Postgres | First build |
| Sign-in | Who is signed in, and whether they hold the platform-admin entitlement; passed to every server call as the `Caller` | Existing application | | Interface unknown: depends on the existing application |
| Directory | People and groups, by immutable directory ID | Existing application, reached through a connection | | Interface unknown: depends on the existing application |
| Message service | Email and Slack | Existing application, reached through an adapter | | Interface unknown: depends on the existing application |
| Mock systems | Seven connectors over state in memory, one per kind of example, each with at most two switches (E-12, E-33) | Engine | | Development and test hosts only |

## The engine's two packages

For engineers only: the engine's code packages and the rules between them.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  fe["frontend<br/>editor and pages"]
  core["@workflow/core<br/>engine/packages/core"]
  cel["@marcbachmann/cel-js 8.0.0"]
  server["@workflow/server<br/>engine/packages/server"]
  mocks["server src/mock<br/>in-memory mock connectors"]
  hosts["Development host<br/>and test host"]

  fe -->|"local package"| core
  fe -.->|"HTTP only"| server
  server --> core
  core -->|"only src/cel/environment.ts"| cel
  hosts --> server
  hosts -->|"register the mock connectors"| mocks
```

*D3b. Which package may use which?*

- **core** (`engine/packages/core`) is pure TypeScript with no I/O and no Node-only or browser-only API, so it runs in a browser and on the server (E-3). Every function is synchronous and deterministic: no I/O, no clock, no randomness (`contract/core-api.md` section 1).
- **server** (`engine/packages/server`) holds the Postgres store, the turn transaction, the jobs, the connectors, the inbound hook and the HTTP API. It imports core. It is the authority: at publish it runs the check and the compile again and stores its own result (E-3).

| Rule | How it is held |
|---|---|
| core imports no Node built-in and uses no Node or browser API. | ESLint, a boundaries test in core, and core's TypeScript settings (`types: []`, `lib: ["ES2022"]`) (`engine/README-dev.md`) |
| Only core's `src/cel/environment.ts` imports the expression library; everything else goes through that wrapper (E-18). | The same two checks |
| Platform code never imports the server's `src/mock`; the hosts register the mock connectors, and production registers none of them. | `engine/design/mock-systems.md` section 1 |
| Platform code never names a customer workflow or a connector; both are data. | Root `README.md`; E-10 |
| The frontend uses core as a package and reaches the server only through the authoring and runtime APIs. | E-3; the contract |

**How the frontend consumes core.** The frontend depends on core by a local path (`"@workflow/core": "file:../engine/packages/core"`). It can use core's TypeScript source through the export condition `workflow-source`, or the built `dist` after core is built (`engine/README-dev.md`); the frontend uses the source. The frontend wraps core's synchronous functions in its own asynchronous interface and may run them in a Web Worker. Every server response names the core version it runs; the browser's must match it exactly, or the editor marks its findings as possibly out of date and publish is refused (`contract/core-api.md` section 13). core has two entries (E-26). `@workflow/core` is the contract surface, with the authored-format and catalogue types; the frontend imports only this one. `@workflow/core/kernel` holds the stored formats, `decide`, `evolve`, the turn function, the schema validator, the kernel publish check, the in-memory host and the call-result check, for the server and the hosts; its shapes may change between minor versions. One root cannot hold both, because the two share names with different meanings (`Status`, `ValueKind`, `MessagePart`) (`contract/core-api.md` section 14).

## Where state lives

For engineers only: every table and what it can be rebuilt from.

Twelve tables (data model). Two are the source of truth: `events` and `definitions`. They are never updated and never deleted. Connections, secrets and the catalogue are configuration held in memory, not tables.

| Store | Holds | Kind | Rebuildable from | Kept |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `events` | Every request's history | History, source of truth | Nothing: everything else is worked out from it | For ever |
| `definitions` | Each published version, keyed by the workflow's ID (not its name) and the version: the compiled definition with its `types` block and origin map, form schemas, the authored source, the draft revision it came from, the core and authored-format versions that compiled it, the catalogue version, who published it | History, source of truth | Nothing | For ever |
| `workflows` | The server's workflow ID, name, description, who created it | Configuration | Nothing | For ever; archiving is not designed |
| `drafts` | One draft per workflow, its revision and its To do counts | Working copy, replaced on each save | Nothing; earlier revisions are not kept | Until the next save |
| `workflow_settings` | `authors`, `stuck_requests_go_to`, paused bindings | Configuration, not versioned | Nothing | For ever |
| `settings_log` | Each change to a workflow's settings, a pause or resume of a binding included, with who and when | Log | Nothing | For ever |
| `requests`, `open_waits` | One row per request (status, stuck state, values, a person's start token) for lists; the open tasks and calls, for My tasks | Read tables | `events`, by replay, except the start token | Rebuilt at will |
| `pending_calls` | Calls opened and not yet answered: attempts, the outside job's reference | Working state | Partly: rows for open calls from `WaitOpened` | Until the result is recorded |
| `jobs` | Call, notify and publish jobs | Working state | Nothing | Until done |
| `attempts_log`, `inbound_log` | Refused attempts; every event received on the inbound hook, with its result or code and the event, the start dedupe included | Logs | Nothing | Not deleted in the first build |
| Browser memory | Try it's test requests | Test state | Nothing | While the page is open |

- **A read table reads events only**: never another read table, never the live version, never the clock. So it can be rebuilt for one request or for all, and a new one can be added later and filled for every existing request (data model section 4).
- **Outbound payloads are not stored.** They are worked out from `events` when a turn's events are posted.

## The development host

For engineers only: how the engine runs before it lives in the existing application.

The development host is the server itself, on PGlite, with the in-memory mock connectors, a seeded directory and the development sign-in. One command starts it, and it serves both APIs on one port (E-33; `engine/design/mock-systems.md`).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  browser["Browser<br/>editor and pages"]
  subgraph proc["One Node process: the development host"]
    eng["Engine server<br/>both APIs, the inbound hook, job workers"]
    pglite[("PGlite<br/>Postgres in WebAssembly")]
    mocks["Seven mock connectors, in memory<br/>Directory, Service catalog, Helpdesk, Jira,<br/>Deploy pipeline, Email and Slack, Reporting"]
  end

  browser -->|"HTTP /api/workflow/v1"| eng
  eng ---|"in process"| pglite
  eng ---|"in process, through the connector interface"| mocks
```

*D3c. What does the development host run?*

| | Development host | Test host | Production |
|---|---|---|---|
| Database | PGlite, in process | PGlite; real Postgres for the cases that test concurrency | Postgres; which server: unknown: depends on the existing application |
| Outside systems | The seven in-memory mocks | The same, reset to their seed before every case | Real systems through their connectors |
| Connections | From the host's seed configuration | The same | From the deployment's configuration at start-up |
| Clock | The system clock | An injected clock that moves only when a case moves it | The system clock |
| Sign-in | `signInAs`: pick a person from the host's list | Each case names the person who makes each API call | The existing application's |
| `{base}`, `{hooks}` | `/api/workflow/v1`; the server's own origin, one port | The same | Unknown: depends on the existing application |

**What needs real Postgres.** PGlite serves one connection, so it cannot show two transactions racing. The cases that test concurrency run on real Postgres with two connections, such as two deliveries of one event at once (integrated-sample case I23). Every other integration case runs on PGlite.

Try it does not use the development host or the mocks: it runs in the browser on core's in-memory host and answers from the catalogue's samples (E-4).
## Browser parts

The browser runs the editor, the pages people use, and engine code for everything the editor works out on each edit. It holds no state of its own beyond the open page: drafts, versions and requests are on the server, and Try it's test requests live in the page's memory. Document 8, [Frontend design](08-frontend-design.md), gives the detail: its modules (D21), what happens on one edit (D22), and what each screen asks of the contract (D23).

| Part | What it does | Owner | Talks to | Build |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Editor | The workflows list, the diagram and stage panel, In words, Values, the form editor, To do and Publish, Settings, Try it, the read-only Connections list. The draft is one document, changed only through named commands, saved with its revision. | Frontend | core (in process), authoring API, the catalogue | Foundation built; the main screen is being built |
| Pages | Start a request, My tasks, the request page, request lists, Stuck requests with Retry and Close | Frontend | Runtime API; core's `formState` for a form being filled in | Not built |
| core, in the browser | `check`, `facts`, `formState`, `evaluate`, `diff` and the Try it host, which compiles the draft in Try it mode, run on the draft as the author edits (E-3, E-4, E-27) | Engine | Nothing: no I/O | Built (`diff` since E-28); the frontend imports it as source |
| Stand-in | Plays the server and the outside systems until the pages reach the real server, behind the same services interface the server will sit behind. Checks, Try it and live requests run on core; the stand-in keeps its data in the browser's local storage. It is replaced as the server arrives. | Frontend | Nothing outside the browser | Built; development only |

Every screen reaches the engine side through that one services interface, never directly: the editor never calls `fetch` itself, and words are chosen in the browser from the codes the engine sends (E-7).

Sources: decisions E-3 to E-33 ([Decisions: engine](11-decisions-engine.md)); kernel spec v2.20 with `architecture.md` and `kernel/data-model.md` in `workflow-platform/engine` (its copy is in `engine/spec/`); `engine/design/integrations-shapes.md`, `mock-systems.md`, `integrated-sample.md`; `engine/README-dev.md`; `contract/core-api.md`, `authoring-api.md`, `runtime-api.md`.
===\ndocs/03-life-of-a-workflow.md\n===
# The life of a workflow

Owner: Engine owner.

Answers: How does a draft become a running request and a history?

A workflow exists in three forms. The author edits a **draft**. Publishing turns the draft into a **published version** (the engine calls it a definition), which the engine runs and which never changes. Each use of a version is a **request**, and everything that happens to it is recorded, in order and for good, as its **history**. This document follows one workflow through the three forms, says which code does each step and where it runs, and marks what is in the first build, what is held as a shape only, and what is later. It describes a design; nothing in it has run.

Four engine words are used below. An **input** is one thing that comes into a request: a start, a button pressed, a connection's result, an admin's retry or close. A **turn** is how the engine handles one input: in one database transaction it records the input and every consequence. **`decide`** is the engine function that works out those consequences; **`evolve`** is the function that rebuilds a request's state by reading its recorded history back.

## Three forms and the steps between

| Form | What it is | Where it is kept | Can it change? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Draft | The workflow in the authored format (`contract/authored-format.md`): stages, tasks, forms, buttons, actions, arrows, values, lists, in the editor's words. It may be unfinished. | On the server, one per workflow, with a revision number. | Yes. Every save replaces it. |
| Published version | The compiled definition (engine stages, waits, transitions, rules, and a `types` block with the type of every data path, constant and operation result), the form schemas, the origin map (which authored item each compiled part came from), and the authored source it was compiled from. | On the server, one row per version (`definitions`). | Never. The next publish makes a new version. |
| Request history | The events recorded for one request, in order. | On the server (`events`). | Only by adding events at the end. |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph browser["In the browser, on core"]
    edit["Edit<br/>the author changes the draft"]
    check["Check<br/>To do and Worth knowing"]
    try["Try it<br/>test requests in memory"]
  end
  draft[("Draft<br/>authored format")]
  publish["Publish<br/>the server checks and<br/>compiles again"]
  version[("Published version<br/>never changes")]
  start["Start<br/>a person or another system"]
  act["Act<br/>a button, a result, an admin"]
  history[("Request history<br/>events, only added to")]
  show["Show<br/>lists, request page, story"]

  edit -->|"save"| draft
  draft --> check
  check -.->|"To do at the item"| edit
  draft --> try
  draft -->|"no To do left"| publish
  publish --> version
  version -->|"names the version"| start
  start -->|"record"| history
  start -->|"then"| act
  act -->|"record"| history
  history --> show
```

*D4. What are the three forms of a workflow, and which steps lead from one to the next?*

| Step | What happens | Code | Runs in |
|---|---|---|---|
| Edit | The editor changes the draft and saves it. The server refuses a save based on an old revision (`stale-revision`) and a document that is not in the authored format (`invalid-document`). An unfinished draft saves. | Editor (frontend); authoring API with core's `parse` and `check` (engine) | Browser; server at each save |
| Check | core's `check` returns findings. A **To do** stops publishing; a **Worth knowing** does not. Each finding is a code, a location in the draft, and parameters. `facts` adds which arrows send back and which values can be read where. | core | Browser, on every edit. Server, at every save (to store the counts) and at publish (authoritative). |
| Try | A test request runs on the draft in the editor, with every connection pretended. See [Try it](#try-it). | core's test host | Browser only |
| Publish | The server upgrades the draft to its own core's authored format, checks and compiles it with the catalogue it holds, refuses on any To do, and stores the new version. | Authoring API, core's `compile` | Server. It is the authority (E-3). |
| Start | A person submits the start form, or an event from another system fits a "Starts when" binding. The start turn records `RequestStarted`, naming the workflow and the version. | Runtime API or the inbound hook; core's turn function inside a server transaction | Server |
| Act | A person presses a button, a connection's result comes back, or an admin retries or closes. Each is one input and one turn. | Runtime API, the inbound hook, the call's job; core's turn function | Server |
| Record | In one transaction the turn validates the input, appends it and every consequence `decide` works out, updates the tables that lists read with the stuck state worked out after it, and queues the jobs that send calls, messages and events. | core (`decide`) inside the server's transaction | Server and Postgres |
| Show | Lists, My tasks, the request page and its story are worked out from the history and named through the version's origin map. The page turns codes into words using that version's authored source. | Server reads, with core's `story`; pages (frontend) | Server, then browser |

The same core package runs in the browser and on the server (E-3). It has no I/O and no clock, so what the browser's check and Try it say is what the server will say. What the browser computes is still only a preview: at publish the server runs `check` and `compile` again and stores only its own result. Every server response carries the core version it runs (`Engine-Core-Version`). If the browser's version differs, the editor marks its findings and Try it as possibly out of date, saving still works, and publishing is refused with `core-version-mismatch` (`contract/core-api.md` section 13).

## What the compiler does to one stage

An author sees one stage. The engine runs a short chain of **engine stages** made from it, in a fixed order: the actions of "When this stage starts", the tasks, the actions of "After they respond", and a **routing step** that holds the arrows. A task that may ask a group has a membership read beside it, in the tasks step itself. A `members` step, or an "is in group" test inside a condition, is a separate recorded read in its own engine stage, placed just before the step that uses it, so it sees a group saved earlier in the same stage. A step the stage does not need is left out; the routing step is always there (`engine/design/compiler.md` section 2; E-23). The Domain approval stage of the change request becomes three engine stages:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph authored["Authored stage: Domain approval"]
    a1["Task<br/>Who is asked: Primary domain's approvers"]
    a2["After they respond<br/>Notify Requester, only when Reject"]
    a3["Arrows<br/>Approve, Reject, Request changes"]
  end
  subgraph compiled["Engine stages in the published version"]
    subgraph e2["st_domain_approval__tasks"]
      w1["Person wait<br/>tk_domain_approval"]
      w2["Call wait tk_domain_approval__members<br/>directory read, recorded,<br/>onFailure: outcome"]
    end
    e3["act_notify_requester_rejected__run<br/>a notification rule matches its entry"]
    e4["st_domain_approval__route<br/>ar_da_approve, ar_da_reject,<br/>ar_da_request_changes"]
  end
  inArrow["From Request form:<br/>In all other cases"] --> e2
  e2 -->|"st_domain_approval__answered:<br/>every task answered;<br/>an open read is cancelled"| e3
  e3 -->|"next"| e4
  e4 --> outNext["Create Jira issue, Rejected,<br/>or Request form, sent back"]
  a1 -.->|"origin"| w1
  a1 -.->|"origin"| w2
  a2 -.->|"origin"| e3
  a3 -.->|"origin"| e4
```

*D4b. What does one authored stage become in the published version, and how is each piece tied back to it?*

- **IDs carry through.** The task ID is the wait's ID, each button ID an outcome ID, each arrow ID a transition ID, each value ID a data path, each status ID the status ID. Names the compiler adds are `<authored item ID>__<local name>`; authored IDs never contain a double underscore, so the two can never clash. An authored ID is at most 40 characters, so every compiled name fits the 64-character limit. A rename changes nothing published (E-14, E-23).
- **One status for the whole chain.** Every step carries the stage's status, so people see "Waiting for approval" from the tasks step to the routing step. Moves between the engine stages of one authored stage make no entry in the story.
- **The membership read beside the task.** "Who is asked" here is a group, so the compiler opens a read of the group's members, `tk_domain_approval__members` (`membersOf@1` on the directory connection, `onFailure: outcome`), in the task's own engine stage, together with the task. The task is open and visible at once; the read only tells, from history, whether anybody can answer it. The published version's `nobodyToAsk` block names the task and its read. Who can answer is the people asked directly plus the recorded members of the groups asked, less the Requester where the Requester may not answer. When that set is empty the request is stuck with `nobody-to-ask`, shown at the task's "Who is asked". A read that fails contributes nobody from its groups; a person asked directly still counts (E-23, E-24; `engine/spec/integrations.md` section 11.5). "People in [group]" under "Who is asked" is the same as asking the group: it gets this read and no other, so Retry for nobody-to-ask always reads the group again (E-24).
- **The tasks step leaves when every task is answered.** Its exit, `st_domain_approval__answered`, is an explicit condition that every task is answered, never "in all other cases", so a membership read still pending can never hold up an answered task. Leaving the step cancels the read; its result, if it comes, is recorded late (E-23).
- **Two tasks that fill the same value.** Within one stage, the later task in the document wins, whichever answered later (E-23).
- **"After they respond" runs before the arrows are checked** (E-22). If no arrow fits, those actions have already run and the request is stuck with `nothing-fits`.
- **A second copy** of the chain, with every step name ending in `Back`, is made when an arrow sends requests back to a stage and that stage shows another status then, or is the start stage. In the change request only the Request form has one, `st_request_form__tasksBack`, whose status is "Needs changes".
- The compiler emits the kernel's elements directly (E-19).

**The origin map.** The published version stores, for every compiled element and, where needed, each field of it, the authored item and part it came from (E-18). Everything the engine reports reaches the author through this map; nothing names a compiled element (E-7). An element is keyed by its kind and ID, such as `wait:st_domain_approval__tasks.tk_domain_approval`; a single field of it by `<element key>#<JSON Pointer>`, such as `wait:st_domain_approval__tasks.tk_domain_approval#/assignees`. For the stage above (`engine/design/compiler.md` sections 12 and 15.4):

| Compiled element | Origin: authored item, part | What the author is shown there, for example |
|---|---|---|
| Stage `st_domain_approval__tasks` | Domain approval, `tasks` | |
| Person wait `tk_domain_approval` | The task; its `assignees`: `whoIsAsked`; its `may` rule: `requesterCanAnswer` | A press by someone not asked is refused at "Who is asked"; nobody to ask is shown at "Who is asked" |
| Call wait `tk_domain_approval__members` | The task; its `groups` argument: `whoIsAsked` | Nobody can answer (nobody asked directly, and the read lists no member able to answer or fails): the request is stuck, reason `nobody-to-ask`, at the task's "Who is asked" |
| Outcomes `btn_da_approve`, `btn_da_reject`, `btn_da_request_changes` | Each button; the look-up of the Eng lead answer: the question Eng lead, `choices` | An Eng lead who is not in the engineering group is refused (`choice-unknown`) at that question |
| Transition `st_domain_approval__answered` (when every task is answered) | Domain approval, `tasks`; each value it saves: the question's `savedAs` | |
| Stage `act_notify_requester_rejected__run` and its notification rule | The Notify action; the rule's condition: `onlyWhen` | A condition that cannot be worked out sends nothing and writes a log line, located at the Notify's "Only when" |
| Stage `st_domain_approval__route` and its transitions | Domain approval, `arrows`; each transition: its arrow | No arrow fits: stuck with `nothing-fits` at the stage's arrows. The story's "moved" entry names the arrow taken. |

Why it is built this way: stage, wait and transition IDs are recorded in histories for ever, and a later compiler may lay the chain out differently for later publishes (compiler section 1.5). Because every reader goes through the origin map of the request's own version, no reader depends on the shape of an ID, and an author is always shown their own stage, task, button or arrow.

## What publish checks

Both layers of checks are in core.

| Layer | What it checks | When it runs | What comes of it |
|---|---|---|---|
| core's `check` | What the author can fix: a part needed to run is missing (nobody asked, an arrow that goes nowhere); a broken reference; a formula that does not parse or gives the wrong kind; a button, or a combination of buttons, that fits no arrow; a value that may be empty where an empty value stops or silently drops something (who is asked, a notification's recipient, a directory group, a needed connection input; `value.mayBeEmpty`); a stage with no way to an ending; a loop with no task; a catalogue entry that does not exist or whose connection is not set up; a "Starts when" binding that leaves a needed question unanswered; any construct the compiler has no rule for, such as two results of one action saved as the same value, or a binding mapping whose question's "Show when" reads "Started on" (the list is in `engine/design/compiler.md`). The full list: `contract/core-api.md` section 4. | Browser on every edit; server at every save and at publish | Findings, To do or Worth knowing |
| The kernel's publish checks (spec section 6) | The compiled definition: every expression type-checks, data is read only where it is set, every stage can reach a final stage, every cycle passes a wait, every write call has a key scope or an explicit key, every data path, constant and operation result has a declared type, and the blocks for bindings, things told and nobody-to-ask are well formed. | Server, at publish only, on the compiler's result | Core's check is designed so that all of them hold (compiler section 14). If one fails, that is a bug in core; the finding for a bug in core is `compile.internal`. |

Publishing is refused, and nothing is stored, when the browser's core version differs from the server's (`core-version-mismatch`), when the draft changed after the revision the author published (`stale-revision`), or when any finding is a To do (`has-todo`, carrying the server's findings). Worth knowing never stops it. If the catalogue changed since the author's last check, the server's findings win (`contract/authoring-api.md` section 5).

**How a problem reaches the right spot.** Every finding carries a `Location`: the ID of an item in the draft (a stage, task, question, button, action, arrow, binding) and the part of it (`whoIsAsked`, `goTo`, `onlyWhen.2`, `inputs.summary`). The editor shows the To do on that item, at that part, in its own words; the engine sends codes and never sentences (E-7). For example, if Domain approval's Request changes button had no arrow, `check` would return `stage.buttonHasNowhereToGo` located at the button `btn_da_request_changes`, with its task as a parameter. Problems found while a request runs use the same `Location`, through the origin map: a refused press, a stuck request, an entry in the story. Document 6 (The contract) draws the edit loop as D14.

## Versions over time

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  v1["Version 1<br/>older: no request open on it"]
  v2["Version 2<br/>older: requests still running on it"]
  v3["Version 3, live<br/>the highest: new starts by default;<br/>its Starts when bindings are live"]
  draft["Draft<br/>based on version 3, being edited"]
  v4["Version 4<br/>made by the next publish"]
  r2["A request started on version 2<br/>runs on version 2 to its end"]
  form["A start form shown from version 2<br/>and sent after version 3 was published"]

  v1 -->|"publish"| v2
  v2 -->|"publish"| v3
  v3 -.->|"edited from"| draft
  draft -.->|"publish"| v4
  r2 --- v2
  form -->|"starts on version 2"| v2
```

*D5. Which version does each request run on while the workflow keeps changing?*

- **A version never changes, and a request never changes version.** `decide` reads only the request's own version; the version is read from the request's events, never assumed (spec section 8; data model section 2).
- **A start names the version whose start form was shown.** Any published version can be started, so a publish while someone is filling in the form refuses nothing. A start that names no version uses the highest (architecture section 4; `contract/runtime-api.md` section 3.3).
- **Only the highest version's "Starts when" bindings are live.** A binding keeps its paused state across versions, by its ID (E-17; `contract/authoring-api.md` section 5).
- **Old versions keep running.** The engine must run a version for as long as a request on it is open. So the definition format, its expression profile (`cel-1`) and its form-schema validator are fixed per format, publish writes every default out, and an operation version such as `jira.createIssue@1` never changes shape (spec section 7). `listVersions` shows how many requests are still open on each version.
- **The draft is kept after publish** and stays the author's working copy. It records the live version it was based on. Publishing an unchanged draft still makes a new version. core's `diff` lists what changed between two authored documents.

Some things about a workflow are settings, kept outside every version:

| Setting | Kept in | Why it is not versioned |
|---|---|---|
| Name, description | The server's workflow record | Renaming a workflow is not an edit to any version (authored format). |
| Authors | Workflow settings | They decide who may edit and publish, not how a request runs. |
| "Stuck requests go to" (the engine's workflow admins) | Workflow settings | A change must apply at once to every running request on every version: who is told, who may retry and close (E-14; data model section 2). |
| Paused bindings | Workflow settings | A workflow admin pauses a binding without publishing (E-17). |
| Connections, their secrets, the addresses that receive outbound events | The deployment's configuration, read at start-up | They belong to the platform. An author uses what the catalogue offers and never sets these (E-10, E-17, E-19). |

A change to a workflow's settings, each pause or resume of a binding included, is recorded with who made it and when (`settings_log`) (E-23).

## Try it

Try it runs test requests on the draft inside the editor, with no server state (E-4). core's `createTestHost(draft, catalogue, fakes)` compiles the draft in Try it mode and returns a host held in browser memory. Each input goes through the same turn function the server runs: validate, append, `decide`, then the stuck state worked out. `decide`, `evolve`, the expression environment, the schema validator, the nobody-to-ask rule and the rules for messages and things told are the same code as on the server. Only I/O is replaced (`contract/core-api.md` section 10):

| On the server | In Try it |
|---|---|
| Group memberships and choices from the directory | `fakes.groups`: who is in each group during the test |
| Choices from a connection | `fakes.sources`, else the catalogue's sample items |
| A connection action ("Look up", Create Jira issue, "Wait for") | Per operation: the catalogue's sample result, a chosen result, a failure code, or hold until the author answers it |
| Email and Slack, "Tell other systems" | The test outbox |
| The clock | `startAt`, then one second later per turn |
| "Stuck requests go to" | `fakes.stuckRequestsGoTo` |

| What Try it shows | What it does not show |
|---|---|
| Where a request goes and why: every arrow checked, in order, with what it read, including the arrows that did not fit. A live request records only the arrow taken. | Any real connection. Nothing leaves the browser, and the mock systems are not used. |
| Refusals, with the runtime's codes in the runtime's order. | A directory or data source that cannot be reached: `membership-unavailable` and `source-unavailable` never occur. |
| Stuck, with its reason; Retry for `action-failed` and `nobody-to-ask`, and Close. | A call that times out or answers "don't know": the fakes offer a sample, a result, a failure, or hold. Sending again and status questions belong to the server's call jobs. |
| What would be sent: each call's inputs, each message with its recipients, each thing told with its values. | Outbound event envelopes and posting them to other systems. |
| A start from a "Starts when" binding, given what the other system would send (`startFrom`). | The inbound hook's own checks: signatures, body size, parsing. |
| An unfinished draft. A request that reaches a part whose To do stops it from running is stuck with reason `unfinished`. Words and labels never stop it (E-20). Nor does a task with nobody asked, which the request reaches and is stuck at with `nobody-to-ask`, nor a question with no choices or choices from a list with no rows, which the tester sees and cannot answer properly (E-28). | Anything kept: test requests last while the page is open, and a changed draft needs a new host. Saving or sharing them is not designed. |

A test run on the server is later; it can be added without changing the contract (E-4).

## A request's history is the source of truth

In each turn the engine records the input and every consequence `decide` worked out, as events, in the order they happened. Nothing is changed or removed afterwards.

| What is recorded | Events |
|---|---|
| What came in | `RequestStarted` (who started it, or which connection and binding; the `workflow` and the version; the start answers). `WaitCompleted` (the button and answers, who pressed it, the groups that let them, each choice as looked up; or a connection's result). `CallResultLate` (a result that arrived after the request moved on). `Overridden` (an admin's retry or close, with who and why). |
| What the engine decided | `TransitionFired` (the arrow, and every value its condition read), `StageEntered` (with the status shown), `StageExited`, `WaitOpened` (who is asked, as worked out then; or the connection, operation, arguments and idempotency key), `WaitCancelled`, `WaitSkipped`, `DataSet` (values saved; removing a value that is not there records nothing, so a person's start records no empty "remove" for the Requester, E-24), `Faulted`, `RequestClosed` |
| On every event | The request, its position `seq`, the time `at` (the only clock the engine has), the `turn`, the event's schema version, the engine build |

Outside data enters only as recorded results: a connection's result, the group lookup when a person acts, the look-up of an answer chosen from a data source. `decide` never reads live data (E-9).

Not in the history: messages sent, events told to other systems (worked out from history and posted, not stored), refused attempts (a log), `decide`'s note of the arrows that did not fit, and what pages read live (people search, choices while a form is open, display names).

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  ev[("Request history<br/>events")]
  src[("Published version<br/>origin map, authored source")]
  proj["requests, open_waits<br/>updated in the turn's transaction"]
  lists["Lists, stuck list, My tasks"]
  page["Request page and its story<br/>the events folded again"]
  notifier["Notifier<br/>messages, values as at the event"]
  pub["Event publisher<br/>payload worked out at each send"]

  ev --> proj
  proj --> lists
  ev --> page
  src -.->|"author's words and places"| page
  ev --> notifier
  ev --> pub
```

*D4c. What is worked out from a request's history, and by whom?*

- **Replaying never re-runs workflow logic.** `evolve` folds events into state. It never evaluates an expression and never reads a definition, because `decide` spelled out every consequence as events when it happened. The cost: a bug in `decide` is recorded as fact. It is repaired by an admin turn, never by rewriting history (architecture section 3).
- **The tables lists read can be rebuilt.** `requests` and `open_waits` are updated in each turn's transaction. Deleting a request's rows and replaying its events gives the same rows. A new list or report is a new table filled the same way, for every existing request (data model section 4).
- **Readers speak the author's words.** The request page and the story fold the request's events and name every element through the origin map of the request's own version; the page renders words and forms from that version's authored source (E-6, E-7). Try it and live requests use the same `story` function.
- **Messages and things told read the past.** Their values are the request's data folded up to the event that set them off, not the data when the job runs (E-14, E-17). Neither can stop or move a request.

## First build and later

| Item | Status |
|---|---|
| Edit, check and Try it in the browser; save and publish on the server; start, act, record, show | First build |
| Several tasks in one stage, send-back arrows and the "If sent back" status, actions inside a stage | First build (E-8) |
| Starts by another system's event, "Wait for" calls, outbound events | First build in their thinnest form, beyond the MVP's requirements at the product owner's request (E-9, E-33) |
| "Everyone in a group must answer" | Later (E-33) |
| Erasing personal data | Later (E-33) |
| A Try it run on the server | Later (E-4) |
| Moving a running request to another version | Later (E-33) |
| Timers, deadlines, reminders, scheduled starts | Later: the engine has no clock (E-9) |
| Draft history, locks and merging between two editors | Later; each save replaces the draft (`contract/authoring-api.md` sections 4 and 7) |
| Archiving a workflow | Not designed |

Sources: decisions E-3 to E-33 ([Decisions: engine](11-decisions-engine.md)); kernel spec v2.20 and its `architecture.md` and `kernel/data-model.md` in `workflow-platform/engine` (its copy is in `engine/spec/`); `engine/design/compiler.md`, `definition-format.md`, `integrations-shapes.md`; `contract/core-api.md`, `authoring-api.md`, `runtime-api.md`, `authored-format.md`.
===\ndocs/04-word-map.md\n===
# Word map

Owner: Frontend owner; the Engine owner checks.

Answers: What does each editor word mean in the engine and in the contract?

Every word an author sees in the editor has exactly one meaning in the saved workflow and one in the engine. This document is that mapping. Read a row from left to right: what the author means by the word, where the editor saves it, what the engine turns it into or checks it with, and where it is recorded when a request runs.

Four terms used in the columns:

- The **authored format** is the workflow as the editor saves it: a JSON document in the editor's own words (`contract/authored-format.md`). Field names below are its fields.
- The **compiler** turns a published draft into a **definition**, the form the engine runs. It lives in the engine's shared core, which also runs in the browser.
- The **history** is the list of events the engine records for each request, in order, for good. Event names below (`StageEntered`, `DataSet` ...) are its entries. Nothing is ever changed in it, only added.
- A **projection** is a table rebuilt from the history for fast reading, such as the list of requests.

## The words, one row each

### Workflow, versions and requests

| Editor word | What the author means | Authored field | Engine concept | Recorded at run time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Workflow** | What I build. | The document's root: `id`, `formatVersion`, and everything below. Its name, description and "Stuck requests go to" live in the server's workflow record, not in the document. | A definition per published version. | Each request names its definition version in `RequestStarted`. |
| **Draft** ("Draft (not live)") | The version I am changing. Saved as I type. | The whole document, stored with a revision number. It may be unfinished. | Not run. Checked on every edit. | Not at run time. |
| **Version** ("Version 3 is live") | What people use now. It never changes. | The authored document, stored beside its compiled definition. | A published definition. A request stays on the version it started on. | The `definitions` table. |
| **Publish** | Make my draft the live version. | None: an operation of the authoring API on the draft. | The server runs the check and the compiler again, refuses while anything is To do, and stores the definition, the form schemas and the origin map (which compiled part came from which authored item). | A new row in `definitions`. |
| **Request** | One use of my workflow, from start form to ending. | Not in the document. | A request: its history of events. | The history (`events`), and the `requests` projection. |

### Stages

| Editor word | What the author means | Authored field | Engine concept | Recorded at run time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Stage** | A box on the diagram where a request sits. | `stages[]` | A chain of engine stages: actions on arrival, the tasks, actions after they respond, then a routing step that holds the arrows (E-14; see [D4b](#fig-d4b)). Engine IDs are made from the stage's ID, so renaming changes nothing. | `StageEntered` and `StageExited`. |
| **Kind** (of stage): Form, Approval, Work, Automatic, Blank | What sort of stage this is. It pre-fills the stage. | `kind` | Nothing of its own. A kind changes no rule; an Automatic stage is simply one with no tasks. The compiler emits the engine's elements directly; it does not use the spec's Approval and Task composites. | Not recorded. |
| **Ending** | A box where a request finishes. | A stage with `kind: "ending"`: name and status only. | A final stage. | `StageEntered`, then `RequestClosed` naming the ending. |
| **Status** | The words and colour people see for where a request is. | `statuses[]`, and a stage's `status` and `ifSentBackStatus`. | A stage's status, `{ id, label }`. Pages key on the status ID, never on the stage. | Inside `StageEntered`. |
| **When this stage starts** / **After they respond** | Things done in order, before anyone is asked / once, when the stage finishes. | `whenThisStageStarts[]` / `afterTheyRespond[]` | The first and third links of the stage's chain. | The entries of each action (below). |

### Tasks and forms

| Editor word | What the author means | Authored field | Engine concept | Recorded at run time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Task** | The part of a stage that asks people. | `tasks[]` | A person wait that must be answered (an obligation). | `WaitOpened`, `WaitCompleted`, or `WaitCancelled`. |
| **Who is asked** | The person or group the task goes to. | `whoIsAsked`, with `ifEmptyUse`; `groupRule: "firstAnswerDecides"`; `requesterCanAnswer`. | The wait's assignees, worked out when it opens. "The requester can't answer" is a rule on who may act. Whether someone is in the group is checked when they act. When a task may ask a group, the compiler adds a recorded read of the group's members beside the task, in the task's own step; it decides only whether anybody is able to answer, and a read that fails counts as nobody to ask. | Assignees in `WaitOpened` (groups are not expanded). The membership read, as a call's result. The person's group membership, looked up when they act, as evidence in `WaitCompleted`. |
| **Form** | The questions a task shows. | `form.pages[]` | A JSON Schema and a set of checks for each button (E-6). | The answers in `WaitCompleted`. |
| **Page** (of a form) | One page of questions. | `pages[]`, with `title` and `showWhen`. | Part of the conditional checks. | Not separately. |
| **Question** | One item on a form. | `items[]` with `type: "question"`: `label`, `kind`, `savedAs`, `choices`, `showWhen`. | A field of the answers, keyed by the question's ID; then copied to its value. | `WaitCompleted`, then `DataSet`. |
| **Choices from** (a connection) | A question whose choices come from another system each time the form opens. | `choices` with `from: "source"` and a catalogue `source`. | A catalogue data source (door 5). While the form is shown, the page asks the engine and the engine reads the source. When the person presses, the chosen item is looked up again. The author is told that only the answer is kept, so a later change in the other system does not change a request's answer. | The answer, `{ stored, label }`, with the source's label at the moment of pressing, and the lookup as evidence in `WaitCompleted`. The list is never recorded. |
| **Button** | How a person finishes a task. | `buttons[]` | An outcome. Its ID is the button's ID. | `WaitCompleted.outcome`. |
| **Needed to press** | Which questions must be answered before this button can be pressed. | `neededToPress` on the button; `neededForEveryButton` on a question; "Also only when" is `enabledWhen`. | The outcome's required fields and checks. | Nothing in the history: a refused press goes to the attempts log. |
| **Button pressed**, **Answered by** | Two more answers every task gives. | `savesButtonPressedAs`, `savesAnsweredByAs` | Writes of the outcome and the actor to values. | `DataSet`. |

### Arrows

| Editor word | What the author means | Authored field | Engine concept | Recorded at run time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Arrow** ("When ... go to ...") | Where a request goes next, and when. | `arrows[]`: `when`, `goTo`, `words`. Listed order is checked order. | A transition. The first one that fits fires. | `TransitionFired`, with what its condition read. |
| **In all other cases** | The arrow for everything the others do not cover. | `when: { "type": "inAllOtherCases" }` | An `otherwise` transition. | `TransitionFired`. |
| **+ only when ...** | Keeps a button's arrow to some requests. | `onlyWhen` on the arrow. | Added to the transition's condition. | What it read, in `TransitionFired`. |
| **When done** | An Automatic stage's way out. | `when: { "type": "whenDone" }` | A transition with no condition, after the actions. | `TransitionFired`. |
| **Send-back** ("sends it back") | An arrow to an earlier stage; the people there are asked again. | Not stored. An arrow sends back when every request must already have passed its target to reach it; the engine works this out (E-14). | A transition into a stage entered before. Re-entry gives fresh tasks. A stage with an "If sent back" status is compiled twice, once per way in. | `StageEntered` again, with the sent-back status. |
| **Don't wait for the others** | Go as soon as this arrow fits, even if other tasks are open. | `goAsSoonAsTrue` | A transition checked after every answer, which cancels the tasks still open. | `WaitCancelled` for each task still open. |

### Actions and connections

| Editor word | What the author means | Authored field | Engine concept | Recorded at run time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Action** | Something the workflow does by itself. | An entry of `whenThisStageStarts[]` or `afterTheyRespond[]`, with `type` and an optional `onlyWhen`. | By type, below. Actions run in listed order. | By type, below. |
| **Save a value** | "Save [what] as [value]". | `type: "saveValue"`: `save`, `as`. | A Set: a write to the request's data, placed on the transition out of the step that holds the action. | `DataSet`. |
| **Notify** | Send a message to a person or group. | `type: "notify"`: `to`, `message`. | A notification rule in the published version, matched on the recorded entry into the step that holds the action. The notifier sends it with the values as they were at that moment. It never stops a request. | Nothing of its own in the history. What was sent is kept in `notifications_sent`. |
| **Tell other systems** | Announce that something happened ("Change released") to every system that listens. | `type: "tellOtherSystems"`: `tell` (an entry of `thingsTold`), `values`. | Like Notify, a rule in the published version (an `events` block beside the notification rules), matched on the recorded entry into the step that holds the action. The event publisher builds the outbound message from that entry, with the values as they were then, and delivers it to listening systems (door 7) as one type, `request.told`, carrying the thing told as `{ id, words }` and the named values. Each value goes out exactly as the request holds it: a choice from a connection with its stored value and its label, a person as a directory reference. The built-in tellings (started, status changed, stuck, no longer stuck, ended) carry IDs, status and reason only, never answers. It never stops a request. | Nothing of its own: the stage entry it is matched on is the record. |
| **Connection** | Another system the platform is linked to, set up by an administrator. | Never named directly: only catalogue IDs such as `jira.createIssue@1` in `operation`, `trigger` or `source`. | A connection: a configured instance of a connector (the code for one kind of system). The catalogue lists what it offers, in four sorts (next four rows). | The connection and operation, in `WaitOpened` of the call. |
| **Gives data**: **Look up** | Read something from another system and save it as values. | `type: "useConnection"` with a read operation; `saveResults`. | A call wait of sort read. | Arguments in `WaitOpened`; the result in `WaitCompleted`; the saved values in `DataSet`. |
| **Does something** (e.g. Create Jira issue) | Have another system do something; the request moves on when it is done. | `useConnection` with a write operation; `inputs`, `saveResults`, `ifStageEntersAgain`. | A call wait of sort write, sent with an idempotency key (a key that lets the other system ignore a repeat). "Once" (`keyScope: request`) keeps the key for the whole request; "again" (`keyScope: activation`) makes a new one each time the stage is entered. The catalogue gives the default, shown and editable on the action; it is a To do only when the catalogue gives none and the author chose none. | As for Look up, plus the key. A result that arrives after the request moved on: `CallResultLate`. |
| **Does something and waits**: **Wait for** | Ask another system to do something and keep the request here until it reports back. | `useConnection` with an await operation. | An ordinary call wait; "waits" is a property of the catalogue entry (sort await). The engine asks the other system to start a job, then takes a result only by asking for the job's status; a callback from the other system only brings that question forward. | As for Look up: an ordinary action call. |
| **Can start a request**: **Starts when** | Another system's event starts a request, as if the start form were filled in. | `start.startsWhen[]`: `trigger`, `onlyWhen`, `answers`, `button`, `requester`. | A trigger binding: the event's fields are mapped onto the start form, and its button is pressed. | `RequestStarted`, naming the trigger; the starter is the connection. |
| **If it fails** | What happens when an action that uses a connection fails. | `ifItFails`: `"stuck"` or `"carryOn"`, with `saveFailureAs`. | The call's `onFailure`: `fault` (the request stops) or `outcome` (the failure is an ordinary result an arrow can test). | The failed result in `WaitCompleted`; then either `Faulted` (stuck), or the failure saved as values by `DataSet`. |
| **Pretended** (Try it) | What a connection would have done, shown instead of doing it. | None. | The test host's fakes: answer with the catalogue's sample, a chosen result, a failure, or hold until the author answers. | Only in the Test outbox. |

### Values and conditions

| Editor word | What the author means | Authored field | Engine concept | Recorded at run time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Value** | A named piece of data the workflow remembers. | `values[]` holds only `id` and `name`. A value is filled by `savedAs`, `as`, `saveResults`, `saveFailureAs`, `savesButtonPressedAs` or `savesAnsweredByAs`. | A data path in the request's data; its first segment is the value's ID. A value is present or absent, never null. Within one stage, when two tasks fill the same value, the later task in the document wins, not the later answer in time. | `DataSet`; the current values in the `requests` projection. |
| **Kind** (of value) | What sort of value: text, number, Yes/No, date, person ... | Never stored: it comes from what fills the value. | A type in the formula language, and a JSON Schema fragment. | Not recorded. |
| **List** (the Domains list) | A small table kept with the workflow. | `lists[]`: `columns`, `rows`. | Constants compiled into the published version. | Not per request. A list choice records the chosen row. |
| **If empty, use** | What to use when a value has nothing in it. | `ifEmptyUse` on a reference. | A fallback in the compiled expression. | What was read, where the expression is recorded. |
| **When ...** (a sentence) | The condition built from chips: "Risk is High". | A sentence: `allOf` or `anyOf` clauses. | An expression in the formula language (CEL). | What it read, in `TransitionFired` or the check's evidence. |
| **Formula** | The typed way to say a "when ..." or a value. | `{ formula, readsAs }`; `readsAs` is the plain sentence shown instead. | A CEL expression. | What it read. An error that cannot be evaluated faults the request. |

### Checking, trying, and when things go wrong

| Editor word | What the author means | Authored field | Engine concept | Recorded at run time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **To do** | Must be done before publishing. | Not stored: worked out from the draft. | A finding of the check with severity `todo`: a code, a location in the authored format, and parameters. Publishing is refused while any exists. | Not at run time. |
| **Worth knowing** | Good to know; does not stop publishing. | Not stored. | A finding with severity `worthKnowing`. | Not at run time. |
| **Try it** | Run a test request inside the editor. | None. | The test host: the same engine core, run in the browser, with every connection pretended and a test outbox (E-4). | Nowhere: held in memory while the page is open. |
| **Sample request** | The request the editor uses for every sample. | `sampleRequest` | Ignored by the compiler. Used for formula samples and Try it. | Not at run time. |
| **Stuck** | A request that cannot move until someone acts. | None on the stage. | One state, `stuck { reason, at }`, the same in the history, the request view and lists. Reasons: `action-failed`, `nobody-to-ask` (nobody was asked, or the group's recorded membership read finds nobody able to answer, or that read failed), `nothing-fits` (no arrow fits), `error`. Inside, the kernel keeps its own distinction: a failure is a fault, while nobody to ask is an open task that nobody can answer, which the engine reports as stuck. Retry and Close are admin turns. Retry is offered only for `action-failed` and `nobody-to-ask`; Close for any open request (see below the table). | `Faulted` for a failure; the one stuck message, `request.stuck`, with the reason, to the people who look after stuck requests; `Overridden` for a retry or close; `RequestClosed`. |
| **Stuck requests go to** | Who is told about stuck requests and may close them, or retry them where that can help. | Not in the document: only in the workflow's settings record. | The workflow's admins, a setting outside the published definition. A change applies at once to running requests. | The `workflow_settings` table. |

**Retry and Close, by reason.** Retry is offered only where running again can help. `action-failed`: the action is tried again. `nobody-to-ask`: who is asked is worked out again, the group's members are read again, and the stage's tasks are asked again. For `nothing-fits` and `error` only Close is offered: running again would read the same values and go wrong the same way, so the fix is in the workflow, for the next request. Close is offered for any open request, stuck or not. Two limits in the first build: if nobody is asked because a value is empty, Retry reads the same empty value, so Close is the only way out; and in a stage with several tasks, Retry asks all of them again.
