If the cause was an empty group and someone is then added to it, that person can simply answer, and the request stops being stuck when the task is answered.

Everyone signed in can open a request's page and see that it is stuck, and why. The Stuck requests list, the technical detail, and Retry and Close are for the people who look after stuck requests and for platform admins.

## One stage, annotated

The picture is the editor with the Domain approval stage open. Its panel on the right always shows the same sections in the same order. The numbers mark each part of the stage, on the panel and on the diagram.

<img src="assets/d6-stage-annotated.png" alt="The editor with the Domain approval stage selected. Numbered callouts mark the parts of the stage panel and of the diagram: kind, name, status, to-dos, Reached from, When this stage starts, Who is asked, the group rule, the Domains-list mapping, the stage box, its buttons, an action, three arrows, an Automatic stage and an ending.">

*D6. One stage, annotated: each part of the stage mapped to its field and its engine element*

| # | What you see | Authored field | Engine element |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Kind badge and its one line: "Approval: asks someone to approve or reject." | `kind: "approval"` | None: the kind only pre-filled the stage. |
| 2 | Stage name, "Domain approval" | `name` | None. Engine IDs come from the stage's ID (`st_domain_approval`), so a rename changes nothing published. |
| 3 | Status people see, "Waiting for approval" | `status`, pointing into `statuses[]` | The stage's status, recorded in `StageEntered`. |
| 4 | This stage's to-dos ("Nothing to do on this stage") | None: worked out | Check findings whose location is in this stage. |
| 5 | Reached from: Request form, by the arrow "In all other cases" | None: worked out from other stages' arrows | The transitions that lead into this stage. |
| 6 | When this stage starts (empty here) | `whenThisStageStarts[]` | The arrival link of the stage's chain. |
| 7 | Task: Who is asked, "Primary domain's approvers" | `tasks[0].whoIsAsked` | The person wait's assignees, recorded in `WaitOpened`. |
| 8 | "One answer is enough: the first person in the group to answer decides." | `groupRule: "firstAnswerDecides"` | One wait with the group as assignee; the first answer completes it. |
| 9 | "Depends on the answer to Primary domain": the Domains list's Approvers column | `whoIsAsked: { value: "v_primary_domain", steps: [{ column: "col_approvers" }] }` and `lists[]` | An expression worked out when the wait opens; the result is recorded as the assignees. |
| 10 | The stage box on the diagram | The `stages[]` item | A chain of engine stages ([D4b](#fig-d4b)). |
| 11 | Buttons: Approve, Reject, Request changes | `buttons[]`, each with `neededToPress` | Outcomes, each with its own required answers. |
| 12 | "Notify Requester (when Reject)" | An `afterTheyRespond` action: `notify` with `onlyWhen` | A notification rule, matched on the entry into the after-response step. Never stops the request. |
| 13 | The arrow "Approve pressed" | `arrows[]`, `when: { type: "buttonPressed" }`, `goTo` | A transition, recorded in `TransitionFired`. |
| 14 | The arrow "In all other cases" (out of Request form) | `when: { type: "inAllOtherCases" }` | An `otherwise` transition. |
| 15 | The dashed arrow "Request changes pressed", which sends the request back | An arrow whose `goTo` is an earlier stage | A transition into a stage entered before: fresh tasks, the "If sent back" status. |
| 16 | An Automatic stage, Create Jira issue, which saves the new issue as Jira issue | `kind: "automatic"`; `whenThisStageStarts: [useConnection jira.createIssue@1]`; `saveResults: { key: "v_jira_issue" }` | A call wait of sort write, then a data write (`DataSet`), then the "When done" transition. |
| 17 | An ending, Rejected | `kind: "ending"` | A final stage; `RequestClosed`. |

Below the visible part, the panel goes on with the task's **Form** (a summary with Edit form), its **Buttons** and what each needs, **After they respond**, and **Then go to** (the arrows). They map as in the tables above.

## One authored stage becomes a chain of engine steps

An author sees one stage; the engine runs a short chain of stages made from it: actions on arrival, the tasks, actions after they respond, then a routing step that holds the arrows. Where a task may ask a group, a read of the group's members sits beside the task, in the task's own step. Diagram [D4b](#fig-d4b) in document 3 ([The life of a workflow](03-life-of-a-workflow.md)) draws it, with the origin map that lets the engine report every problem back at the author's own stage.

## Words the engine has that the editor never shows

The engine's words stay in the engine and its documents. An engineer reading the history will meet them; an author never does. Each has an editor word a person sees instead.

| Engine word | What it is | What a person sees instead |
|---|---|---|
| **Wait** | Something open that a request is waiting on: a person wait (a task) or a call wait (an action that uses a connection). | Task; the action's name, such as "Create Jira issue" |
| **Outcome** | How a wait finishes. | Button; for an action, done or failed |
| **Transition** | A move from one stage to another, with its condition. | Arrow |
| **Otherwise** | A transition taken when no other fits. | "In all other cases" |
| **Call** | A request to another system, recorded with its result. | Look up, Create Jira issue, Wait for |
| **Read, write, await** | The three sorts of call. | Gives data, Does something, Does something and waits |
| **Trigger** | An outside event that can start a request. | Starts when |
| **Event**, **history** | One recorded entry; all of a request's entries in order. | The request page's timeline; "So far" in Try it |
| **Set**, **data path** | A write to the request's data; where in the data it goes. | Save a value; Value |
| **Fault** | The request is stopped by a failure or an error until an admin clears it. | Stuck (one of its reasons) |
| **Activation** | One entry into a stage. Re-entering a stage gives a new activation with fresh waits. | Nothing: the stage is simply entered again ("sends it back") |
| **Idempotency key**, **keyScope** | The key that lets another system ignore a repeat; whether it lasts the whole request or one entry of the stage. | "Once per request" or "again on every entry" |
| **Final stage** | A stage that closes the request. | Ending |
| **Workflow admins** | Who may retry or close a request, and who gets the alerts. | Stuck requests go to |
| **Definition** | The compiled, published form of a workflow. | Version |
| **Connector** | The code that talks to one kind of system. | Connection |
| **Composite** | A reusable pattern expanded at publish, such as the spec's Approval. Kept for hand-written definitions; the compiler does not use them. | Nothing: the stage's kind only pre-fills it |
| **Origin map** | The table from each compiled element back to the authored item it came from. | Nothing: problems are always shown at the author's own stage, button or arrow |

===\ndocs/05-integrations.md\n===
# Integrations

Owner: Engine owner.

Answers: How do data and events get in and out of the platform, upstream and downstream, and how is each way set up and wired?

This chapter covers everything that crosses the platform's edge: another system starting a request, a person's answer, a look-up, an action in another system, a message to people, and an event sent to other systems. For each it says who sets it up and where the settings are kept, what happens at run time, what the engine records, and what happens when something fails.

It describes a design. The first build shows every door working in its thinnest form, against mock systems; the fuller designs are kept for later (E-33, [Reserved for later](#reserved-for-later)). The sources are the engine decisions in [Decisions: engine](11-decisions-engine.md) (E-9 to E-33), kernel spec v2.20 and its `integrations.md` (whose copy is in `engine/spec/`), the server's side in [integrations-shapes.md](../engine/design/integrations-shapes.md), the mock systems in [mock-systems.md](../engine/design/mock-systems.md), the worked sample in [integrated-sample.md](../engine/design/integrated-sample.md), and the catalogue [catalogue.json](../contract/fixtures/catalogue.json). Field-level shapes stay in those files; this chapter names them.

**How to read it.** The sections up to "One request through every door" are for every reader. Each door then has a table at a glance and one worked example. A part that is for connection builders or engineers says so; the product owner can skip it. Names in code type, such as `WaitCompleted` or `pending_calls`, are the engine's records, tables and codes, for engineers.

**Build status.**

| Mark | Meaning |
|---|---|
| First build | Part of what this repository builds first. |
| First build \* | Built in its thinnest form because the product owner asked to see every kind of integration working against mock systems. Beyond `requirements/mvp.md` (E-9, E-33). |
| Later | Designed enough not to block it; not built. |

## Words used here

| Word | What it is |
|---|---|
| Request history | Everything the engine records for one request, in order, never changed. Arrows, checks and conditions read only this. |
| Door | One of the seven ways data or control crosses the platform's edge (E-9). |
| Turn | One input to a request and everything the engine records for it at once: a start, a button pressed, a result from another system, an admin's Retry or Close. |
| Connection | Another system the platform is linked to, such as Jira. A platform admin writes each one in the deployment's configuration. Authors use what it offers and never see how it is reached. The code that talks to the other system is a **connector**, written by a **connection builder**, an engineer. |
| What a connection offers | In the editor's words: **Gives data** (a question's choices, "From a connection", or a "Look up" action), **Does something** (an action named after what it does, such as "Create issue"), **Does something and waits** (a "Wait for" action, such as "Run the pipeline and wait"), and **Can start a request** ("Also start it from another system" on the start stage). Each thing offered has a fixed version, such as `jira.createIssue@1`. The action "Tell other systems" needs no connection. |
| The compiler | The part of the engine that turns the author's draft into the published version that requests run on. It adds a few things the author does not, such as the read below. |
| The people who look after stuck requests | The people and groups in the workflow's "Stuck requests go to" setting; when it is not set, the authors. They are told when a request is stuck and can retry or close it. The engine calls them **workflow admins**. |
| Platform admins | Holders of the existing application's platform-admin entitlement. They write the connections and the addresses that receive outbound events. |
| Stuck | A request that cannot move until someone acts. There are four reasons; see [When a request is stuck](#when-a-request-is-stuck). A request that is only waiting for a slow system is not stuck. |
| The key | Every call to another system carries a key, so the other system can recognise a repeat of the same call and not act twice. A call that gets no answer is sent again with the same key. When the request comes back to the stage, either the key is kept for the whole request (**"once"**: the other system returns its earlier result) or each entry gets a new key (**"again"**: it acts again). What a connection offers sets the default; the editor states it on the action. A "Look up" always reads again. |
| Accepted | The answer a system gives when asked to do something it will finish later (a "Wait for"): it has started a job, here is the job's reference, such as `run-5001`. Nothing is recorded yet; the engine asks about the job until it ends. |
| The read the compiler adds | For every task that may ask a group, the engine reads the group's members when the task opens, beside the task, and records the answer, so history shows whether anybody can answer the task. The task can be answered while the read is still pending. It is a read call (door 3); this chapter describes it under door 4. |
| Log line | A structured line the server writes for engineers. Problems that tell nobody, such as a refused start or a slow call, are log lines. |

## The idea in one page

Data and control cross the platform's edge through seven doors. Nothing enters a request's history any other way (E-9).

| # | Door | What the author sees | What crosses | Build |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Start | The start form; "Also start it from another system", which adds a "Starts when" card | A person submits the start form, or another system's event is mapped onto it | Person: first build. Another system: first build \* |
| 2 | Act | A task's form and buttons | A person's answers and the button they pressed | First build |
| 3 | Call | "Look up", an action that does something such as "Create issue", "Wait for", each added from a stage's "+ Add" menu | The engine asks another system; the result comes back and is recorded | Look up, Does something: first build. Wait for: first build \* |
| 4 | Membership | A task whose "Who is asked" shows a group | Who is in the group, read when the task opens; which groups a person is in, when they press a button | First build |
| 5 | Choices | A question whose "Choices" are "From a connection" or "People from the directory" | The list while the form is open; the chosen item, looked up again when the person presses | First build |
| 6 | Notification | "Notify"; the built-in messages | Messages to people through email and Slack | First build |
| 7 | Event out | "Tell other systems"; the built-in events | Public events posted to the addresses a platform admin lists | First build \* |

Pages also read live data that is recorded nowhere: people search, choices while a form is open, names for display. Those reads are not doors. What they return reaches history only through door 2 or door 5.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph up["Upstream: into the platform"]
    direction TB
    subgraph upc["Control: starts or moves a request"]
      d1["1 Start<br/>a person fills in the start form: first build<br/>another system, Starts when: first build *"]
      d2["2 Act<br/>a person presses a task's button<br/>first build"]
      l1["Later: a scheduled start,<br/>a timer, a message<br/>to a running request"]
    end
    subgraph upd["Data: recorded when it arrives"]
      d3r["3 Call: Gives data, Look up<br/>the engine asks,<br/>the data comes back in<br/>first build"]
      d4["4 Membership<br/>who is in a group<br/>first build"]
      d5["5 Choices<br/>Choices from, on a question<br/>first build"]
    end
  end
  eng["Engine<br/>keeps each request's history"]
  subgraph down["Downstream: out of the platform"]
    direction TB
    subgraph dnc["Control: makes something happen elsewhere"]
      d3w["3 Call: Does something,<br/>such as Create Jira issue: first build<br/>Does something and waits,<br/>Wait for: first build *<br/>the result comes back in"]
      d7["7 Event out<br/>Tell other systems<br/>first build *"]
    end
    subgraph dnd["Data: tells people, never waited on"]
      d6["6 Notification<br/>Notify<br/>first build"]
    end
  end
  key["How to read this<br/>* beyond the MVP, at the product owner's request<br/>dashed box: later<br/>door 3 is drawn twice: a Look up only brings data in,<br/>an action that does something acts in another system"]
  up --> eng --> down
  classDef later fill:#ffffff,stroke:#a0a6b1,stroke-dasharray:4 3,color:#464d5e
  classDef legend fill:#f4f5f7,stroke:#a0a6b1,color:#1c2030
  class l1 later
  class key legend
```

*D7. Where does each door sit: upstream or downstream, data or control, first build or later?*

### Three rules that never bend

| Rule | What it means in the engine | What follows for an author |
|---|---|---|
| **Nothing outside moves a request unless the workflow asked.** | Another system can start a request (door 1) or answer a call the engine made (door 3). Nothing else reaches a running request. | To wait for another system, use a "Wait for" action: the engine asks about the job until it ends. |
| **No clock.** | `decide`, the kernel function that works out what a turn does, never reads the time. Each event carries the time it was recorded. Jobs use a clock for retries and polls, never to move a request. | No deadlines, reminders, timers or scheduled starts in the first build. A formula has no "today"; it can read the day the request started. |
| **Outside data is recorded when it arrives.** | A call's result, a membership lookup and a choice lookup are written into history in the turn that uses them. `decide` never reads live data, and replay never calls out. | Arrows and checks see a value as it was when it was looked up. The label of a chosen item is the source's label at the moment the person pressed. |

A notification or an outbound event never stops or holds up a request. A door can make a request stuck in two ways only: an action that uses a connection fails and its "If it fails" is "stuck" (door 3), or a task is open that nobody can answer (doors 2 and 4). History is append-only: what went wrong is put right by a Retry or Close, recorded as a new event.

## When a request is stuck

Everyone who can see a request sees that it is stuck and the reason. The detail, and the buttons Retry and Close, are for the people who look after stuck requests and the platform admins (E-19, E-23). Stuck is worked out from the request's state after each turn, never recorded (E-33).

| Reason | What it means | What can be done |
|---|---|---|
| Action failed (`action-failed`) | An action that uses a connection failed clearly, and its "If it fails" is "stuck". The detail gives the failure code the connection returned. | Retry: the action is tried again. Close. |
| Nobody to ask (`nobody-to-ask`) | A task is open and nobody can answer it: the people asked directly plus the recorded members of the groups asked, less the Requester where the Requester may not answer. A group whose read failed counts as no one (E-24). | Retry: the groups are read again and the stage's tasks asked again. Close. |
| Nothing fits (`nothing-fits`) | Nothing is open and no arrow out of the stage fits. | Close only. |
| Error (`error`) | Something in the workflow could not be worked out, such as a formula, or one turn took more than 50 arrows. | Close only: running again would repeat the same result. |

**Who is told.** When a request becomes stuck, for any reason, the people who look after stuck requests get the built-in message `request.stuck` with the reason, and systems listening to outbound events get `request.stuck@1`. That is the one alert in the first build. Everything else that goes wrong at the edge (a refused start, a slow or unclear call, a directory or data source that cannot be reached, a rule that cannot be worked out) is a log line on the server, and nobody is told (E-33).

Close is offered for any open request, stuck or not. A request that is only waiting for a slow call is not stuck and cannot be retried; it is waited for or closed (E-20).

## One request through every door

The running example is the integrated sample workflow, "Service change" (`contract/fixtures/integrated-sample.authored.json`), run against the in-memory mock systems. Its stages:

- **Request form**, the start stage. A Helpdesk ticket of category "Service change" also starts it.
- **Find service owner**: "Look up a service" in the Service catalog, saving the owner and tier as values.
- **Approve change**, for Tier 3 services only: the Platform team approves. Not on the path below.
- **Deploy**: "Wait for" the Deploy pipeline; then "Tell other systems" "Change deployed" if it succeeded.
- **Fix deployment**, if the deploy failed: "Create Jira issue", "Notify" the owner (or the Platform team when there is none), then a task with the buttons Mark fixed and Deploy again.
- **Deployed**, the ending.

Priya raises a Helpdesk ticket for Ledger, a service with no owner, so the Platform team (Sam and Mei) is asked to fix the failed deploy. The full walk is [integrated-sample.md](../engine/design/integrated-sample.md) section 3.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant HD as Helpdesk
  participant EN as Engine
  participant DIR as Directory
  participant SC as Service catalog
  participant DP as Deploy pipeline
  participant REP as Reporting
  HD->>EN: [door 1] ticket HD-2307 created, signed
  EN->>DIR: who is priya.raman@example.test?
  EN->>SC: [door 5] is Ledger one of the choices?
  Note over EN: start turn, started by connection helpdesk, Requester Priya
  EN-->>HD: [door 1] 200, started, request 1001
  EN->>REP: [door 7] started, status Preparing
  EN->>SC: [door 3 Look up] details of Ledger
  SC-->>EN: no owner, Tier 2
  EN->>REP: [door 7] status Deploying
  EN->>DP: [door 3 Wait for] run the pipeline for Ledger
  DP-->>EN: accepted, run-5001
  EN->>DP: how is run-5001? asked every poll interval
  DP-->>EN: failed, tests-failed
  EN->>REP: [door 7] status Needs fixing
```

*D7b. How does a Helpdesk ticket start a request, and what happens up to the failed deploy?*

The question to the Directory is not a door of its own: the Helpdesk connector resolves the reporter's email while it reads the event, and the result enters history only as the start answer `requester`. The Helpdesk calls the service "Ledger DB"; the lookup at door 5 records the catalog's label, "Ledger".

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant EN as Engine
  participant JI as Jira
  participant DIR as Directory
  participant MS as Email and Slack
  actor MEI as Mei, Platform team
  participant DP as Deploy pipeline
  participant REP as Reporting
  EN->>JI: [door 3 Does something] Create Jira issue, key kept for the request
  JI-->>EN: OPS-101
  EN->>DIR: [door 3 read, added by the compiler] members of Platform team
  DIR-->>EN: Sam, Mei
  EN->>MS: [door 6] deploy failed, fix issue OPS-101, and a new task, to Sam and Mei
  MEI->>EN: [door 2] presses Deploy again
  EN->>DIR: [door 4] Mei's groups now
  DIR-->>EN: Platform team
  EN->>REP: [door 7] status Deploying
  EN->>DP: [door 3 Wait for] run the pipeline, new key
  DP-->>EN: accepted, run-5002
  EN->>DP: how is run-5002?
  DP-->>EN: succeeded
  EN->>REP: [door 7] told Change deployed, status Deployed, ended
```

*D7c. How does the request go on from the failed deploy to Deployed?*

Ledger has no owner, so Fix deployment asks the Platform team; the compiler adds the read of its members, so history shows whether anybody can answer. On this path Reporting receives every event in order, the request sends 4 messages and nobody is alerted. "Deploy again" sends the request back to Deploy with a new key, so the pipeline starts a new run. The Tell is published only on the pass that succeeded.

## What a connection is, and who sets one up

A connection joins three things: connector code written by an engineer, a configuration entry written by a platform admin, and the catalogue entries that tell the editor what the connection offers. Authors use what it offers and never see how a connection is reached (E-10, E-19).

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  builder["Connection builder<br/>an engineer"]
  padmin["Platform admin"]
  author["Workflow author"]
  code["Connector code<br/>mock-jira<br/>never recorded"]
  conf["Connection jira<br/>deployment configuration:<br/>connector, label, settings, status,<br/>the name of its secret"]
  start["Server start-up<br/>reads the configuration,<br/>holds connections and entries in memory"]
  test["Snapshot test<br/>fails the build if an entry's<br/>shape changes under its version"]
  entry["Offer, a catalogue entry<br/>jira.createIssue@1<br/>Does something,<br/>fields in and out, failure codes, sample"]
  editor["Editor<br/>Create Jira issue action"]
  hist["Published version and history<br/>name connection jira and<br/>operation createIssue@1"]
  builder -->|"writes; ships with a deployment"| code
  padmin -->|"writes"| conf
  code --> start
  conf --> start
  code --> test
  start --> entry
  entry -->|"the editor reads the offers: GET catalogue"| editor
  author --> editor
  editor -->|"publish"| hist
```

*D12. What is a connection made of, and who adds one and how?*

| Who | Does | Kept in |
|---|---|---|
| Connection builder | Writes a connector and the catalogue entries for what it offers. Production and the development host register different sets; platform code names none. | Repository code |
| Platform admin | Writes each connection: its ID, which connector, a label, its settings, whether it is ready, and where its secret is. Names which connection is the directory and which carries messages. Lists the addresses that receive outbound events. | The deployment's configuration, read at start-up only. No table and no screen (E-33). |
| Workflow author | Uses what connections offer in actions, questions' choices and "Starts when" cards. Chooses "Stuck requests go to". | The draft, then the published version; the workflow's settings, each change recorded with who and when (`settings_log`) |
| The people who look after stuck requests | Pause or Resume a "Starts when" card; see refused starts and "Run again" one. | The workflow's settings; the inbound log |

A connection that is not set up is listed to authors but cannot be used: using it is a To do at publish. A disabled one holds its calls, and its address for incoming events answers "try again later". **Try it** pretends every connection from the samples its catalogue entries carry, in the browser; nothing reaches another system (E-4).

For engineers: the connection ID matches `^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{1,39}$` and is never renamed; `directoryConnection` and `notifyConnection` are platform settings in the same configuration. An entry's shape (its fields, ignoring labels) never changes under one version; a new shape is a new version (`createIssue@2`). A snapshot test over every declared entry fails the build when a shape changes under its ID. The catalogue's version is worked out at start-up.

## Door 1: a request starts

A request starts when a person submits the start form, or when another system's event fits one of the workflow's "Starts when" cards. The event's fields fill in the start form, and the request goes on as if a person had pressed Submit.

| | |
|---|---|
| Who sets it up | The author adds a "Starts when" card to the start stage: what starts it, "Only when", and "Fill in the form from the ticket", the Requester being one row. A connection builder writes the trigger entry and the connector's `verify` and `parse`; a platform admin writes the connection and gives the other system its address and secret. |
| At run time | One address per connection, `{hooks}/hooks/v1/events/{connection}`. The event is handled while the sender waits: checked, mapped, and the request started in one transaction per workflow. The sender gets a synchronous answer with one result per workflow: `started`, `duplicate`, `notMatched`, `paused` or `refused`. |
| What is recorded | `RequestStarted`, by the connection, with the binding and the sender's event ID as its trigger. Every event received is one row of the inbound log, with its result or its code. |
| The same event twice | Starts nothing: the answer is `duplicate` with the first request. |
| Paused | The people who look after stuck requests can Pause a card. An event it would take is refused with `paused` and not kept; the other system must send it again after Resume. |
| When it fails | A final refusal (a mapping that fails, or the start form's rules) leaves no request and is listed on the Stuck requests page for 30 days, where "Run again" runs it on the live version, usually after a publish. A sending refused at the door (unreadable, too big, a bad signature, an unknown connection) is answered with a code. If the platform cannot reach a system it needs, it answers 503 and the sender sends again. Each of these is a log line; nobody is told. |

**Worked example.** A Helpdesk ticket arrives, and then the same ticket again after a lost answer.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant HD as Helpdesk
  participant HK as Engine hook
  participant DIR as Directory
  participant SC as Service catalog
  participant EN as Engine start turn
  HD->>HK: POST /hooks/v1/events/helpdesk, webhook-id HD-2307.created, signed
  Note over HK: size, connection, signature and timestamp checked
  HK->>DIR: find the user with the reporter's email
  DIR-->>HK: Priya
  Note over HK: binding Helpdesk ticket fits. Answers mapped
  HK->>SC: look up svc-ledger by its stored value
  SC-->>HK: found, label Ledger
  HK->>EN: start on version 1, by connection helpdesk
  Note over EN: one transaction: the start turn and its inbound-log row, unique per connection, event and workflow
  EN-->>HK: request 1001
  HK-->>HD: 200, service-change started, request 1001
  HD->>HK: the same event again
  Note over HK: the inbound log already holds a started row
  HK-->>HD: 200, service-change duplicate, request 1001
```

*D10a. What happens when a Helpdesk ticket arrives, and when the same ticket arrives twice?*

The starter is the connection. The Requester the card names is a start answer that only a connection may supply; a person who sends it is refused. "The requester can't answer their own request" compares the person acting with that Requester. For engineers: a person's start is `POST {base}/requests` with a client token made when the form opened; one token starts at most one request.

## Door 2: a person acts

A person answers a task: fills in its form and presses a button.

| | |
|---|---|
| Who sets it up | The author: the task's form, buttons, "Who is asked", "The requester can't answer their own request". |
| At run time | The lookups a press needs (the person's groups, door 4; the chosen items, door 5) are made before the request is locked, after a check that the task is open; the task is checked again under the lock. The press is then checked in order: still open, the person's groups, among those asked, the task's rule, the answers fit the form, the chosen items, the button's checks. |
| What is recorded | `WaitCompleted`: the button, the answers, who acted, and evidence (the groups they belong to among those asked, what each check read, each item looked up). A refused press is written to the attempts log. |
| When it fails | Refused with its code; nothing changes in history. A second press of the same task is refused `wait-not-open`, naming who answered. A lookup that cannot be made is refused "try again". |

**Worked example.** Mei presses Deploy again on Fix deployment: her groups are looked up (Platform team), the press is recorded with them as evidence, and the arrow back to Deploy is taken. Diagram [D9](#fig-d9), under door 4, draws it.

## Door 3: the workflow calls another system

An action that uses a connection: "Look up" reads data and saves it under "Save the results as"; an action that does something makes another system act, such as "Create issue"; "Wait for" asks another system to do something and keeps the request in the stage until it reports the result. The sort is set by what the connection offers (E-10).

| | |
|---|---|
| Who sets it up | A connection builder writes the entry and the connector's `call` (and `status`, for "Wait for"); a platform admin writes the connection; the author adds the action from the "+ Add" menu and sets its inputs, "Save the results as" and "If it fails". |
| At run time | The turn that enters the stage records the call (connection, operation, arguments, key) and creates one job for it. The job sends the call with the recorded key. An answer becomes a new turn. No answer, or an unclear one, means the job runs again later with the same key, without limit. A "Wait for" is answered "accepted" with a job reference, and the same job asks for the job's status every poll interval until it ends. |
| What is recorded | `WaitOpened` when the stage is entered; `WaitCompleted` (`ok`, or `failed` with the failure code) when the result arrives; `CallResultLate` for a result after the stage was left, which no arrow reads. "Accepted", the job reference and polls are not recorded. |
| When it fails | A clear failure follows "If it fails": stuck (`action-failed`), or "Carry on, saving the problem as" values an arrow can test. No answer is never a failure and never stuck. A slow call is waited for; past the time the connection says to expect, the server writes a log line. |
| Leaving the stage | Tells the other system nothing. A call never sent, and a "Look up", are dropped. An action sent with no clear answer is kept and asked again until it answers, and its result is recorded late. |
| Retry and Close | Retry, only for a request stuck with `action-failed` or `nobody-to-ask`, re-enters the stuck step: under "once" the same key is sent, so the other system returns the earlier result or acts again if that key failed; under "again" a new key is used. Close closes every open task and call; outside jobs are not stopped. |

**Worked example: Does something, no answer, a failure, Retry.**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant EN as Engine
  participant JB as Call job
  participant JI as Jira
  participant MS as Email and Slack
  actor SAM as Sam, looks after stuck requests
  Note over EN: Fix deployment entered. Recorded: Create Jira issue opened, key K
  JB->>JI: create issue, key K
  Note over JB: no answer in 30 s. Not recorded. The job runs again later
  JB->>JI: create issue again, same key K
  JI-->>JB: 403 permission denied
  JB->>EN: failed, permission-denied, as a new turn
  Note over EN: recorded. If it fails is stuck. Stuck, action failed
  EN->>MS: request stuck, to the people who look after stuck requests
  SAM->>EN: Retry, with a reason
  Note over EN: recorded. The step entered again, same key K
  JB->>JI: create issue, key K
  JI-->>JB: 201 OPS-101
  JB->>EN: ok, OPS-101
  Note over EN: recorded. Fix issue saved. No longer stuck
```

*D8. What happens when an action reaches another system, gets no clear answer, fails, and is retried?*

**A "Wait for" is polled.**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant EN as Engine
  participant JB as Call job
  participant DP as Deploy pipeline
  Note over EN: Deploy entered. Recorded: Run the pipeline opened, key K1
  JB->>DP: run the pipeline, key K1
  DP-->>JB: accepted, run-5001
  Note over JB: the job reference is kept. Not recorded. The job runs again after the poll interval
  JB->>DP: how is run-5001?
  DP-->>JB: running
  JB->>DP: how is run-5001?
  DP-->>JB: failed, tests-failed
  JB->>EN: failed, tests-failed, as a new turn
  Note over EN: recorded. If it fails is carry on. Saved as values, the arrow goes to Fix deployment
```

*D10b. How does the workflow wait for another system?*

An answer counts only if it names the job the call holds, so a result about an earlier run never completes the wait of a later one.

**The documented exception.** The other system must honour the key. The sample's Jira create does not: it creates without looking for an earlier issue, so if Jira creates the issue and the answer is lost, the next try creates a second one; an admin closes the extra by hand (spec `integrations.md` section 3). The mock shows this, unfixed.

## Door 4: the directory says who can answer

Who is in a group. It is read when a task asked of a group opens (the read the compiler adds), to tell whether anybody can answer it; and when a person presses a button on such a task, to check which groups they are in now.

| | |
|---|---|
| Who sets it up | A platform admin names the directory connection. The author picks the group in "Who is asked". |
| At run time | The membership read opens with the task, so the task is visible at once and a slow directory delays nobody; its result decides "nobody to ask", never who may press. At a press, the person's groups are looked up before the lock. |
| What is recorded | The read's result, as a call result; at a press, the groups among those asked that the person belongs to, as evidence. |
| When it fails | The read fails: its groups count as no one; if nobody else can answer, the request is stuck `nobody-to-ask` and Retry reads the group again. The directory cannot be reached at a press: refused `membership-unavailable` ("try again"), nothing written, a log line. |
| Who is told about a task | The people asked, less anyone who may not answer it (the Requester where the Requester can't answer). |

**Worked example.**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant EN as Engine
  participant JB as Call job
  participant DIR as Directory
  actor MEI as Mei
  Note over EN: Fix deployment entered. Recorded: the task opened, asked of Platform team, and beside it the membership read
  JB->>DIR: members of Platform team
  alt the directory answers
    DIR-->>JB: Sam, Mei
    JB->>EN: the result, as a new turn
    Note over EN: recorded. Somebody can answer, so not stuck
  else the read fails
    JB->>EN: failed, as a new turn
    Note over EN: recorded. Platform team counts as no one. Stuck, nobody to ask. Retry reads the group again
  end
  MEI->>EN: presses Deploy again
  EN->>DIR: Mei's groups now, before the lock
  alt the directory answers
    DIR-->>EN: Platform team
    Note over EN: lock taken, the task checked again. Recorded, with her groups as evidence
  else the directory cannot be reached
    EN-->>MEI: try again. Nothing is written
  end
```

*D9. Who is in a group: when is it read, and what is recorded?*

The membership read is a snapshot: a person added to the group after it can still answer, while the request shows "nobody to ask" until they do.

## Door 5: choices from another system

A question whose choices come from a connection's data source ("From a connection") or from the members of a directory group ("People from the directory"). The list is read live while the form is open; the chosen item is looked up again when the person presses, so the label recorded comes from the source and not from the browser (E-17, E-20).

| | |
|---|---|
| Who sets it up | A connection builder writes a data source with list and get; the author sets the question's choices: the source, its filters, the stored and label fields, or the group. |
| At run time | The page asks for choices by question, never by source (`POST {base}/choices`); lists are cached for a minute. When the person presses, each answer is looked up again by its stored value with the same inputs. |
| What is recorded | The answer as `{stored, label}` with the source's label; a person as `{type: "user", id}`; the lookup as evidence. The list is never recorded. |
| When it fails | The list cannot be read: no choices shown. The item is not found: refused `choice-unknown`. The source cannot be asked at a press: refused `source-unavailable` ("try again"), nothing written, a log line. |

**Worked example.**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  actor PR as Priya
  participant PG as Start form page
  participant EN as Engine
  participant SC as Service catalog
  PR->>PG: types led in Service
  PG->>EN: POST /choices, question Service, search led
  EN->>SC: list services, status active, search led
  SC-->>EN: Ledger
  EN-->>PG: choices. Not recorded
  PR->>PG: picks Ledger, presses Submit
  PG->>EN: POST /requests, Service svc-ledger with the label shown
  EN->>SC: get svc-ledger, status active
  SC-->>EN: found, name Ledger
  Note over EN: recorded: the answer with the source's label, and the lookup as evidence
  EN-->>PG: 201, request started
```

*D9b. Where do a question's choices come from, and how is the answer checked when the person presses?*

## Door 6: notifications

Messages to people. The author's "Notify" sends a message, with values in it, to a person or group, optionally "only when". The built-in messages are `task.assigned` (a task opens) and `request.stuck` with its reason.

| | |
|---|---|
| Who sets it up | The author writes Notify actions. The words of the built-in messages are the frontend's. Which connection carries messages is a platform setting, `notifyConnection`. |
| At run time | One job per turn whose events could match a rule. It reads the request's values as they were at the event, not later; expands groups when sending; leaves out anyone a task's rule says may not answer it. |
| What is recorded | Nothing in history. |
| When it fails | The job runs again; a crash can send a message twice. A rule that cannot be worked out sends nothing and writes a log line. It never holds the request. |

**Worked example.** When Fix deployment is entered, its Notify sends "The deploy of Rotate Ledger database credentials failed with code The tests failed. Fix issue: OPS-101." to Sam and Mei (the owner is empty, so the Platform team), and `task.assigned` tells them about the task. Diagram [D11](#fig-d11) draws the notifier beside the publisher.

## Door 7: events out

Other systems learn what happened to requests, without asking. Every request publishes the built-in events; the author's "Tell other systems" adds `request.told@1`.

| | |
|---|---|
| Who sets it up | The author adds "Tell other systems": "What happened", "With these values", "Only when". A platform admin lists the addresses that receive events; authors never choose who listens. |
| At run time | One job per turn. Each event of the turn is posted, in the request's order, to every address in the configuration, signed, one event per POST, at least once. |
| What is recorded | Nothing. Each event's `id` is its request, the event's number and the rule, so a repeat has the same `id` and subscribers dedupe on it. |
| When it fails | An address that does not answer 2xx fails the job, which runs again later and posts the turn's events again; that request's later events wait. It never holds the request. |

| Type | Published when | `data` |
|---|---|---|
| `request.started@1` | The request starts | `startedBy`, `trigger` |
| `request.statusChanged@1` | The status after the turn differs from before it | `from`, `to` |
| `request.stuck@1` | The request becomes stuck, or stuck another way | `reason`, `stage` |
| `request.unstuck@1` | It was stuck and is not | `reason`, `stage`, `by` |
| `request.ended@1` | The request closes | `status`, `stage`, `closedBy`, `by` |
| `request.told@1` | A "Tell other systems" is reached and its "Only when" is true | `told: {id, words}`, `values` |

**Worked example.**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant EN as Engine turn
  participant NT as Notify job
  participant MS as Email and Slack
  participant PB as Publish job
  participant REP as Reporting
  Note over EN: the turn commits and queues one notify job and one publish job
  NT->>EN: read the turn's events and the values as they were then
  NT->>MS: Notify, one message per person
  PB->>EN: read the turn's events
  PB->>REP: POST status Needs fixing, signed
  REP-->>PB: 503
  Note over PB: the job runs again after 10 s, 30 s, 1 min, 5 min, then every 15 min
  PB->>REP: POST the same event again, same id
  REP-->>PB: 204
```

*D11. How does the platform tell people and other systems what happened?*

## What other systems must promise, and what the platform promises them

For connection builders and engineers.

**A connector and its system must promise:** every answer fits the entry's fields; a timeout or "don't know" is `unknown`, never `failed`; a Look up has no outside effect; an action honours the key (for a key that succeeded, return that result; for a key that failed, act again); a "Wait for" starts at most one job per key and names the job in every answer; a data source's get finds only what its list would return; a trigger's event ID is the same on every redelivery, and a signed timestamp more than 300 s away is refused.

**The platform promises:** one call is always sent with the same key, at least once; one event starts at most one request per workflow, for ever, and the answer says per workflow what became of it, with codes and authored locations; an outbound event is posted at least once, in its request's order, with the same `id` on every send and `time` when it happened.

| Endpoint | Who calls it | Answers |
|---|---|---|
| `POST {hooks}/hooks/v1/events/{connection}` | A system that starts requests | `200` with a result per workflow; `400`, `401`, `404`, `413`, `503` |
| `POST <a configured address>` | The platform | The subscriber answers 2xx to acknowledge |
| `GET {base}/catalogue` | The editor | The connections, every entry with defaults written, and which connection is the directory and which carries messages |

## The mock systems

For engineers. Seven mock systems, one per kind of example, live in memory behind the connector interface, each with at most two switches: fail the next call, and be down (E-12, E-33). Tests drive them directly; the dev host is the server itself on PGlite with these connectors, a seeded directory and the development sign-in, serving both APIs on one port.

| Mock | Door | What it shows | Switches |
|---|---|---|---|
| Directory | 3, 4, 5 | Who is in a group; who may act; directory choices; finding a ticket's reporter | Be down |
| Service catalog | 5, 3 Look up | Choices from outside data and the check at pressing; a Look up saved as values | Fail the next call; be down |
| Helpdesk | 1 | A signed ticket event that starts a request | None: a test sends it, again, or badly signed |
| Jira | 3 Does something | The key, a clear failure, stuck, Retry; the duplicate a plain create makes | Fail the next call; be down |
| Deploy pipeline | 3 Wait for | Accepted, polling, a new run after a send-back | Fail the next call; be down |
| Email and Slack | 6 | Notifications, kept to inspect | Be down |
| Reporting | 7 | Receiving events in order; a report built from status changes | Be down |

## Open points

| Point | Needs |
|---|---|
| Where `{base}` and `{hooks}` are mounted, and the deployment URI that names the platform in outbound events | The existing application |
| The directory's API, the email and Slack service's interface, and where the configuration and its secrets live | The existing application |
| The real Helpdesk's signing scheme. Without a signed timestamp an old event that never started a request can be replayed. | The existing application |
| A paused "Starts when" drops events; a slow call tells nobody; "nobody to ask" for a group is a snapshot. | The product owner: accepted for the first build (E-33) |

## Reserved for later

Not built in the first build, with each item's full design archived: held events and re-runs for a paused card, signing-key rotation, callbacks from a "Wait for" job, the reconciler and call log, outbound positions with a pull feed, subscriptions and delivery logs, a catalogue registry with shape hashes, connections and secrets in the database, the alert kinds, and mock systems as HTTP servers. Also later: timers, scheduled starts, and stopping an outside job.

The list, how each would be added and which kept convention makes that cheap is `workflow-platform/research/reserved-for-later.md`, section "Integrations"; the archived designs are in `workflow-platform/research/later/integrations-full/`.
===\ndocs/06-the-contract.md\n===
# The contract

Owner: Frontend owner; the Engine owner supplies D16.

Answers: What exactly passes between frontend and engine?

The frontend (the editor and the pages people use) and the engine (everything that runs requests) are built by two teams. They meet at one contract: the files in the repository's `contract/` folder. This document says what is in it, who may change each part, and how the two sides stay in step. It describes the contract at the level of operations and shapes; the files hold every field. Everything here is a design: the engine has not run, and the frontend runs only against its own stand-in for the engine ([Frontend design](08-frontend-design.md)).

## Why there is a contract, and its one rule

The two sides are built at the same time, by different people, and must still agree on every byte that crosses between them: the saved workflow, every problem the engine finds, every refusal, every line of a request's history. The contract writes that agreement down, so each side can be built and tested against it without waiting for the other.

**The one rule: the engine reports codes, places and values; the frontend chooses every word.** A problem is never a sentence from the engine. It is a **code** (such as `stage.buttonHasNowhereToGo`), a **place**, and **parameters**. The place is always a `Location`, `{ item, part? }`: the ID of an item in the author's own workflow (a stage, a task, a button, an arrow) and, where needed, the field of that item (`whoIsAsked`, `goTo`, `onlyWhen.2`). It never names one of the engine's compiled parts. The published version keeps an **origin map** from every compiled part back to the authored item it came from, so even a problem found while a request runs is reported at the author's own stage, button or arrow (decision E-7 in [Decisions: engine](11-decisions-engine.md)).

Three kinds of text pass through as they are, because they are someone's own words rather than the engine's: the author's own message on a button that cannot be pressed yet, the author's words inside a Notify message, and, only to the people who look after stuck requests, the other system's own failure text.

### One example, end to end

In the Change request sample, the author keeps Approve's only arrow to risky changes with "+ only when Risk is High". A request where Approve is pressed and Risk is Medium would have nowhere to go. The engine's check, which runs in the browser on every edit, returns this finding:

```json
{ "code": "stage.buttonHasNowhereToGo",
  "severity": "todo",
  "location": { "item": "btn_da_approve" },
  "params": { "task": { "item": "tk_domain_approval" } } }
```

That is all the engine says. The frontend looks the button up in the draft, finds its stage's arrows for that button, works out the case none of them covers, and writes:

| Where the author sees it | Words |
|---|---|
| Under the Domain approval box, and in the stage panel's strip | add an arrow for Approve |
| In the To do list, with its fix | When Approve is pressed and Risk is not High, the request goes nowhere. Add an arrow for it. |

The sentences come from `frontend/src/model/describe/finding.ts`, with the words in `frontend/src/words/findings.ts` (`findings.stage.buttonHasNowhereToGo.short`, `findings.fix.addArrowForIt`) and `frontend/src/words/describe.ts` (`describe.nowhereToGo`). The names in them (Approve, Risk, High) are read from the draft at that moment, so a rename shows at once and the engine never needs to know it. These files are part of the editor's main screen, which is being built.

## The four parts

The contract has four parts, A to D, plus one file of shared words. Each has one pen: the side that writes it. The other side reviews and asks for changes.

| Part | What it is | Pen | Where it lives |
|---|---|---|---|
| A. Authored workflow format | An author's workflow as the editor saves it | Frontend owner; the engine makes it compilable | `contract/authored-format.ts` (the source of truth) and `authored-format.md` |
| B1. Core package | The engine's functions that run in the browser, and again on the server | Engine owner | `contract/core-api.md`; the code in `engine/packages/core` |
| B2. Authoring API | The server's side of authoring: workflows, drafts, publish, versions, settings | Engine owner | `contract/authoring-api.md` |
| C. Runtime API | What the pages people use read and send, and the endpoint where other systems start requests | Engine owner | `contract/runtime-api.md` |
| D. Catalogue of connections | What the connections offer authors, as data | Engine owner | `contract/catalogue.ts`; the sample `contract/fixtures/catalogue.json` |
| Shared words | The words of the messages the engine sends to people | Frontend owner | `contract/words/notifications.json` |

### A. The authored workflow format

**What it is.** The draft as data, in the editor's own words: stages and their kinds, tasks, who is asked, forms, buttons, actions, arrows and their conditions, statuses, lists, the sample request, and where the author placed things on the diagram. Values are not declared; a value exists because something fills it. Other systems appear only as catalogue references such as `jira.createIssue@1`. A draft may be unfinished: an arrow may go nowhere yet, nobody may be asked yet. Saying what is missing is the check's job, not the format's. The [Word map](04-word-map.md) gives each editor word with its field.

**What is fixed.** Every item has an ID that is made once, never reused, and kept through renames and moves. The ID's prefix says what it names (`st_` a stage, `btn_` a button). An ID is at most 40 characters and never contains a double underscore, which is kept for names the compiler adds. These IDs become the engine's own IDs and the names of values in every request's history, so they are kept for ever. How each kind of value is written as JSON is fixed for the same reason (`core-api.md` section 2.4): a person is always `{ "type": "user", "id": ... }`, an empty value is a missing key and never `null` or `""`.

**What is cheap to change.** Adding an optional field. The format carries its own version (`formatVersion`, 0 today); the engine upgrades an older draft when it reads it, so a later version is a change of code, not of stored drafts.

### B1. The core package

**What it is.** One package of engine code, `engine/packages/core`, that runs both in the browser and on the server (E-3). It has no input or output, no clock and no randomness: the same arguments give the same answer everywhere. That is how the editor can check a draft on every edit, and how Try it can promise to behave like a live request. Its functions, by what the editor uses them for:

| For | Functions |
|---|---|
| Reading a saved draft | `parse`: is this an authored workflow at all; `upgrade`: bring an older draft up to date |
| To do and Worth knowing | `check`: every problem, as findings |
| What the diagram, the panel and the value picker show | `facts`: per stage, the arrows into it and whether it can be reached; per arrow, whether it can be used and whether it sends a request back; per value, its kind and where it is filled and used. `valuesInScope`: which values exist at a point, and whether each is always filled, may be empty, or is never filled there |
| Formulas and samples | `checkFormula`, `evaluate` (the value of anything for the sample request), `evaluateSent` (the same for a "Starts when", over what the other system sends), `sampleValues` |
| Forms | `formState`: which questions show and which buttons can be pressed, for the form editor's preview, Try it and the live pages alike |
| What changed since the live version | `diff` |
| Try it | `createTestHost`: a test request run in the browser (D15 below) |

`compile`, which turns a draft into the published definition, runs only on the server. Nothing in core returns a sentence.

**What is fixed.** What each code means and what its parameters mean: a code's parameters never change meaning. The formula language's functions and rules, which are pinned per published-definition format, so a request reads the same years later (`core-api.md` section 6.4).

**What is cheap to change.** Adding a code: every list of codes is open, a new one may arrive in a minor version of core, and the frontend shows a plain general sentence for a code it does not know yet.

### B2. The authoring API

**What it is.** The server's side of authoring: list and create workflows; read and save the one draft each workflow has; publish; list and read versions; read and save the workflow's settings (name, description, authors, "Stuck requests go to"); the server's core version; and the catalogue. Eleven operations in all.

Two of them carry the design. **Save** takes the whole draft and the revision it was based on; if someone saved in between, it is refused as `stale-revision`, and the refusal carries the current draft. Nothing is merged: one author at a time. **Publish** makes the server run the check and the compiler again with its own copy of core and its own catalogue, refuse if anything is To do, and store the new version, its compiled definition, its form schemas, its origin map and its authored source. The server's result is the one that counts (E-3).

Every server call answers in one shape: the value, or a list of errors, each a code with its parameters and, where it applies, a `Location`.

**What is fixed.** A workflow's server ID never changes; a published version never changes. **What is cheap to change.** Paths, size limits, and who may author, which is an assumption the product owner has not decided (`authoring-api.md` section 2).

### C. The runtime API

**What it is.** Everything the pages people use read and send:

| Group | Operations |
|---|---|
| Start a request | The workflows a person can start; the start form; start (with a token made when the form opened, so a double submit starts one request); the choices for a question whose choices come from another system or the directory |
| Tasks | My tasks; one task; act (press a button). An act is checked in a fixed order, and the first failing step decides, so the page shows every problem of that step at once |
| Stuck requests | Retry (only for a failed action or nobody to ask) and Close (any open request), each with a reason and the page's `lastSeq`, so an admin never acts on a page that is out of date |
| "Starts when" | List a workflow's bindings; pause or resume one; list the starts a paused binding held; list refused starts and run one again |
| Reads | A version's authored source (from which every form and every word on a page is drawn); request lists with filters; one request, with its open tasks, its stuck state and its story |
| Session and directory | Who is signed in; people search and names, for pickers and display |

The same file fixes the one endpoint other systems call to start a request, and the exact answers they get (`runtime-api.md` section 8; [Integrations](05-integrations.md), door 1).

**What is fixed.** The inbound endpoint and its answers: other systems hold them, so fields may be added but none is removed or renamed. **What is cheap to change.** The transport: the operations are plain functions, and HTTP is one way of calling them (E-11). Polling and paging.

### D. The catalogue of connections

**What it is.** The list of connections and what each offers, as data: operations (read, write, or await: "Look up", "Does something", "Wait for"), data sources ("Choices from"), triggers ("Starts when"), and event sinks (the systems that listen). Each entry has a versioned ID, its input and result fields in the editor's own kinds of value, its failure codes, its defaults, and a sample that Try it and the editor's examples use. The catalogue also names which connection is the directory. The editor reads it from the server and hard-codes no connection (E-10): adding a connection changes neither the editor nor the engine.

**What is fixed.** An entry's shape under its ID (`jira.createIssue@1` never changes shape; a new shape is `@2`). **What is cheap to change.** Labels, descriptions, defaults, timeouts and samples.

### The shared words

`contract/words/notifications.json` holds the words of every message the engine sends to people: `task.assigned`, `request.stuck` (one message for every stuck reason), `start.refused`, and one per alert. The frontend writes them; the engine's notifier and alert sender send from the file and never write their own. Each message has named placeholders (`{request}`, `{stage}`, `{reason}`), which the engine fills; a new placeholder is agreed before the words use it.

## The four parts at a glance

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph browser["In the browser"]
    editor["Editor<br/>workflows list, diagram and panel,<br/>forms, To do, Publish, Try it"]
    pages["Pages people use<br/>start, My tasks, a task,<br/>request page, stuck requests"]
    bcore["B1 core<br/>check, facts, formState,<br/>evaluate, diff, test host"]
  end
  subgraph server["On the server"]
    auth["B2 Authoring API<br/>drafts, publish, versions,<br/>settings, catalogue"]
    run["C Runtime API<br/>start, act, retry, close,<br/>bindings, reads"]
    score["B1 core<br/>the same package; compile;<br/>the authority at publish"]
    workers["Notifier and alert sender"]
    words[("Shared words<br/>notifications.json")]
  end
  other["Other systems"]

  editor -->|"in process"| bcore
  pages -->|"formState"| bcore
  editor -->|"A: the draft;<br/>D: the catalogue"| auth
  pages --> run
  auth --> score
  run --> score
  workers --> words
  other -->|"the inbound endpoint"| run
```

*D13. Which side calls which part of the contract, and where the browser ends*

The browser holds the same core the server runs, so the editor's To do list and Try it agree with what the server will say. The server stays the authority: at publish it checks and compiles again and stores only its own result, and a person's press is always judged on the server.

## One edit, through the contract

Document 8 draws the same moment from the frontend's side, with its modules ([D22](#fig-d22)). Here it is seen through the contract: which function is called, and which code comes back.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  actor A as Author
  participant ED as Editor
  participant CO as core in the browser
  participant AU as Authoring API
  A->>ED: narrows Approve's arrow to Risk is High
  ED->>CO: check(draft, catalogue)
  CO-->>ED: Finding stage.buttonHasNowhereToGo<br/>at btn_da_approve
  Note over ED: worded at the button's place
  ED->>CO: facts(draft, catalogue)
  CO-->>ED: Reached from, send-backs, value kinds
  ED->>AU: saveDraft(workflow, baseRevision 12, draft)
  alt revision 12 is current
    AU-->>ED: 200 SavedDraft: revision 13,<br/>To do and Worth knowing counts
  else someone saved revision 13 first
    AU-->>ED: 409 stale-revision, with the current draft
    Note over ED: the author is shown the current draft
  end
```

*D14. One edit in the editor: the check, the facts, and the save with its revision*

The server also runs `parse` on every save, and refuses a document that is not an authored workflow (`invalid-document`). It runs `check` too, only to store the counts the workflows list shows; an unfinished draft always saves.

## Try it, through the contract

Try it runs a test request on the draft without the server. The test host is part of core and runs the same code a live request runs; only what would leave the platform is replaced. Every connection is pretended from the catalogue's samples, or from what the author chooses for it. What would have been sent collects in a test outbox (E-4).

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  actor A as Author
  participant TI as Try it screen
  participant TH as Test host, in the browser
  A->>TI: starts a test request as Priya
  TI->>TH: createTestHost(draft, catalogue, fakes)
  TH-->>TI: the host, and the stages still unfinished
  TI->>TH: start(Priya, Submit, answers)
  Note over TH: the same turn as live. An action it<br/>reaches is answered from its fake
  TH-->>TI: ok, the test request's ID
  TI->>TH: request(id, as Marcus)
  TH-->>TI: RequestView: status, open tasks,<br/>story entries started, moved, task.opened
  Note over TI: each entry worded:<br/>Priya Raman pressed Submit, so it went to Domain approval
  TI->>TH: outbox()
  TH-->>TI: messages, done in other systems,<br/>other systems told
```

*D15. Try it: the test host in the browser, pretended connections, and the story the author reads*

- **The story** is a list of entries, each a code, a place and parameters: `started`, `task.opened`, `task.answered`, `moved` (which arrow, from where to where, whether it sent the request back, and what its condition read), `action.waiting`, `action.done`, `action.failed`, `value.saved`, `status.changed`, `stuck`, `retried`, `closed`, `ended`. The live request page gets the same entries from the runtime API, so one piece of frontend code words both. In Try it, a `moved` entry also lists the arrows that did not fit and what they read, which a live request does not record.
- **Pretended connections.** For each operation the author can choose: answer with the sample, answer with a chosen result, fail with one of the operation's failure codes, or hold, so a "Wait for" can be answered later by hand.
- **The outbox** holds three kinds of entry: calls ("Done in other systems"), messages, and things told to other systems.
- **An unfinished draft** can be tried. A test request that reaches a part whose To do stops it from running is stuck with the reason `unfinished`, which only Try it uses.

## Publish, then a person acts

What happens between the editor's publish and a person's press on a task of a request that runs on the published version. The server checks and compiles again with the same core package the browser runs, and stores the version with its authored source. A task page later renders its form from that source and works out its state with core; the engine judges the press and answers in authored terms. Names are those of `authoring-api.md` and `runtime-api.md`. Drawn by the engine owner (`contract/D16-publish-then-act.md`); only line breaks were added here.

```mermaid
%%{init: {"sequence": {"width": 100, "actorMargin": 24}}}%%
sequenceDiagram
  participant ED as Editor
  participant AU as Authoring API
  participant SC as core on the server
  actor P as Person
  participant PG as Task page, with core
  participant RT as Runtime API
  participant LK as Directory and<br/>data sources
  ED->>AU: publish(workflow, revision,<br/>coreVersion), POST {base}/<br/>workflows/{id}/versions
  AU->>SC: check and compile<br/>the draft again, with<br/>the server's catalogue
  SC-->>AU: compiled definition,<br/>form schemas, origin map,<br/>no To do
  Note over AU: one transaction:<br/>the version stored in<br/>definitions with its<br/>authored source
  AU-->>ED: 201 PublishResult,<br/>the version and the<br/>worth-knowing findings
  P->>PG: opens a task of<br/>a request on that version
  PG->>RT: getTask(requestId,<br/>task)
  RT-->>PG: TaskView, with version,<br/>values, lookups,<br/>buttonStates
  PG->>RT: publishedSource(<br/>workflow, version)
  RT-->>PG: PublishedSource,<br/>the authored form<br/>of that version
  Note over PG: core.formState works<br/>out which questions show<br/>and which buttons<br/>can be pressed
  P->>PG: presses a button
  PG->>RT: act(requestId, task,<br/>button, answers)
  RT->>LK: before the lock:<br/>the person's groups,<br/>and each chosen item<br/>by its stored value
  LK-->>RT: groups and<br/>items found
  Note over RT: lock taken. Checked<br/>in the kernel's order: still<br/>open, groups, asked, may,<br/>answers, choices, checks.<br/>Recorded in one transaction
  RT-->>PG: 200 TurnDone, or errors:<br/>a Refusal with its code<br/>and authored Location
```

*D16. What happens when an author publishes, and then a person acts on a live request?*

The task page makes two calls: the task first, for the state of this request, then the version's source, which never changes and is cached for good. A refusal comes back as a code at a place in that source, and the page words it there: `not-assignee`, for example, comes back at the task's "Who is asked", and the page says in its own words that this person is not among those asked.

## How the two sides keep in step

**Shared fixtures.** Both sides test against the same files in `contract/fixtures/`: four sample workflows in the authored format (`change-request`, `blank`, `several-at-once`, `integrated-sample`), `records.json` (each sample's name, description and "Stuck requests go to", standing in for the server's workflow records) and `catalogue.json` (the sample catalogue, with the mock systems' connections). The frontend's tests load them today; the engine's cases are written against them and have not run.

**The fixture check.** `contract/check` proves the fixtures still fit the format: `npm run verify` type-checks each fixture's typed source against `authored-format.ts`, confirms each `.json` is exactly what its source produces, and checks that every ID is unique, follows the ID rule and that no reference points at a missing ID.

**Versions on every response.** Every server response carries the core version it runs (`Engine-Core-Version`) and the published-definition format (`Engine-Definition-Format`). The browser's core must be exactly the server's. When it is older or newer:

| What still works | What does not |
|---|---|
| Editing and saving the draft | Publishing, refused with `core-version-mismatch` |
| The check and Try it, marked as possibly out of date | |

The editor asks the author to reload the page, which brings the matching core. The exact-match rule is cheap to relax later.

**Changing a contract file.** Each file has one pen, as the table of the four parts says; the other side asks for a change rather than making it. Asks and answers are written down (`contract/CHANGES-draft2.md` holds the latest round). An edit to `contract/*.ts` that changes a type is made in one commit, after a line to the other side, because the frontend's build type-checks those files straight from the working folder (E-22).

## Every family of codes that crosses

Codes are spelled two ways (`core-api.md` section 1.1): a code that is recorded or sent outside the platform is kebab-case (`choice-unknown`, `nobody-to-ask`); a code that only passes between core, the server and the frontend uses dots and camel case (`stage.buttonHasNowhereToGo`, `task.opened`).

| Family | Raised by | Worded by | Where the words live | Two examples | Full list |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Findings: To do and Worth knowing | core's `check`, in the browser and again on the server | Frontend | `frontend/src/words/findings.ts` | `stage.buttonHasNowhereToGo`, `value.mayBeEmpty` | `core-api.md` section 4 |
| Problems reading a saved draft | core's `parse`, on every save | Frontend | Not worded yet | `parse.badId`, `parse.duplicateId` | `core-api.md` section 3 |
| Errors and refusals | The authoring and runtime APIs, and the test host | Frontend | Each screen's words file; publish refusals in `frontend/src/words/todo.ts` | `stale-revision`, `not-assignee` | `core-api.md` section 2.6 |
| Stuck reasons | The engine, from a request's history | Frontend | On pages: the pages' words, not written yet. In messages: `reasons` in `contract/words/notifications.json` | `action-failed`, `nobody-to-ask` | `core-api.md` section 8 |
| Story entries | core's story, in the test host and the runtime API | Frontend | The Try it and request page words, not written yet | `task.answered`, `moved` | `core-api.md` section 9 |
| Changes since the live version | core's `diff` | Frontend | `frontend/src/words/todo.ts` | `item.added`, `part.changed` | `core-api.md` section 11 |
| Built-in messages and alerts | The engine's notifier and alert sender | Frontend, sent by the engine | `contract/words/notifications.json` | `request.stuck`, `alert.call-overdue` | `contract/words/README.md` |
| Answers to other systems | The inbound endpoint | Nobody: read by machines | None | `started`, `refused` with `mapping-error` | `runtime-api.md` section 8 |

## Settled, and still open

**Settled** in the contract as of this writing: the four parts and their pens; the one rule of codes, places and values; the authored format's IDs and value JSON; one stuck state with four reasons (five in Try it), Retry only for a failed action or nobody to ask, Close for any open request; choices from another system read live and looked up again when the person acts; one stuck message; the order of checks when a person acts, with no call to another system while a request is locked; the inbound endpoint's answers. Every decision behind these is still pending the product owner's review.

**Still open**, with who decides:

| Open point | Who decides |
|---|---|
| Who may author: today any signed-in person may create a workflow; its authors and platform admins may edit and publish | Product owner |
| Whether every signed-in person should see the answers, action results and whole story of every request (the first build says yes) | Product owner |
| Archiving a workflow; keeping draft history; recording which catalogue version a version was checked against | Engine owner (not designed yet) |
| Sign-in, the base paths, the platform-admin entitlement, the request and readable IDs' storage and display, the directory's API and limits, where a notification's link points, how the real Helpdesk signs its deliveries | The existing application's owners |
| The formula functions `days` and `asDate`, and refusing `\p` in patterns, are part of the formula language but not yet in the engine's code | Engine owner |
| Failed expressions must record what failed, and the origin map must reach a field, for a stuck request's place and detail | Engine owner, as a change to the kernel spec |
| A choice is looked up with inputs read before the lock; whether to compare them again under the lock | Engine owner |
| Test requests in Try it cannot be saved or shared | Engine owner (cheap to add) |
| Does the workflows list need each "Starts when" binding and whether it is paused, or only the systems it uses? | Frontend owner |
| Which page shows pausing a "Starts when" and the refused starts? | Frontend owner |
| Does the condition builder hide directory steps on the start form, or show them and rely on the To do? | Frontend owner |
| Does any page need the messages sent for a request, or the attempts log? Neither is offered | Frontend owner |
| Is "the directory cannot be reached" on each button usable, or should the task page get one flag? | Frontend owner |
| The stuck list for admins only, while every row shows its stuck state to everyone: is a page-level restriction enough? | Frontend owner |
| Does the settings page need the history of changes, or only the last one? | Frontend owner |


`contract/CHANGES-draft2.md` records the latest round: sections (d2) and (d3) say what was settled after decisions E-21 to E-24, section (e) the engine's asks of the frontend, which are met (the integrated sample's fixture fixes, the 40-character IDs, the comments that E-20 and E-23 had made untrue, the words file, the diagram captions), and section (f) the frontend's open questions listed above. The open points of each API are at the end of its file.

# Engine design

Owner: Engine owner.

Answers: How does the engine process one input, store it, and recover?

**Reading path.** The product owner's reading path is documents 0, 1, 5 and 4: [Start here](00-start-here.md), [Context](01-context.md), [Integrations](05-integrations.md) and [Word map](04-word-map.md). This document is mostly for engineers; each section meant only for them says so in its first line.

This is the engine as designed: the server side that runs requests, keeps their history and talks to other systems. It follows the kernel spec v2.20 (`workflow-platform/engine/kernel/kernel-spec.md`; its copy is in `engine/spec/`), its data model and architecture, the formats in `engine/design/`, and decisions E-1 to E-33 in [Decisions: engine](11-decisions-engine.md). Core and the server are built and run in the engine packages' own tests and on the development host, against in-memory mock systems; nothing runs yet inside the existing application. The editor's word comes first; the engine's term follows in brackets where an engineer needs it.

## The model in a page

A **request** is one use of a published version of a workflow. For each request the engine keeps a **history**: a numbered list of events, appended to and never changed, kept for ever. Everything else the engine knows about a request is worked out from its history.

| Thing | What it is | What an author sees |
|---|---|---|
| Stage | A named place where a request sits. Under the root stage exactly one stage is active. Each entry is a new *activation* with fresh waits. Entering a final stage closes the request. The compiler turns one authored stage into a short chain of engine stages: arrival actions, tasks, after-response actions, then a routing step that holds the arrows (E-14). | Stage, ending |
| Wait | Something the request waits on, opened when its stage is entered and cancelled when the stage is left. A *person wait* asks someone to answer. A *call wait* is a request the engine sent to another system through a connection. | Task; an action that uses a connection ("Look up", "Create Jira issue", "Wait for") |
| Outcome | How a wait finishes. | Button; for an action, done or failed |
| Transition | A move to another stage, with a condition in the expression language (CEL) and optional writes to the request's data (Set). The first transition whose condition is true fires. | Arrow; "Save a value" |
| Turn | One input, processed under a lock on the request, in one Postgres transaction. | Nothing: one press of a button, one answer from another system |

A request changes only through one of four inputs:

| Input | Recorded as | Who sends it |
|---|---|---|
| Start | `RequestStarted`, then the start task's `WaitCompleted` | A person submitting the start form, or a connection through a live "Starts when" (trigger binding) |
| A person answers | `WaitCompleted` | The person asked, through the runtime API |
| A call returns | `WaitCompleted`, or `CallResultLate` if the wait has already closed | A connection, through the call's job |
| An admin steps in | `Overridden` | A workflow admin ("Stuck requests go to") or a platform admin: Retry or Close |

Two pure functions in `engine/packages/core` do the work (E-3). Neither does I/O; both run in the browser for Try it and on the server.

- **`decide`** takes the published definition, the request's current state and one input, works out every consequence and returns them as events. It evaluates expressions. It has no clock and never reads live data: outside data reaches it only as recorded events. Beside the events it returns a trace for "why did it go there", which is not recorded (E-15).
- **`evolve`** folds one event into the state. Replaying a request is folding its events from the first. `evolve` never evaluates an expression, never reads the definition and never calls out.

Why it is split this way: **history is the truth, and replay never re-runs workflow logic.** Every consequence is written out as an event, so a request reads the same years later, on any build of the code, without its definition or any outside system. Every other table can be deleted and rebuilt from history, or re-derived. The cost: a bug in `decide` is recorded as fact. It is repaired by an admin turn, never by rewriting history.

## One input, end to end

For engineers only: the steps of one turn inside the server.

The running example is the change request demo, case D1 (`workflow-platform/engine/workflows/change-request-demo/test-cases.yaml`). Rita started the request; in the stage Pending (status "Pending approval") the task `primary.decision` asks the group `grp-a` (Alice and Rita), and its recorded membership read has listed them; the requester may not answer it. Alice presses Approve and names Lee as eng lead.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  autonumber
  actor Alice
  participant API as Runtime API
  participant DB as Postgres
  participant Dir as Directory
  participant Core as decide
  Alice->>API: POST act: task Pending.primary.decision, button approve, engLead Lee
```
