<section class="doc" data-file="06-the-contract.md"><h1 id="doc-06-the-contract">The contract</h1>
<p class="doc-meta doc-owner">Owner: Frontend owner; the Engine owner supplies D16.</p>
<p class="doc-meta doc-answers">Answers: What exactly passes between frontend and engine?</p>
<p>The frontend (the editor and the pages people use) and the engine (everything that runs requests) are built by two teams. They meet at one contract: the files in the repository's <code>contract/</code> folder. This document says what is in it, who may change each part, and how the two sides stay in step. It describes the contract at the level of operations and shapes; the files hold every field. Everything here is a design: the engine has not run, and the frontend runs only against its own stand-in for the engine (<a href="#doc-08-frontend-design">Frontend design</a>).</p>
<h2 id="06-the-contract--why-there-is-a-contract-and-its-one-rule">Why there is a contract, and its one rule</h2>
<p>The two sides are built at the same time, by different people, and must still agree on every byte that crosses between them: the saved workflow, every problem the engine finds, every refusal, every line of a request's history. The contract writes that agreement down, so each side can be built and tested against it without waiting for the other.</p>
<p><strong>The one rule: the engine reports codes, places and values; the frontend chooses every word.</strong> A problem is never a sentence from the engine. It is a <strong>code</strong> (such as <code>stage.buttonHasNowhereToGo</code>), a <strong>place</strong>, and <strong>parameters</strong>. The place is always a <code>Location</code>, <code>{ item, part? }</code>: the ID of an item in the author's own workflow (a stage, a task, a button, an arrow) and, where needed, the field of that item (<code>whoIsAsked</code>, <code>goTo</code>, <code>onlyWhen.2</code>). It never names one of the engine's compiled parts. The published version keeps an <strong>origin map</strong> from every compiled part back to the authored item it came from, so even a problem found while a request runs is reported at the author's own stage, button or arrow (decision E-7 in <a href="#doc-11-decisions-engine">Decisions: engine</a>).</p>
<p>Three kinds of text pass through as they are, because they are someone's own words rather than the engine's: the author's own message on a button that cannot be pressed yet, the author's words inside a Notify message, and, only to the people who look after stuck requests, the other system's own failure text.</p>
<h3 id="06-the-contract--one-example-end-to-end">One example, end to end</h3>
<p>In the Change request sample, the author keeps Approve's only arrow to risky changes with &quot;+ only when Risk is High&quot;. A request where Approve is pressed and Risk is Medium would have nowhere to go. The engine's check, which runs in the browser on every edit, returns this finding:</p>
<pre><code class="language-json">{ &quot;code&quot;: &quot;stage.buttonHasNowhereToGo&quot;,
  &quot;severity&quot;: &quot;todo&quot;,
  &quot;location&quot;: { &quot;item&quot;: &quot;btn_da_approve&quot; },
  &quot;params&quot;: { &quot;task&quot;: { &quot;item&quot;: &quot;tk_domain_approval&quot; } } }
</code></pre>
<p>That is all the engine says. The frontend looks the button up in the draft, finds its stage's arrows for that button, works out the case none of them covers, and writes:</p>
<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead>
<tr>
<th>Where the author sees it</th>
<th>Words</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Under the Domain approval box, and in the stage panel's strip</td>
<td>add an arrow for Approve</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>In the To do list, with its fix</td>
<td>When Approve is pressed and Risk is not High, the request goes nowhere. Add an arrow for it.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><p>The sentences come from <code>frontend/src/model/describe/finding.ts</code>, with the words in <code>frontend/src/words/findings.ts</code> (<code>findings.stage.buttonHasNowhereToGo.short</code>, <code>findings.fix.addArrowForIt</code>) and <code>frontend/src/words/describe.ts</code> (<code>describe.nowhereToGo</code>). The names in them (Approve, Risk, High) are read from the draft at that moment, so a rename shows at once and the engine never needs to know it. These files are part of the editor's main screen, which is being built.</p>
<h2 id="06-the-contract--the-four-parts">The four parts</h2>
<p>The contract has four parts, A to D, plus one file of shared words. Each has one pen: the side that writes it. The other side reviews and asks for changes.</p>
<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead>
<tr>
<th>Part</th>
<th>What it is</th>
<th>Pen</th>
<th>Where it lives</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>A. Authored workflow format</td>
<td>An author's workflow as the editor saves it</td>
<td>Frontend owner; the engine makes it compilable</td>
<td><code>contract/authored-format.ts</code> (the source of truth) and <code>authored-format.md</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>B1. Core package</td>
<td>The engine's functions that run in the browser, and again on the server</td>
<td>Engine owner</td>
<td><code>contract/core-api.md</code>; the code in <code>engine/packages/core</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>B2. Authoring API</td>
<td>The server's side of authoring: workflows, drafts, publish, versions, settings</td>
<td>Engine owner</td>
<td><code>contract/authoring-api.md</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>C. Runtime API</td>
<td>What the pages people use read and send, and the endpoint where other systems start requests</td>
<td>Engine owner</td>
<td><code>contract/runtime-api.md</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>D. Catalogue of connections</td>
<td>What the connections offer authors, as data</td>
<td>Engine owner</td>
<td><code>contract/catalogue.ts</code>; the sample <code>contract/fixtures/catalogue.json</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Shared words</td>
<td>The words of the messages the engine sends to people</td>
<td>Frontend owner</td>
<td><code>contract/words/notifications.json</code></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><h3 id="06-the-contract--a-the-authored-workflow-format">A. The authored workflow format</h3>
<p><strong>What it is.</strong> The draft as data, in the editor's own words: stages and their kinds, tasks, who is asked, forms, buttons, actions, arrows and their conditions, statuses, lists, the sample request, and where the author placed things on the diagram. Values are not declared; a value exists because something fills it. Other systems appear only as catalogue references such as <code>jira.createIssue@1</code>. A draft may be unfinished: an arrow may go nowhere yet, nobody may be asked yet. Saying what is missing is the check's job, not the format's. The <a href="#doc-04-word-map">Word map</a> gives each editor word with its field.</p>
<p><strong>What is fixed.</strong> Every item has an ID that is made once, never reused, and kept through renames and moves. The ID's prefix says what it names (<code>st_</code> a stage, <code>btn_</code> a button). An ID is at most 40 characters and never contains a double underscore, which is kept for names the compiler adds. These IDs become the engine's own IDs and the names of values in every request's history, so they are kept for ever. How each kind of value is written as JSON is fixed for the same reason (<code>core-api.md</code> section 2.4): a person is always <code>{ &quot;type&quot;: &quot;user&quot;, &quot;id&quot;: ... }</code>, an empty value is a missing key and never <code>null</code> or <code>&quot;&quot;</code>.</p>
<p><strong>What is cheap to change.</strong> Adding an optional field. The format carries its own version (<code>formatVersion</code>, 0 today); the engine upgrades an older draft when it reads it, so a later version is a change of code, not of stored drafts.</p>
<h3 id="06-the-contract--b1-the-core-package">B1. The core package</h3>
<p><strong>What it is.</strong> One package of engine code, <code>engine/packages/core</code>, that runs both in the browser and on the server (E-3). It has no input or output, no clock and no randomness: the same arguments give the same answer everywhere. That is how the editor can check a draft on every edit, and how Try it can promise to behave like a live request. Its functions, by what the editor uses them for:</p>
<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead>
<tr>
<th>For</th>
<th>Functions</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Reading a saved draft</td>
<td><code>parse</code>: is this an authored workflow at all; <code>upgrade</code>: bring an older draft up to date</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>To do and Worth knowing</td>
<td><code>check</code>: every problem, as findings</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What the diagram, the panel and the value picker show</td>
<td><code>facts</code>: per stage, the arrows into it and whether it can be reached; per arrow, whether it can be used and whether it sends a request back; per value, its kind and where it is filled and used. <code>valuesInScope</code>: which values exist at a point, and whether each is always filled, may be empty, or is never filled there</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Formulas and samples</td>
<td><code>checkFormula</code>, <code>evaluate</code> (the value of anything for the sample request), <code>evaluateSent</code> (the same for a &quot;Starts when&quot;, over what the other system sends), <code>sampleValues</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Forms</td>
<td><code>formState</code>: which questions show and which buttons can be pressed, for the form editor's preview, Try it and the live pages alike</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>What changed since the live version</td>
<td><code>diff</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Try it</td>
<td><code>createTestHost</code>: a test request run in the browser (D15 below)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><p><code>compile</code>, which turns a draft into the published definition, runs only on the server. Nothing in core returns a sentence.</p>
<p><strong>What is fixed.</strong> What each code means and what its parameters mean: a code's parameters never change meaning. The formula language's functions and rules, which are pinned per published-definition format, so a request reads the same years later (<code>core-api.md</code> section 6.4).</p>
<p><strong>What is cheap to change.</strong> Adding a code: every list of codes is open, a new one may arrive in a minor version of core, and the frontend shows a plain general sentence for a code it does not know yet.</p>
<h3 id="06-the-contract--b2-the-authoring-api">B2. The authoring API</h3>
<p><strong>What it is.</strong> The server's side of authoring: list and create workflows; read and save the one draft each workflow has; publish; list and read versions; read and save the workflow's settings (name, description, authors, &quot;Stuck requests go to&quot;); the server's core version; and the catalogue. Eleven operations in all.</p>
<p>Two of them carry the design. <strong>Save</strong> takes the whole draft and the revision it was based on; if someone saved in between, it is refused as <code>stale-revision</code>, and the refusal carries the current draft. Nothing is merged: one author at a time. <strong>Publish</strong> makes the server run the check and the compiler again with its own copy of core and its own catalogue, refuse if anything is To do, and store the new version, its compiled definition, its form schemas, its origin map and its authored source. The server's result is the one that counts (E-3).</p>
<p>Every server call answers in one shape: the value, or a list of errors, each a code with its parameters and, where it applies, a <code>Location</code>.</p>
<p><strong>What is fixed.</strong> A workflow's server ID never changes; a published version never changes. <strong>What is cheap to change.</strong> Paths, size limits, and who may author, which is an assumption the product owner has not decided (<code>authoring-api.md</code> section 2).</p>
<h3 id="06-the-contract--c-the-runtime-api">C. The runtime API</h3>
<p><strong>What it is.</strong> Everything the pages people use read and send:</p>
<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead>
<tr>
<th>Group</th>
<th>Operations</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Start a request</td>
<td>The workflows a person can start; the start form; start (with a token made when the form opened, so a double submit starts one request); the choices for a question whose choices come from another system or the directory</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Tasks</td>
<td>My tasks; one task; act (press a button). An act is checked in a fixed order, and the first failing step decides, so the page shows every problem of that step at once</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Stuck requests</td>
<td>Retry (only for a failed action or nobody to ask) and Close (any open request), each with a reason and the page's <code>lastSeq</code>, so an admin never acts on a page that is out of date</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>&quot;Starts when&quot;</td>
<td>List a workflow's bindings; pause or resume one; list the starts a paused binding held; list refused starts and run one again</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Reads</td>
<td>A version's authored source (from which every form and every word on a page is drawn); request lists with filters; one request, with its open tasks, its stuck state and its story</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Session and directory</td>
<td>Who is signed in; people search and names, for pickers and display</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><p>The same file fixes the one endpoint other systems call to start a request, and the exact answers they get (<code>runtime-api.md</code> section 8; <a href="#doc-05-integrations">Integrations</a>, door 1).</p>
<p><strong>What is fixed.</strong> The inbound endpoint and its answers: other systems hold them, so fields may be added but none is removed or renamed. <strong>What is cheap to change.</strong> The transport: the operations are plain functions, and HTTP is one way of calling them (E-11). Polling and paging.</p>
<h3 id="06-the-contract--d-the-catalogue-of-connections">D. The catalogue of connections</h3>
<p><strong>What it is.</strong> The list of connections and what each offers, as data: operations (read, write, or await: &quot;Look up&quot;, &quot;Does something&quot;, &quot;Wait for&quot;), data sources (&quot;Choices from&quot;), triggers (&quot;Starts when&quot;), and event sinks (the systems that listen). Each entry has a versioned ID, its input and result fields in the editor's own kinds of value, its failure codes, its defaults, and a sample that Try it and the editor's examples use. The catalogue also names which connection is the directory. The editor reads it from the server and hard-codes no connection (E-10): adding a connection changes neither the editor nor the engine.</p>
<p><strong>What is fixed.</strong> An entry's shape under its ID (<code>jira.createIssue@1</code> never changes shape; a new shape is <code>@2</code>). <strong>What is cheap to change.</strong> Labels, descriptions, defaults, timeouts and samples.</p>
<h3 id="06-the-contract--the-shared-words">The shared words</h3>
<p><code>contract/words/notifications.json</code> holds the words of every message the engine sends to people: <code>task.assigned</code>, <code>request.stuck</code> (one message for every stuck reason), <code>start.refused</code>, and one per alert. The frontend writes them; the engine's notifier and alert sender send from the file and never write their own. Each message has named placeholders (<code>{request}</code>, <code>{stage}</code>, <code>{reason}</code>), which the engine fills; a new placeholder is agreed before the words use it.</p>

<p>The browser holds the same core the server runs, so the editor's To do list and Try it agree with what the server will say. The server stays the authority: at publish it checks and compiles again and stores only its own result, and a person's press is always judged on the server.</p>

<p>The server also runs <code>parse</code> on every save, and refuses a document that is not an authored workflow (<code>invalid-document</code>). It runs <code>check</code> too, only to store the counts the workflows list shows; an unfinished draft always saves.</p>
<h2 id="06-the-contract--try-it-through-the-contract">Try it, through the contract</h2>
<p>Try it runs a test request on the draft without the server. The test host is part of core and runs the same code a live request runs; only what would leave the platform is replaced. Every connection is pretended from the catalogue's samples, or from what the author chooses for it. What would have been sent collects in a test outbox (E-4).</p>

font-size: 16px; font-weight: 400;">other systems told</text><line x1="691" y1="719" x2="340" y2="719" class="messageLine1" data-et="message" data-id="i11" data-from="TH" data-to="TI" stroke-width="2" stroke="none" marker-end="url(#mmd-22-arrowhead)" style="stroke-dasharray: 3, 3; fill: none;"></line><line x1="686" y1="719" x2="686" y2="719" stroke-width="0" marker-start="url(#mmd-22-sequencenumber)"></line><text x="686" y="723" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12px" text-anchor="middle" class="sequenceNumber">9</text></svg></div><figcaption class="figure-caption"><span class="fig-id">D15.</span> Try it: the test host in the browser, pretended connections, and the story the author reads</figcaption></figure>
<ul>
<li><strong>The story</strong> is a list of entries, each a code, a place and parameters: <code>started</code>, <code>task.opened</code>, <code>task.answered</code>, <code>moved</code> (which arrow, from where to where, whether it sent the request back, and what its condition read), <code>action.waiting</code>, <code>action.done</code>, <code>action.failed</code>, <code>value.saved</code>, <code>status.changed</code>, <code>stuck</code>, <code>retried</code>, <code>closed</code>, <code>ended</code>. The live request page gets the same entries from the runtime API, so one piece of frontend code words both. In Try it, a <code>moved</code> entry also lists the arrows that did not fit and what they read, which a live request does not record.</li>
<li><strong>Pretended connections.</strong> For each operation the author can choose: answer with the sample, answer with a chosen result, fail with one of the operation's failure codes, or hold, so a &quot;Wait for&quot; can be answered later by hand.</li>
<li><strong>The outbox</strong> holds three kinds of entry: calls (&quot;Done in other systems&quot;), messages, and things told to other systems.</li>
<li><strong>An unfinished draft</strong> can be tried. A test request that reaches a part whose To do stops it from running is stuck with the reason <code>unfinished</code>, which only Try it uses.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="06-the-contract--publish-then-a-person-acts">Publish, then a person acts</h2>
<p>What happens between the editor's publish and a person's press on a task of a request that runs on the published version. The server checks and compiles again with the same core package the browser runs, and stores the version with its authored source. A task page later renders its form from that source and works out its state with core; the engine judges the press and answers in authored terms. Names are those of <code>authoring-api.md</code> and <code>runtime-api.md</code>. Drawn by the engine owner (<code>contract/D16-publish-then-act.md</code>); only line breaks were added here.</p>

<p>The task page makes two calls: the task first, for the state of this request, then the version's source, which never changes and is cached for good. A refusal comes back as a code at a place in that source, and the page words it there: <code>not-assignee</code>, for example, comes back at the task's &quot;Who is asked&quot;, and the page says in its own words that this person is not among those asked.</p>
<h2 id="06-the-contract--how-the-two-sides-keep-in-step">How the two sides keep in step</h2>
<p><strong>Shared fixtures.</strong> Both sides test against the same files in <code>contract/fixtures/</code>: four sample workflows in the authored format (<code>change-request</code>, <code>blank</code>, <code>several-at-once</code>, <code>integrated-sample</code>), <code>records.json</code> (each sample's name, description and &quot;Stuck requests go to&quot;, standing in for the server's workflow records) and <code>catalogue.json</code> (the sample catalogue, with the mock systems' connections). The frontend's tests load them today; the engine's cases are written against them and have not run.</p>
<p><strong>The fixture check.</strong> <code>contract/check</code> proves the fixtures still fit the format: <code>npm run verify</code> type-checks each fixture's typed source against <code>authored-format.ts</code>, confirms each <code>.json</code> is exactly what its source produces, and checks that every ID is unique, follows the ID rule and that no reference points at a missing ID.</p>
<p><strong>Versions on every response.</strong> Every server response carries the core version it runs (<code>Engine-Core-Version</code>) and the published-definition format (<code>Engine-Definition-Format</code>). The browser's core must be exactly the server's. When it is older or newer:</p>
<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead>
<tr>
<th>What still works</th>
<th>What does not</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Editing and saving the draft</td>
<td>Publishing, refused with <code>core-version-mismatch</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>The check and Try it, marked as possibly out of date</td>
<td></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><p>The editor asks the author to reload the page, which brings the matching core. The exact-match rule is cheap to relax later.</p>
<p><strong>Changing a contract file.</strong> Each file has one pen, as the table of the four parts says; the other side asks for a change rather than making it. Asks and answers are written down (<code>contract/CHANGES-draft2.md</code> holds the latest round). An edit to <code>contract/*.ts</code> that changes a type is made in one commit, after a line to the other side, because the frontend's build type-checks those files straight from the working folder (E-22).</p>
<h2 id="06-the-contract--every-family-of-codes-that-crosses">Every family of codes that crosses</h2>
<p>Codes are spelled two ways (<code>core-api.md</code> section 1.1): a code that is recorded or sent outside the platform is kebab-case (<code>choice-unknown</code>, <code>nobody-to-ask</code>); a code that only passes between core, the server and the frontend uses dots and camel case (<code>stage.buttonHasNowhereToGo</code>, <code>task.opened</code>).</p>

<td>None</td>
<td><code>started</code>, <code>refused</code> with <code>mapping-error</code></td>
<td><code>runtime-api.md</code> section 8</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><h2 id="06-the-contract--settled-and-still-open">Settled, and still open</h2>
<p><strong>Settled</strong> in the contract as of this writing: the four parts and their pens; the one rule of codes, places and values; the authored format's IDs and value JSON; one stuck state with four reasons (five in Try it), Retry only for a failed action or nobody to ask, Close for any open request; choices from another system read live and looked up again when the person acts; one stuck message; the order of checks when a person acts, with no call to another system while a request is locked; the inbound endpoint's answers. Every decision behind these is still pending the product owner's review.</p>

<section class="doc" data-file="07-engine-design.md"><h1 id="doc-07-engine-design">Engine design</h1>
<p class="doc-meta doc-owner">Owner: Engine owner.</p>
<p class="doc-meta doc-answers">Answers: How does the engine process one input, store it, and recover?</p>
<p><strong>Reading path.</strong> The product owner's reading path is documents 0, 1, 5 and 4: <a href="#doc-00-start-here">Start here</a>, <a href="#doc-01-context">Context</a>, <a href="#doc-05-integrations">Integrations</a> and <a href="#doc-04-word-map">Word map</a>. This document is mostly for engineers; each section meant only for them says so in its first line.</p>
<p>This is the engine as designed: the server side that runs requests, keeps their history and talks to other systems. It follows the kernel spec v2.20 (<code>workflow-platform/engine/kernel/kernel-spec.md</code>; its copy is in <code>engine/spec/</code>), its data model and architecture, the formats in <code>engine/design/</code>, and decisions E-1 to E-33 in <a href="#doc-11-decisions-engine">Decisions: engine</a>. Core and the server are built and run in the engine packages' own tests and on the development host, against in-memory mock systems; nothing runs yet inside the existing application. The editor's word comes first; the engine's term follows in brackets where an engineer needs it.</p>
<h2 id="07-engine-design--the-model-in-a-page">The model in a page</h2>
<p>A <strong>request</strong> is one use of a published version of a workflow. For each request the engine keeps a <strong>history</strong>: a numbered list of events, appended to and never changed, kept for ever. Everything else the engine knows about a request is worked out from its history.</p>
<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead>
<tr>
<th>Thing</th>
<th>What it is</th>
<th>What an author sees</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Stage</td>
<td>A named place where a request sits. Under the root stage exactly one stage is active. Each entry is a new <em>activation</em> with fresh waits. Entering a final stage closes the request. The compiler turns one authored stage into a short chain of engine stages: arrival actions, tasks, after-response actions, then a routing step that holds the arrows (E-14).</td>
<td>Stage, ending</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Wait</td>
<td>Something the request waits on, opened when its stage is entered and cancelled when the stage is left. A <em>person wait</em> asks someone to answer. A <em>call wait</em> is a request the engine sent to another system through a connection.</td>
<td>Task; an action that uses a connection (&quot;Look up&quot;, &quot;Create Jira issue&quot;, &quot;Wait for&quot;)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Outcome</td>
<td>How a wait finishes.</td>
<td>Button; for an action, done or failed</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Transition</td>
<td>A move to another stage, with a condition in the expression language (CEL) and optional writes to the request's data (Set). The first transition whose condition is true fires.</td>
<td>Arrow; &quot;Save a value&quot;</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Turn</td>
<td>One input, processed under a lock on the request, in one Postgres transaction.</td>
<td>Nothing: one press of a button, one answer from another system</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><p>A request changes only through one of four inputs:</p>
<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead>
<tr>
<th>Input</th>
<th>Recorded as</th>
<th>Who sends it</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Start</td>
<td><code>RequestStarted</code>, then the start task's <code>WaitCompleted</code></td>
<td>A person submitting the start form, or a connection through a live &quot;Starts when&quot; (trigger binding)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>A person answers</td>
<td><code>WaitCompleted</code></td>
<td>The person asked, through the runtime API</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>A call returns</td>
<td><code>WaitCompleted</code>, or <code>CallResultLate</code> if the wait has already closed</td>
<td>A connection, through the call's job</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>An admin steps in</td>
<td><code>Overridden</code></td>
<td>A workflow admin (&quot;Stuck requests go to&quot;) or a platform admin: Retry or Close</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><p>Two pure functions in <code>engine/packages/core</code> do the work (E-3). Neither does I/O; both run in the browser for Try it and on the server.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong><code>decide</code></strong> takes the published definition, the request's current state and one input, works out every consequence and returns them as events. It evaluates expressions. It has no clock and never reads live data: outside data reaches it only as recorded events. Beside the events it returns a trace for &quot;why did it go there&quot;, which is not recorded (E-15).</li>
<li><strong><code>evolve</code></strong> folds one event into the state. Replaying a request is folding its events from the first. <code>evolve</code> never evaluates an expression, never reads the definition and never calls out.</li>
</ul>
<p>Why it is split this way: <strong>history is the truth, and replay never re-runs workflow logic.</strong> Every consequence is written out as an event, so a request reads the same years later, on any build of the code, without its definition or any outside system. Every other table can be deleted and rebuilt from history, or re-derived. The cost: a bug in <code>decide</code> is recorded as fact. It is repaired by an admin turn, never by rewriting history.</p>
<h2 id="07-engine-design--one-input-end-to-end">One input, end to end</h2>
<p>For engineers only: the steps of one turn inside the server.</p>
<p>The running example is the change request demo, case D1 (<code>workflow-platform/engine/workflows/change-request-demo/test-cases.yaml</code>). Rita started the request; in the stage Pending (status &quot;Pending approval&quot;) the task <code>primary.decision</code> asks the group <code>grp-a</code> (Alice and Rita), and its recorded membership read has listed them; the requester may not answer it. Alice presses Approve and names Lee as eng lead.</p>

fill: none;"></line><line x1="630" y1="894" x2="630" y2="894" stroke-width="0" marker-start="url(#mmd-24-sequencenumber)"></line><text x="630" y="898" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12px" text-anchor="middle" class="sequenceNumber">13</text></svg></div><figcaption class="figure-caption"><span class="fig-id">D17.</span> One input, end to end inside the engine: what happens when a person approves</figcaption></figure>
<ul>
<li><strong>The lock.</strong> One request is changed by one turn at a time. A start inserts the row instead of locking it; a start through &quot;Starts when&quot; also inserts its started row in the inbound log, whose unique index stops a second start for the same event and workflow. If the lock is not obtained in 5 s the answer is <code>busy</code>. The primary key <code>(request_id, seq)</code> on <code>events</code> is a second guard: two turns cannot both write the same <code>seq</code>.</li>
<li><strong>Lookups before the lock.</strong> The lookups made when a person acts, the person's groups and each chosen item, happen before the request is locked, after an unlocked check that the task is open. The task is checked again under the lock. No outside call is made while a request is locked (E-23). An act on a task that is no longer open is answered <code>wait-not-open</code> even while the directory is down, because the unlocked check comes first.</li>
<li><strong>The checks.</strong> The refusal reasons come in a fixed order: <code>wait-not-open</code>, <code>membership-unavailable</code>, <code>not-assignee</code>, <code>may</code>, <code>invalid-data</code>, <code>source-unavailable</code>, <code>choice-unknown</code>, <code>check</code> (runtime API section 4.3); the lookups' results are applied at their place in that order. A refused act rolls back and writes one <code>attempts_log</code> row in its own transaction; history is untouched. A lookup that cannot be made (<code>membership-unavailable</code>, <code>source-unavailable</code>) writes nothing at all and is answered &quot;try again&quot;.</li>
<li><strong>What is recorded with the answer.</strong> <code>WaitCompleted.evidence</code> holds the asked groups Alice belongs to (<code>memberOf</code>), what each check read, and each answer looked up in a data source (<code>lookups</code>).</li>
<li><strong>One input, many events.</strong> <code>decide</code> fires transitions until none is enabled. More than 50 firings in one turn is an error. The stuck state is then worked out from the new state and written to the request's row.</li>
<li><strong>Jobs.</strong> The engine's own <code>jobs</code> table, written inside the turn's transaction and taken by polling workers (E-30). A notify job is inserted for the turn when any new event could match a notification rule, and a publish job for every turn. Each opened call gets its own call job.</li>
</ul>
<p>After the commit, the jobs carry on. A call's result is a new input and therefore a new turn.</p>

<p>A start takes the same path as D17: starting a request is acting on the start task (the start wait). The start turn appends <code>RequestStarted</code>, enters the root and the first stage, opens its waits, completes the start task, then decides as usual. Who is asked by the start task is not checked at start; its <code>may</code>, schema, lookups and checks are. A refused start leaves no request. Delivery of outbound events to subscribers is drawn in document 5, <a href="#doc-05-integrations">Integrations</a>.</p>
<h2 id="07-engine-design--the-event-vocabulary">The event vocabulary</h2>
<p>For engineers only: the recorded event shapes.</p>
<p><strong>These shapes are kept for ever once the first request runs</strong> (<code>engine/design/event-payloads.md</code>). No field may be removed, renamed, retyped or given a new meaning; such a change is a new schema version <code>v</code> of that event type, and readers upcast older versions when they read. Every type starts at <code>v: 1</code>. Adding a value to an open list (a cause, a wait kind) is not a new version.</p>
<p>Every event carries an envelope: <code>requestId</code> (matching <code>^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}$</code>), <code>seq</code> (1, 2, 3 ... per request, without gaps), <code>at</code> (the time of the turn's transaction, the engine's only clock), <code>turn</code> (the <code>seq</code> of the input that caused it), <code>v</code>, <code>engineBuild</code>. A person, connection or the engine itself is written <code>by: {type, id}</code>, with <code>type</code> one of <code>user</code>, <code>connection</code>, <code>system</code>. A person or group in data is always <code>{type, id}</code> with the directory's immutable object ID (E-20).</p>
<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead>
<tr>
<th>Event</th>
<th>Kind</th>
<th>What it means</th>
<th>Who causes it</th>
<th>Fields that matter</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>RequestStarted</code></td>
<td>Input</td>
<td>A request began.</td>
<td>A person, or a connection through &quot;Starts when&quot;</td>
<td><code>workflow</code> (the workflow's ID), <code>version</code>, <code>readableId</code> (the request number people see), <code>by</code>, <code>input</code> (button and answers), <code>trigger</code> (null for a person; the binding, connection, trigger and the sender's event ID otherwise)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>WaitCompleted</code></td>
<td>Input</td>
<td>A task was answered, or a call returned a result.</td>
<td>The person who answered; a connection for a call</td>
<td><code>wait</code> (element, activation, key, seq), <code>outcome</code>, <code>data</code> (answers, the call's result, or <code>{code, message}</code> for a failure), <code>by</code>, <code>evidence</code> (<code>memberOf</code>, <code>checks</code> with their reads, <code>lookups</code>; null for a call)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>CallResultLate</code></td>
<td>Input</td>
<td>A call's result arrived after its wait had closed. No condition ever reads it.</td>
<td>A connection</td>

</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>Overridden</code></td>
<td>Input</td>
<td>An admin stepped in.</td>
<td>A workflow admin or platform admin</td>

</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>TransitionFired</code></td>
<td>Decision</td>
<td>An arrow was taken.</td>
<td>The engine (<code>decide</code>)</td>
<td><code>transition</code>, <code>stage</code>, <code>activation</code>, <code>reads</code> (every path its condition read, with its value or &quot;absent&quot;)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>StageEntered</code></td>
<td>Decision</td>
<td>The request entered a stage.</td>
<td>The engine</td>
<td><code>activation</code>, <code>stage</code>, <code>status</code> (<code>{id, label}</code> or null), <code>parentActivation</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>StageExited</code></td>
<td>Decision</td>
<td>The request left a stage. Not written when the request closes.</td>
<td>The engine; an admin's re-entry gives <code>forced</code></td>
<td><code>activation</code>, <code>stage</code>, <code>mode</code> (<code>normal</code> or <code>forced</code>)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>WaitOpened</code></td>
<td>Decision</td>
<td>A task or a call was opened, with everything resolved at that moment.</td>
<td>The engine</td>
<td><code>wait</code>, <code>kind</code>, <code>role</code>; for a task: <code>assignees</code> (who is asked, groups not expanded), <code>outcomes</code>; for a call: <code>connection</code>, <code>op</code> (<code>createIssue@1</code>), <code>effect</code>, <code>args</code>, <code>idempotencyKey</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>WaitCancelled</code></td>
<td>Decision</td>
<td>An open task or call was closed because the stage was left or the request closed.</td>
<td>The engine; Close</td>
<td><code>wait</code>, <code>cause</code> (<code>stage-exit</code>, <code>request-closed</code>)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>WaitSkipped</code></td>
<td>Decision</td>
<td>An open wait was set aside by an admin.</td>
<td>An admin's Retry, which re-enters a stage with waits still open</td>
<td><code>wait</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>DataSet</code></td>
<td>Decision</td>
<td>Values were written. Removing a value that is not there records nothing, so a person's start records no empty <code>remove</code> for the Requester (E-24).</td>
<td>The engine, on a transition</td>
<td><code>patch</code> (ordered <code>set</code> and <code>remove</code> operations on paths), <code>source</code>, <code>element</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>Faulted</code></td>
<td>Decision</td>
<td>The request stopped on an error.</td>
<td>The engine</td>
<td><code>kind</code> (<code>error</code>), <code>element</code>, <code>error</code> (<code>code</code> such as <code>cel-error</code> or <code>call-failed</code>, <code>field</code>, <code>params</code>, <code>detail</code>). A fault from a failed call has code <code>call-failed</code> and copies the operation's failure code into <code>params</code>.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>RequestClosed</code></td>
<td>Decision</td>
<td>The request ended. Later inputs can still be recorded after it.</td>
<td>The engine at an ending; Close</td>
<td><code>stage</code> (the ending, or null when an admin closed it)</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><p>Order within a turn: the input; then, for each transition that fires, <code>TransitionFired</code>, <code>DataSet</code>, <code>WaitCancelled</code>, <code>StageExited</code>, <code>StageEntered</code>, <code>WaitOpened</code>; then <code>RequestClosed</code> or <code>Faulted</code> if any (spec section 3). The stuck state, the public events and a request's data &quot;as of&quot; an event are worked out from history by every reader the same way; none of them is an event (E-33).</p>
<h2 id="07-engine-design--a-requests-life">A request's life</h2>
<p>A request is <strong>running</strong> while a turn is being processed, <strong>waiting</strong> between turns while a task or a call is open, <strong>stuck</strong> when it cannot move until someone acts, and <strong>ended</strong> once closed.</p>

<p>&quot;Stuck&quot; is one state with four reasons, worked out from history after every turn and never recorded, the same way by the lists, the request page, the notifier and the publisher (E-19, E-20, E-23, E-33; integrations section 11.5). The reason is read from the fault, whatever added the call; nobody-to-ask is the match of the published version's <code>nobodyToAsk</code> block; nothing-fits is a function of the state. The stage a stuck request is reported in is always an authored stage, found through the version's origin map (E-27, E-28). The first that applies wins:</p>
<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead>
<tr>
<th>Reason</th>
<th>State after the turn</th>
<th>Example</th>
<th>Admin actions</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>action-failed</code></td>
<td>A <code>Faulted</code> with code <code>call-failed</code>, not cleared: a call whose &quot;If it fails&quot; is &quot;stuck&quot; failed clearly, whatever added it. The fault's <code>params</code> carry the operation's failure code.</td>
<td>Jira refuses to create the issue (demo D7).</td>
<td>Retry: clears the fault and re-enters the engine stage that stopped, so the action is tried again. With &quot;once&quot; it is sent under the same explicit key, with &quot;again&quot; (<code>keyScope: activation</code>) under a new one. Earlier actions of the authored stage are not repeated. Close.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>error</code></td>
<td>A <code>Faulted</code> with any other code, not cleared: an expression could not be evaluated, or a turn exceeded 50 firings.</td>
<td>An unknown domain has no approver group (demo D9).</td>
<td>Close only. The request sits where its turn began, so running again would repeat the same result, and could repeat an outside action that had already succeeded.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>nothing-fits</code></td>
<td>The request is open, has no fault, and has no open task and no open call, so no arrow fits. After-response actions have already run (E-22).</td>
<td>No arrow covers the answers given.</td>
<td>Close only. The arrows would be checked again over the same values.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>nobody-to-ask</code></td>
<td>An open task matches its rule in the <code>nobodyToAsk</code> block: nobody can answer it. Who can answer is the people asked directly plus the members of the groups asked, as recorded by the task's membership read in the same activation, less the Requester where &quot;The requester can't answer&quot;. A read that failed contributes nobody from its groups; a person asked directly still counts (E-24). Not a fault.</td>
<td>The Platform team holds only the Requester (integrated sample I26b).</td>
<td>Retry: re-enters the task's engine stage, so the group is read again and the stage's tasks are asked again. Close.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><ul>
<li><strong>The membership read.</strong> For every task that may ask a group, the compiler opens a read of the group's members beside the task, in the task's own engine stage: a call wait <code>&lt;task&gt;__members</code> on <code>membersOf@1</code> with <code>onFailure: outcome</code>. The task is open at once; the read only feeds the nobody-to-ask match. A failed read contributes nobody from its groups; people asked directly still count (E-24). &quot;People in [group]&quot; under &quot;Who is asked&quot; is the same as asking the group: no separate directory read is made for it, so Retry for nobody-to-ask always reads the group again. The tasks step leaves by an explicit condition that every task is answered, never by <code>otherwise</code>, so a pending read cannot hold it; leaving the step cancels the read. A stuck rule whose expression errors counts as no match for every reader, and the error is logged.</li>
<li><strong>While stuck.</strong> A request with an error fault (<code>action-failed</code> or <code>error</code>) still accepts and records answers and call results, but <code>decide</code> does not run until an admin turn clears the fault; that turn then decides once over every input kept. <code>nothing-fits</code> is no fault and does not stop <code>decide</code>: it ends as soon as something is open again or the request closes. A request stuck with <code>nobody-to-ask</code> has no fault: if someone is added to the group, they can simply answer.</li>
<li><strong>Retry</strong> is offered only for <code>action-failed</code> and <code>nobody-to-ask</code> (E-23). On a request that is not stuck it is refused <code>not-stuck</code>; on one stuck with <code>nothing-fits</code> or <code>error</code>, <code>not-retryable</code>. It is one admin turn, <code>Overridden {by, reason, actions: [retry]}</code>: the fault, if any, is cleared and the active engine stage re-entered. Open waits there are skipped and opened afresh. Known limits (E-19): an empty value stays empty, so Close is the only way out until values can be changed by hand; in a stage with several tasks every task is asked again.</li>
<li><strong>Close</strong> is offered for any open request, stuck or not: <code>Overridden {actions: [close]}</code>, every open wait cancelled, <code>RequestClosed {stage: null}</code>. Outside jobs are not stopped; their results are recorded late.</li>
<li><strong>A slow call is not stuck.</strong> A call with no result is waited for; after the time its operation says to expect, the server writes a <code>call-overdue</code> log line and nobody is told (E-33). It cannot be retried, which avoids starting a second outside job (E-20).</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="07-engine-design--a-calls-life">A call's life</h2>
<p>For engineers only: how one call is sent.</p>
<p>A call wait is recorded twice: in history (<code>WaitOpened</code> when it opens; <code>WaitCompleted</code> or <code>CallResultLate</code> when a result is recorded) and in working state (one <code>pending_calls</code> row and one <code>call</code> job while no result is recorded). Everything between, sends, &quot;accepted&quot;, the job reference, polls, is working state and never enters history (integrations section 10).</p>

y2="0%"><stop offset="0%" stop-color="#a5abef" stop-opacity="1"></stop><stop offset="100%" stop-color="#c9cdd4" stop-opacity="1"></stop></linearGradient></svg></div><figcaption class="figure-caption"><span class="fig-id">D20.</span> A call's life: sent, accepted, done; no clear answer; a late result</figcaption></figure><div class="table-wrap"><table><thead>
<tr>
<th>Rule</th>
<th>What it means</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>At least once, with a key</td>
<td>Every call carries an idempotency key, recorded in <code>WaitOpened</code>. The connector must honour it: for a key that already succeeded, return that result and do nothing else; for a key that failed, try again. &quot;Once&quot; compiles to an explicit key, <code>'once.' + request.id + '.' + &lt;action ID&gt;</code>, so the two copies of a stage emitted for &quot;If sent back&quot; share it (E-23). &quot;Again&quot; and every read use <code>keyScope: activation</code>: a readable key made of the request and the wait instance (E-33). The Jira connector is a known exception: a plain create, so a lost answer followed by a resend can make a second issue (integrations section 3).</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>One job per call</td>
<td>The job sends the call. A timeout or &quot;don't know&quot; is never a failure: the job runs again after 10 s, 30 s, 1 min, 5 min, then every 15 min, without limit, with the same key. Only a clear refusal is <code>failed</code>. A worker that dies mid-job leaves a stale lock, and the next worker takes the job again.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Await</td>
<td>The connector may answer <code>accepted</code> with the outside job's reference. The same job then asks the job's status every <code>pollSeconds</code>.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Tied to its job</td>
<td>A status answer is recorded only if it names the row's job. An answer naming another job is a <code>job-mismatch</code> log line. So a stale result of a failed job never completes the wait of the job that replaced it.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Tied to its wait</td>
<td>A result is recorded for the one wait whose job got it. Whether that wait already has a result is read from history; a second result is dropped.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Late result</td>
<td>Leaving the stage, Retry or Close tells the outside system nothing. A call never sent, and a read, are dropped when their wait closes. A write or await sent at least once with no clear answer is kept and sent or asked again until it answers, because it may have acted outside; its result is recorded as <code>CallResultLate</code>, which no condition reads, and each try writes a <code>call-outcome-unknown</code> log line.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Overdue</td>
<td>A try past the operation's <code>expectedWithinSeconds</code> writes a <code>call-overdue</code> log line. Nobody is told (E-33).</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><h2 id="07-engine-design--the-data-model">The data model</h2>
<p>For engineers only: the tables.</p>
<p>Twelve tables (data model). <strong>History</strong> is never updated or deleted; <strong>configuration</strong> is set by authors and admins, changeable and not versioned; <strong>read tables</strong> are rebuilt from <code>events</code>; <strong>working state</strong> may be lost; <strong>logs</strong> are append-only records that cannot be rebuilt. The application's database role has no UPDATE or DELETE on <code>events</code>, <code>definitions</code> or the logs. Connections, secrets and the catalogue are configuration read at start-up and held in memory, not tables (E-33).</p>

<td>No</td>
<td>For ever</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>settings_log</code></td>
<td>Log</td>
<td>Each change to a workflow's settings, a pause or resume included: the record before and after, who, when.</td>
<td>No</td>
<td>For ever</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>requests</code></td>
<td>Read table</td>
<td>One row per request: version, status, active stages, data, starter, stuck state, authored stage, last <code>seq</code>; a person's start token. Lists, filters and the lock use it.</td>
<td>Yes, from <code>events</code>, keeping the start token</td>
<td>Rebuilt</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>open_waits</code></td>
<td>Read table</td>
<td>One row per open task or call: who is asked (users and groups, not expanded). The action-item list uses it.</td>
<td>Yes, from <code>events</code></td>
<td>Rebuilt</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>pending_calls</code></td>
<td>Working state</td>
<td>One row per call with no result recorded: its key, the outside job's reference, attempts, last error, whether its wait has closed.</td>
<td>Partly, from <code>WaitOpened</code></td>
<td>Until the result is recorded</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>jobs</code></td>
<td>Working state</td>
<td>Call, notify and publish jobs, with when each may run next.</td>
<td>No</td>
<td>Until done</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>drafts</code></td>
<td>Working state</td>
<td>One draft per workflow, overwritten on each save.</td>
<td>No</td>
<td>Overwritten</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>attempts_log</code></td>
<td>Log</td>
<td>Refused attempts: who, what, the refusal reason. Not history.</td>
<td>No</td>
<td>Not deleted in the first build</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>inbound_log</code></td>
<td>Log</td>
<td>Every event received on the inbound hook, per candidate workflow: its result or code, the request it started, the parsed event; the start dedupe.</td>
<td>No</td>
<td>Not deleted in the first build</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><p>There are no snapshots: a request has a few dozen events, so each turn folds them from the first.</p>
<h2 id="07-engine-design--failure-and-recovery">Failure and recovery</h2>
<p>For engineers only: crashes, repeats and faults.</p>
<p><strong>A crash between any two steps.</strong> Each turn is one transaction, and its jobs are written in it, so a crash leaves one of these states:</p>
<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead>
<tr>
<th>Crash</th>
<th>What is left</th>
<th>How it recovers</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Inside a turn, before COMMIT</td>
<td>Nothing: the transaction rolls back.</td>
<td>The caller sends again. A second act on the same task is refused <code>wait-not-open</code> with who answered, if the first did commit. A person's start is repeated with the same <code>clientToken</code> and returns the first request.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>After COMMIT, before the caller hears</td>
<td>The turn is recorded, with its jobs.</td>
<td>As above: the repeat is recognised.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>A call job, during a send</td>
<td>The job, locked.</td>
<td>Its lock goes stale and the next worker takes it; it is sent again with the same key.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>After the outside system acted, before the result turn commits</td>
<td>The job and its row.</td>
<td>Sent or asked again; the connector returns the earlier result by key. A result for a wait that already has one in history is dropped.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>A notify job, while sending</td>
<td>Some messages sent.</td>
<td>The job runs again and sends again: a double message is accepted.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>A publish job, while posting</td>
<td>Some events posted.</td>
<td>The job runs again and posts the turn's events again; subscribers dedupe on the event <code>id</code>.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>The inbound hook, mid-event</td>
<td>Starts that committed; the sender has no answer.</td>
<td>The sender sends again; the started rows answer <code>duplicate</code>.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Read tables lost or wrong</td>
<td></td>
<td>Rebuild the request's rows from its events.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><p><strong>At least once, and how repeats are recognised.</strong></p>
<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead>
<tr>
<th>What repeats</th>
<th>Recognised by</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>A call sent twice</td>
<td>The idempotency key, at the connector; a second result for the same wait, by reading history.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>A notification</td>
<td>Not recognised; a double message is accepted.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>An outbound event</td>
<td>Its <code>id</code>: the request, the event's number and the rule.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>An inbound event</td>
<td>A started row in the inbound log for (connection, event ID, workflow), written in the start turn's transaction.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>A person's start</td>
<td>The client token on the request's row (starter, <code>clientToken</code>).</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>A person's answer</td>
<td>The task is no longer open: <code>wait-not-open</code>.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><p><strong>What a fault keeps and rolls back.</strong> An expression error, more than 50 firings in a turn, or a call that failed clearly where the author chose &quot;stuck&quot; rolls back the turn's decisions, keeps the input event and appends <code>Faulted {kind: error, element, error}</code>. In a start turn the start itself (entering the first stage, opening its waits, completing the start task) is kept; only the firings are rolled back, so the request exists. An expression error is never treated as false. A fault is cleared only by Retry, which re-enters the stage, or by Close.</p>
<p><strong>How a stuck request is found, and by whom.</strong> Nobody has to look for it:</p>
<ul>
<li>The stuck state is written to <code>requests.stuck</code> in the turn's transaction; the stuck list is the request list filtered to rows whose <code>stuck</code> is set, served by a partial index.</li>
<li>The built-in rule <code>n_stopped</code> (on Stuck, every reason; E-21) sends the message <code>request.stuck</code> with the reason to the workflow admins. It is the one alert in the first build; the other built-in rule, <code>n_task</code>, sends <code>task.assigned</code> when a task opens, to those asked who may answer it.</li>
<li><code>request.stuck@1</code> is posted to every listening system; <code>request.unstuck@1</code> when it ends.</li>
<li>Every signed-in person sees on the request page that it is stuck and why. The detail, Retry and Close are for the workflow admins and platform admins (E-19). For <code>action-failed</code> the detail carries the operation's failure code (E-21). <a href="#doc-09-people-and-permissions">People and permissions</a> has the details.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="07-engine-design--expressions">Expressions</h2>
<p>For engineers only: the expression language and its pinned library.</p>
<p>Every condition, value and mapping an author builds compiles to an expression in <strong>CEL</strong> (Common Expression Language). The definition pins the expression profile <strong><code>cel-1</code></strong> and the form-schema profile <strong><code>jsonschema-1</code></strong> (<code>definition-format.md</code> sections 3.14 to 6). A profile is immutable: a change to any rule, or to a library version behind it, is a new profile and a new definition format.</p>
<p>Why it is pinned per format: the engine must run <code>decide</code> for a published version for as long as any request on it is open, and what a condition read is recorded for ever, so an expression must evaluate the same way for that whole time. The library fails part of the standard conformance tests, and the wrapper depends on library internals outside its type contract, so a library upgrade could change behaviour without warning. The trial also showed that two versions can load side by side, so pinning per format is workable.</p>
<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead>
<tr>
<th><code>cel-1</code></th>
<th>Content</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Library</td>
<td><code>@marcbachmann/cel-js</code> 8.0.0 and <code>@bufbuild/re2</code> 0.6.2, exact versions and integrity hashes, behind an engine-owned wrapper that is the only code importing the library (E-18, E-20)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Replaced by the wrapper</td>
<td><code>matches</code> (RE2: no lookaround, linear time), <code>timestamp()</code> (strict RFC 3339), <code>int()</code> (range-checked), <code>lowerAscii</code> and <code>upperAscii</code> (ASCII only), <code>getDayOfYear()</code> (in UTC)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Added</td>
<td><code>date()</code> for <code>YYYY-MM-DD</code>; <code>days(n)</code>, an int to a duration; <code>asDate(t)</code>, a timestamp to a <code>YYYY-MM-DD</code> string in UTC, which the compiler applies where a formula's result is used as a date; equality for object types</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Function list</td>
<td>Written out in <code>engine/design/definition-format.md</code> and pinned, not &quot;whatever the library registers&quot; (E-23)</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Refused</td>
<td>Time-zone arguments to timestamp getters; <code>\p</code> and <code>\P</code> in patterns (when the formula is checked, E-26); a duration plus a timestamp; <code>json()</code> on bytes; the <code>cel1_</code> prefix; mixing <code>int</code> and <code>double</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Values</td>
<td>Present or absent, never null. JSON is read into CEL by the definition's <code>types</code> block, which declares every data path, constant and operation result: a schema number is a double, an integer an int. Integers stay within +/-(2^53 - 1). UTC only. No clock and no I/O.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Errors</td>
<td>Recorded with the engine's own code, never the library's.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><p><strong>What the trial ran</strong> (<code>engine/packages/core/test/cel/</code>, 2026-11-15, Windows 11, Node 26.13.1, Vitest 5.1.0): 7 test files, 36 tests, all passing. They covered the demo's expressions and the spec's rules through the wrapper (T1 to T26); the cel-spec &quot;simple&quot; conformance tests against the library alone, recorded as a baseline of 1,122 passing, 579 failing, 643 skipped (T27); the whole corpus in a V8 sandbox with no Node globals (T28); the bundle size, 45,991 bytes gzip (T29); and versions 7.6.1 and 8.0.0 side by side (T30). Not run: real browsers, and the library's own test suite.</p>
<p><strong>Kept for ever once written:</strong> the wrapper produces <code>reads</code> as decided (E-20): each path from the request that an expression selected, with the value at its end or absent. Constants are not recorded.</p>
<h2 id="07-engine-design--testing">Testing</h2>
<p>For engineers only: the test cases and what they assert.</p>
<p>The test cases are data, and they are the engine's acceptance criteria. <strong>They run:</strong> core's tests translate the demo cases and the replay-only cases and run them through the kernel and the in-memory host, and the server's tests run the demo cases through the turn transaction on PGlite.</p>
<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead>
<tr>
<th>Cases</th>
<th>Where</th>
<th>What they are written to prove</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>Demo cases D1 to D11</td>
<td><code>workflow-platform/engine/workflows/change-request-demo/test-cases.yaml</code></td>
<td>For each input, the exact events appended in order, or the refusal; the notification rules matched. Calls are faked: results are injected as inputs. D10 deletes the projection rows and replays the events, expecting identical rows.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Replay-only cases</td>
<td><code>workflow-platform/engine/kernel/replay-only.yaml</code></td>
<td><code>evolve</code> folds stored histories that <code>decide</code> does not write today: two active child stages, wait <code>seq</code> above 1, the readable number, a start by a connection. They are to show that those conventions hold.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Integrated sample cases I1 to I30</td>
<td><code>engine/design/integrated-sample.md</code></td>
<td>One workflow through every door, against the in-memory mock systems, through the real hook and APIs with real signatures. Each case is asserted on what a person or an outside system can see: inputs, refusals, the story, messages and outbound events, including every outbound event's <code>id</code> and payload. The exact list of engine events for each case will be produced by the built compiler and engine, reviewed once, and then kept as the expected output. The hand-written event lists in the sample are illustrations and are not renumbered by hand (E-24).</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>Separate tests</td>
<td><code>workflow-platform/engine/architecture.md</code> section 6</td>
<td>What the cases cannot reach: the call job, a duplicate result, a call closed before it was sent; the stuck state and the 50-firing limit; the action-item query; each publish check, with a definition that fails it; the catalogue snapshot; the real connectors.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><p>Tests and the dev host run on PGlite, Postgres compiled to WebAssembly in process (E-11). PGlite serves one connection, so it cannot show two transactions racing. The cases that need <strong>real Postgres</strong> with two connections, such as two deliveries of one event at once (I23), run there. Jobs, and the connectors' checks of an inbound event's signature, read time from a clock the test host moves.</p>
<p>The demo follows the same rules as compiled workflows (E-23): people and groups are <code>{type, id}</code> in its data, call arguments, results and cases, with the <code>nobodyToAsk</code> block and the single stuck rule. The integrated sample's engine stage names must match the compiler's naming (<code>engine/design/compiler.md</code>) before anything is published, since stage IDs are recorded for ever.</p>
<h2 id="07-engine-design--what-the-first-build-includes">What the first build includes</h2>
<p>&quot;First build&quot; means behaviour and tests are in the first build. &quot;Later&quot; is designed enough not to block it and is not built; what the kernel and the integrations no longer build, and how each would be added, is listed in <code>workflow-platform/research/reserved-for-later.md</code> (E-33). Publishing refuses a definition that uses a part that is not built.</p>

<section class="doc" data-file="08-frontend-design.md"><h1 id="doc-08-frontend-design">Frontend design</h1>
<p class="doc-meta doc-owner">Owner: Frontend owner.</p>
<p class="doc-meta doc-answers">Answers: How is the editor built, and how does it stay in step with the engine?</p>
<p>The frontend is everything that runs in the browser: the editor in which authors build workflows, and the pages people use to start requests, answer tasks and look after stuck requests. It is platform code, and its code names no customer workflow. &quot;Change request&quot; and the other sample workflows come from the contract's fixtures: the tests use them, and the development app is seeded with them so that every screen has something to show. This document says how it is put together, what happens on one edit, what each screen asks of the engine side, the ten decisions behind it, how it is tested, and what exists today.</p>
<p>Two documents come first if you have not read them: <a href="#doc-01-context">Context</a> for who uses which screen, and the <a href="#doc-04-word-map">Word map</a> for what each editor word means. Where this document mentions the engine, the details are in the engine owner's documents: <a href="#doc-02-the-parts">2 The parts</a>, <a href="#doc-03-life-of-a-workflow">3 The life of a workflow</a>, <a href="#doc-06-the-contract">6 The contract</a> and <a href="#doc-07-engine-design">7 Engine design</a>.</p>
<h2 id="08-frontend-design--what-the-frontend-is">What the frontend is</h2>
<p>The frontend is three things built from one set of components:</p>
<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead>
<tr>
<th>Part</th>
<th>Who uses it</th>
<th>Screens</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><strong>The editor</strong></td>
<td>Workflow authors</td>
<td>Workflows list; the Diagram with its stage panel; In words; Values; the form editor; To do and Publish; Settings; the read-only Connections list</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>Try it</strong></td>
<td>Workflow authors</td>
<td>The editor's diagram running a test request, with &quot;Acting as&quot;, the task as that person sees it, why each move happened, and the Test outbox</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><strong>The pages people use</strong></td>
<td>Requesters, people asked, the people who look after stuck requests</td>
<td>Start a request; My tasks; the requests list; a request's page; Stuck requests</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><p>The frontend owns every word a person reads. The engine side answers in <strong>codes</strong>: a check result, a refusal or a history entry is a code, a location in the saved workflow, and parameters. The frontend turns each into a sentence. Engine words such as &quot;wait&quot; or &quot;transition&quot; never reach a screen.</p>
<h2 id="08-frontend-design--how-it-is-put-together">How it is put together</h2>
<p>The code is in <code>frontend/src</code>, in seven kinds of folder. Each may import only from the folders below it in this diagram, and the lint step (<code>npm run lint</code>) fails the build if one breaks the rule.</p>

<p>The arrows show the main dependencies. The full rule, as the lint step enforces it:</p>
<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead>
<tr>
<th>Folder</th>
<th>What it holds</th>
<th>May import</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td><code>contract</code></td>
<td>The authored workflow format, the catalogue types and the sample workflows, imported from the repository's <code>contract/</code> folder, never copied</td>
<td>nothing</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>words</code></td>
<td>Every label and sentence, one file per feature plus a shared vocabulary</td>
<td>nothing</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>services</code></td>
<td>The one interface to the engine side: the engine's core, and the stand-in for the server</td>
<td><code>contract</code> and <code>@workflow/core</code>; it is the only folder that may import the engine's core</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>model</code></td>
<td>The draft being edited, the commands that change it, and everything worked out from it</td>
<td><code>contract</code>, <code>services</code>, <code>words</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>ui</code></td>
<td>Design tokens as CSS variables, and primitives: button, field, menu, dialog, popover, tabs, chip, card ...</td>
<td><code>words</code></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>features/*</code></td>
<td>One folder per screen or part of a screen</td>
<td><code>contract</code>, <code>services</code>, <code>model</code>, <code>words</code>, <code>ui</code>, and its own folder; <strong>never another feature</strong></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td><code>app</code></td>
<td>The route table, the editor's top bar and the app frame</td>
<td>everything; nothing imports <code>app</code></td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><p><strong>Features never import each other.</strong> When one screen must show another feature's part, it places a <strong>slot</strong>: a named placeholder declared in <code>model</code>, such as <code>StageActions</code>, which the stage panel shows under &quot;When this stage starts&quot;. <code>app</code> fills each slot with the owning feature's component. The editor's top bar is built the same way: the To do count and Publish come from <code>features/todo</code>, Try it from <code>features/tryit</code>. So several people can build features at once without editing each other's files.</p>
<h2 id="08-frontend-design--what-happens-on-one-edit">What happens on one edit</h2>
<p>An author changes something, for example points an arrow at another stage. Everything else on screen follows from the changed document.</p>

class="figure-caption"><span class="fig-id">D22.</span> One edit: the command, what is worked out again, and the autosave</figcaption></figure>
<p>Four points carry the design:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>The document changes only through named commands.</strong> A command is a small, pure function from one document to the next, with a name such as <code>arrow.setGoTo</code>. A command may refuse (for example, pointing at a stage that no longer exists), and then nothing changes. Undo applies the command's recorded inverse.</li>
<li><strong>Nothing on screen is stored beside the document.</strong> The diagram, &quot;Reached from&quot;, the To do list, the value picker and In words are all worked out from it.</li>
<li><strong>The check and the facts are the engine's,</strong> run in the browser on the engine's own core (decisions E-3 and U-4), so what the editor says is what the server will say at publish. The check waits for a short pause in the typing (150 ms) before it runs.</li>
<li><strong>One author at a time.</strong> The draft is saved after a short pause (800 ms), with the revision it was based on. If someone saved in between, the save is refused, saving stops, and the author is told and can load the newer draft. Nothing is merged. A save that fails for any other reason is tried again every 5 seconds. Today the &quot;server&quot; in this picture is the stand-in described below.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="08-frontend-design--how-the-frontend-uses-the-engines-core">How the frontend uses the engine's core</h2>
<p>The frontend has no engine of its own. Everything that decides what a workflow does comes from the engine owner's package <code>@workflow/core</code>, the same code the server runs (<a href="#doc-02-the-parts">The parts</a>).</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>What is imported, and where.</strong> The frontend links <code>@workflow/core</code> as TypeScript source, so no build of the engine is needed (<code>frontend/src/services/README.md</code> says how). Only <code>src/services</code> may import it, and only its main entry: the lint step fails on any other import. Every screen reaches core through the services interface.</li>
<li><strong>What core does for the editor.</strong> The check (To do and Worth knowing), the facts (Reached from, arrows that can never be used, which arrows send back), values in scope, formulas (checking and sample results), sample values, form state, &quot;what changed&quot; since the live version, and the compile that publishing runs.</li>
<li><strong>Try it</strong> runs on core's own test host in the browser: the same turn, the same story and the same outbox as a live request, with every connection pretended.</li>
<li><strong>Live requests</strong>, until the engine's server can be run, also run in the browser on core: each request has its own test host. A request is kept as the list of moves the engine accepted (a start, a button pressed, an admin's retry or close, an answer from another system) and is replayed on a fresh host after a reload. What a request page shows (its status, tasks, buttons, history and stuck state) is core's view of it.</li>
<li><strong>What is left of the stand-in,</strong> in <code>src/services/standin</code>, only plays the server and pretends the other systems: the workflows with their drafts, versions and settings; the lists of requests and tasks; who is signed in; the sample directory and catalogue; and the pretended answers of other systems. It never decides what a workflow does. It is replaced by the engine's server once that can be run against. Its data is kept in the browser's local storage. The sample requests of the development app are made at start-up by running their moves through the engine, so they cannot disagree with it.</li>
<li><strong>A new code from core.</strong> Words for every finding code, story entry kind and change kind core can give are required by the type checker and by tests that go through every code, so a new code without words stops the build. If a story entry or a refusal that this build does not know still reaches a screen, it gets plain general words, never its code.</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="08-frontend-design--what-each-screen-asks-of-the-contract">What each screen asks of the contract</h2>
<p>The contract between frontend and engine has four parts, described in <a href="#doc-00-doc-plan">About this document set</a> (section 5) and, from the frontend's side, in <code>contract/frontend-needs.md</code>:</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>A. The authored format</strong>: the draft as data.</li>
<li><strong>B. Authoring</strong>: what the core works out in the browser (check, facts, values in scope, formula check, sample values, form state, Try it), and what the server keeps (drafts, publish, versions, workflow settings).</li>
<li><strong>C. Runtime</strong>: start a request, answer a task, retry and close, and the reads for lists, tasks and the request page.</li>
<li><strong>D. Catalogue and directory</strong>: what the connections offer, and people and groups.</li>
</ul>

<h2 id="08-frontend-design--the-ten-decisions">The ten decisions</h2>
<p>Each decision says what was decided, why, and what it costs. The last column says whether it is cheap to change later.</p>
<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead>
<tr>
<th>#</th>
<th>Decision</th>
<th>Why</th>
<th>What it costs</th>
<th>Cheap to change later?</th>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td>F1</td>
<td><strong>React and TypeScript, built as components with a thin development host (Vite).</strong> Nothing depends on Next.js.</td>
<td>The application the platform will live in is Next.js and React; components can be mounted there without rework.</td>
<td>The development host (hash routes, its own frames) is thrown away when the screens are mounted in the application.</td>
<td>The host, yes. React and TypeScript, no.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>F2</td>
<td><strong>One document, changed only through named commands.</strong> The draft sits in one store; every edit is a named, pure function from document to document.</td>
<td>Undo and redo, autosave, a change log and unit tests come with it; no screen can make an edit another screen does not understand.</td>
<td>Every kind of edit needs a command and its tests (about a hundred today).</td>
<td>No: every screen edits through it.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>F3</td>
<td><strong>Everything else on screen is worked out from the document,</strong> by the engine's check and facts where the contract says so, never stored beside it.</td>
<td>One source of truth: the diagram, the panel and In words cannot disagree.</td>
<td>Everything is recomputed on each edit, so the check must be fast (the engine's target: under 50 ms for 30 stages).</td>
<td>Yes: results can be cached later without changing any screen.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>F4</td>
<td><strong>The engine side is reached through one async interface</strong> with two implementations: an in-browser stand-in, and the real one. The real one replaces the stand-in piece by piece.</td>
<td>The two sessions build at the same time; the frontend never waits for the engine.</td>
<td>The stand-in can drift from the engine. It must answer in the same codes and shapes, and it is replaced as each real part arrives.</td>
<td>The implementations, yes. The interface's shapes are used by every screen, so changing them is not.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>F5</td>
<td><strong>All words live in one module:</strong> labels, the Glossary, and the sentence for every check code, refusal code and history entry.</td>
<td>The vocabulary was the hardest-won result of the mockup rounds; one place keeps it consistent and translatable.</td>
<td>Every label is a key, not inline text; a test fails on a key in the wrong file or defined twice.</td>
<td>Yes.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>F6</td>
<td><strong>One form renderer</strong> for the form editor's preview, Try it and the real request page.</td>
<td>What the author previews is what people get.</td>
<td>The renderer must cover every question kind and every way choices are filled, in all three places.</td>
<td>No, once screens depend on it; splitting it later would break the promise.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>F7</td>
<td><strong>The diagram is drawn with a graph library</strong> (<code>@xyflow/react</code>, with <code>dagre</code> for layout): pan, zoom, automatic layout by default, the author's positions kept when they move a stage.</td>
<td>The mockups could not show seven or more stages readably; this is the known gap.</td>
<td>A third-party dependency; positions are saved in the document's <code>diagram</code> field.</td>
<td>Mostly: the library is used only inside <code>features/diagram</code>.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>F8</td>
<td><strong>Look and feel sit behind a seam:</strong> design tokens as CSS variables (from the mockup kit) and a small <code>ui</code> folder of primitives.</td>
<td>The company's standard look replaces the tokens and <code>ui</code>; nothing else changes.</td>
<td>Features must use the primitives and variables, never their own colours or controls.</td>
<td>Yes: that is its purpose.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>F9</td>
<td><strong>Autosave with a revision number.</strong> A stale save is refused; saving stops and the author is offered &quot;Load the latest&quot; (nothing on their screen is replaced until they choose it). One author at a time.</td>
<td>The simplest thing that cannot lose work silently.</td>
<td>Two authors on one draft: the second one's change is refused, not merged.</td>
<td>Yes, towards locking or merging; F2's named commands make merging possible.</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td>F10</td>
<td><strong>Tests at three levels:</strong> commands and derivations; components, rendered; and the tasks from the mockup evaluations, replayed in a real browser.</td>
<td>The evaluation tasks already say what an author must be able to do; they become the acceptance tests.</td>
<td>End-to-end tests need Chrome and are slower (about two minutes for all of them); each covers a task an author or a requester must be able to do, or a defect a verifier found.</td>
<td>Yes.</td>
</tr>
</tbody>
</table></div><h2 id="08-frontend-design--how-it-is-tested-and-how-to-run-it">How it is tested, and how to run it</h2>
<div class="table-wrap"><table><thead>
