# Workflow engine: design package

This folder is the design for a small workflow engine. It is complete enough to plan the build of the engine from. It refers to nothing outside itself.

**Status.** Design only. No engine code exists. The test cases are data and have never been run.

**Your task, if you are planning the build.** Plan the engine described here, to the build scope in section 3. Do not plan what section 4 lists as not designed; note where your plan depends on it. Where this package leaves a choice open (`open-questions.md`), say what you assumed.

## 1. What the engine is for

The product is a platform on which workflow authors build their own workflows: intake, approvals, assigned work, calls to other systems. A workflow is data, published without a deployment. A request is one running instance of a workflow.

The engine is the part that runs requests. It takes four kinds of input (start a request, a person acts, a call returns, an admin intervenes), decides what follows, and records every consequence in an append-only history that is kept forever and is the source of truth.

The first build must run one workflow end to end: a simplified change request (`workflows/change-request-demo/`). It must also run an integrated sample workflow through each kind of integration in `integrations.md`, against mock outside systems: the product owner asked to see an example of each kind working.

## 2. Constraints

- **Stack:** Next.js, React, Node, Postgres. The engine lives inside an existing application and uses its sign-in, its user directory, and its email and Slack service.
- **Team:** two engineers.
- **Scale:** tiny. About one request every ten seconds at most; a request has a few dozen events.
- **Priorities:** simplicity and correctness over throughput. The first build is as small as possible.
- **Expensive versus cheap:** event shapes and IDs are kept forever, so they are specified in full now. A field, event type, action or table no first-build feature uses is added when it is built, unless adding it later would change the meaning or the form of something already written. Everything cheap to change later takes the simplest option.
- **No file storage,** so no attachments.

## 3. Build scope

This table decides what is built. Publishing rejects a definition that uses a part marked "Not built".

Three labels:
- **Build:** behaviour and tests in the first build.
- **Shape only:** the stored state can hold it and `evolve` (replay) handles it, but `decide` never produces it. `kernel/replay-only.yaml` tests these.
- **Not built:** specified for later. Do not plan it.

| Part | Spec | First build |
|---|---|---|
| Stages (root plus one level), stages with no waits, final stages, statuses | 2 | Build |
| Start wait: starting a request is acting on a person wait of `root.initial` | 2 | Build |
| Transitions, `otherwise`, Set on a transition (path segments; a CEL optional removes); values never null | 2 | Build |
| Person waits: assignees, `may`, outcomes with data schemas and per-outcome checks, obligation and option, act-time membership check with evidence | 2 | Build |
| Person waits whose assignees resolve to none (the wait opens; the request waits) | 2 | Build |
| Call waits: read and write, `keyScope` and the derived idempotency key, versioned ops, `onFailure`, dispatcher, reconciler, late results | 2 | Build |
| Await operations: `accepted`, job references, status questions, callbacks as nudges, overdue alerts for every call | 2, integrations | Build |
| `RequestStarted.trigger` with `kind: event`; the `triggers` block; the inbound hook; pausing a binding, its paused deliveries run again on resume; refused starts listed for 30 days and run again | 2, 5, integrations | Build |
| `StageExited.stage`, `TransitionFired.stage`; non-person assignees dropped at open | 2, 5 | Build |
| Act-time lookups: membership (`membership-unavailable`), the outcome's `lookups` by stored value (`choice-unknown`, `source-unavailable`), recorded in `evidence.lookups`, all made before the request is locked; the question-scoped choices call | 2, integrations | Build |
| The stuck state (`action-failed`, `nobody-to-ask`, `nothing-fits`, `error`), the `nobodyToAsk` block and the compiler's membership read; Retry only for `action-failed` and `nobody-to-ask`; Close for any open request; the admin-only detail of a failed action | 6, integrations | Build |
| Outbound events: the `events` block, the six types, the publisher, push delivery, the pull feed | integrations | Build. `request.erased@1` reserved. |

| Platform alerts | integrations | Build |
| Batching and rewinding outbound events; sending a call again; a connection test button; rotating the callback key; telling an outside job to stop; a Requester not in what the event sent; customer-defined connections; saving a connection while the server runs | integrations | Not built |
| Message waits (unsolicited input to a running request); starting a request on a schedule | 2, integrations | Not built. Nothing is reserved for them: wait kinds and trigger kinds are open lists. |
| CEL context and evaluation | 2 | Build |
| Turns: one input, one transaction, per-request lock; event order; the stuck state worked out from the state | 3 | Build |
| Faults: recorded, turn rolled back, inputs kept while faulted | 3 | Build |
| Admin turn: `retry` and `close` | 4 | Build |
| Every event type and the envelope | 5 | Build the shapes and `evolve` for all. `decide` produces `WaitSkipped` only in a retry of a stage with waits still open. |
| `StageEntered.parentActivation`; wait `seq` (always written as 1) | 5 | Build. `decide` writes them on every event; nothing reads more than one level or more than one instance. |
| A second active child stage; a wait `seq` above 1 | 2 | Shape only |
| Publish checks; publish writes every default explicitly; element IDs and the origin map | 6, 7 | Build |
| Notification rules (reading data as of the event, messages as words or parts, alerts to admins) and the notifier | 7, integrations | Build |
| Tables: `events`, `definitions`, `workflows`, `workflow_settings`, `settings_log`, `binding_pauses`, `drafts`, `start_tokens`, `requests`, `open_waits`, `pending_calls`, `notifications_sent`, `attempts_log`, `connections`, `secrets`, `catalogue_entries`, `trigger_deliveries`, `trigger_starts`, `inbound_log`, `call_log`, `outbound_events`, `subscriptions`, `subscription_deliveries`, `rule_errors`, `platform_alerts`; rebuild of projections from events | data model | Build |
| Connections, applied from configuration at start-up: user directory (`membersOf@1`, `groupMembers@1`, act-time membership), Jira (`createIssue@1`), email and Slack through the existing service, the `webhook-sink` connector; the connector interface; the mock systems (development and tests only) | integrations | Build |
| Mock outside systems for the dev host: directory, service catalog, helpdesk, Jira, deploy pipeline, email and Slack, reporting. Each is a small in-process server with real HTTP in and out, and is a catalogue entry like any other; platform code names none of them. | integrations | Build |
| Workflow `change-request-demo` and its test cases | workflows | Build. These are the acceptance tests. |
| An integrated sample workflow that passes through every door of `integrations.md` against the mock systems, with its cases | integrations | Build. Its definition and cases are kept with the authoring design, outside this package. |
| Cutover from the existing product, legacy import | architecture | Not built. The readable-ID range is held. |
| Restricting who can view a request | data model | Not built. Every signed-in user sees every request. |

## 4. Not in this package

The first release of the product also needs an authoring experience: an author builds a workflow without writing code, tries it, and publishes it. Its backend is designed outside this package (the authored format, how it compiles to a definition, drafts, the authoring API, trying a draft); `open-questions.md`, section 1, says which pieces and what each gives the engine. The engine's contract with it is narrow: a published definition (`kernel/kernel-spec.md`, section 2) goes in through the publish API and the publish checks, and the catalogue (`integrations.md`, section 8) comes out.

Also not here: page designs, and the reasoning and history behind the decisions. Where a reason matters to a builder, the doc states it in place.

## 5. Reading order

| # | File | What it gives you |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `architecture.md` | The components, how one input is processed, how the engine is tested. |
| 2 | `kernel/kernel-spec.md` | The rules, in full. The reference; terse on purpose. |
| 3 | `kernel/data-model.md` | Tables, keys, indexes, and the steps of a turn as one transaction. |
| 4 | `workflows/change-request-demo/` | The workflow the first build runs, and its test cases. |
| 5 | `integrations.md` | Directory, Jira, email and Slack, forms, sign-in and admins; then the exact shapes of connections, the catalogue, starts by outside events, await calls, act-time lookups, notifications, outbound events and alerts. |
| 6 | `open-questions.md` | Everything undecided, and who can answer it. |
| 7 | `kernel/replay-only.yaml` | Replay cases for stored state that `decide` does not produce yet. |

## 6. Layering

A level refers only to levels below it: `workflows/` -> `kernel/`. The kernel spec names no workflow. The kernel folder may cite `integrations.md` for blocks that `decide` never reads. Keep code the same way: the engine must not know what an approval is.

## 7. What counts as done for the first build

- Every case in `workflows/change-request-demo/test-cases.yaml` passes: the engine appends exactly the listed events, refuses the listed attempts, and the notifier matches the listed rules.
- Every case in `kernel/replay-only.yaml` passes.
- Every case of the integrated sample workflow passes against the mock systems, including its `publish` lines.
- Deleting a request's projection rows and replaying its events gives the same rows.

# Workflow engine: architecture

How the parts fit, against `kernel/kernel-spec.md` v2.20. The rules are in the kernel spec and the tables in `kernel/data-model.md`; this file does not repeat them.

## 1. Components

```
  pages (not in this package)
      |
  Engine API ............ start, act, admin turn, publish; reads for lists and the request page
      |
  decide / evolve ....... the kernel: pure functions over a definition and a request's events
      |
  Postgres .............. events, definitions (source of truth); read tables; working state; jobs
      |
  jobs .................. one per call (sends, polls an await); one notifier job and one publisher job per turn
      |
  connections ........... configured instances of connector code: directory, Jira, email and Slack,
                          and the in-memory mock systems in development
  hook .................. inbound events (start a request)
```

| Component | Does | Decided |
|---|---|---|
| Engine API | Accepts the four inputs and publish. Each input is one turn. Serves reads from the read tables and from a request's events. | Yes |
| `decide` | Given the definition, the request's state and one input: works out every consequence and returns it as events. Evaluates CEL. | Yes |
| `evolve` | Folds events into state. The only code replay uses. Never evaluates CEL, never reads a definition. | Yes |
| Publish | Compiles the authored workflow, runs the publish checks, stores an immutable definition version. | Yes |
| Read tables | `requests` and `open_waits`, updated in the same transaction as the events, rebuildable by replay. | Yes |
| Call job | One per call: sends it at least once with its recorded key, runs again while there is no clear answer, and polls an await. A result comes back as an input. | Yes |
| Notifier | A job per turn. Applies the definition's notification rules to that turn's events and sends through the existing email and Slack service. Not part of history. | Yes |
| Connections | Configured instances of connector code, one per outside system, read from configuration at start-up and held in memory. A workflow reaches one only through a call. The engine also reads the directory directly for the act-time membership check, the action-item list and the notifier's recipients, and reads data sources for choices and act-time lookups. | Yes: the connector interface and the catalogue, `integrations.md` section 8 |
| Inbound hook | Accepts outside events that start requests through trigger bindings. Authenticates, limits, logs every event in `inbound_log`. | Yes |
| Publisher | A job per turn turns the turn's committed events into public events and posts them, in the request's order, to the configured addresses. Not part of history. | Yes |
| Jobs | The engine's own table, written in the turn's transaction and taken by polling workers. | Yes |

## 2. One input, end to end

A person approves.

1. The API receives: request, wait, outcome, data, and the signed-in user.
2. Before any lock, the request's events are folded and the wait is checked to be open. The user's group memberships are looked up now, and each answer from a data source is looked up by its stored value. A lookup's result, or the failure to get it, is kept: a lookup that cannot be made refuses the act with 'try again' under the lock, at its place in the kernel's order, writing nothing. No outside call is made while a request is locked.
3. The turn opens a transaction, locks the request's row, loads and folds the request's events with `evolve` again, and checks that the wait is still open.
4. The input is validated: the memberships found against the wait's assignees and its `may` rule; the data fits the outcome's schema; each data-source answer takes the source's label; the outcome's checks pass. A refusal rolls back and writes one row to the attempts log.
5. `WaitCompleted` is appended, with the membership lookup and what each check read as evidence.
6. `decide` fires transitions until none is enabled and appends each consequence: which transition fired and what it read, data written, waits cancelled, stage exited, stage entered, waits opened with their resolved parameters.
7. The read tables are updated from the new events, the stuck state among them. Each opened call gets a pending-call row and a call job. One notifier job and one publisher job are inserted for the turn.
8. Commit.

Starting a request takes the same path: the starter acts on the start wait, a person wait of the first stage. The turn appends `RequestStarted`, enters the root and the first stage, opens its waits, completes the start wait, then decides as usual. The start wait's assignees are not checked at start; its `may`, checks and schema are. A refused start leaves no request.

After the commit the call job sends any call, and its result returns as a new input and a new turn. The notifier job reads the turn's events and sends what the rules match.

`kernel/data-model.md`, section 1, gives the same steps against the tables.

## 3. Rules that shape the code

- **`decide` records, `evolve` replays.** Every consequence is spelled out as events, so replaying a history never re-runs workflow logic and never needs the definition. The cost: a bug in `decide` is recorded as fact. It is repaired by an admin turn, never by rewriting history.
- **No unsolicited input.** Every inbound fact closes a wait the engine opened, or starts a request through a live trigger binding. There are no signals and no correlation keys: the engine asks about an outside job it started, and nothing outside can answer a call unasked.
- **Conditions read recorded state.** A join such as "all approved" is an expression over the waits in the stage, checked after every input. There are no trigger events.
- **No clock.** Each event carries its timestamp; that is the only time the engine knows. `decide` never asks what time it is.
- **Outside data enters as recorded results.** A call's result, the act-time membership lookup and the act-time data-source lookup are written into history when they arrive. `decide` and `evolve` never read live data.
- **Errors never count as false.** A failed expression, or a failed call that the workflow did not opt to handle, rolls the turn back and faults the request.
- **Stuck is worked out, not recorded.** It is one function of the request's state after a turn (`integrations.md` section 11.5); every reader uses it.
- **Results belong to one entry of a stage.** Re-entering a stage gives fresh waits. Anything that must persist is written to the request's data.
- **Pages key on a stage's status ID, not its stage ID or label.** Stage IDs may change between definition versions; `StageEntered` records the status as `{id, label}`.
- **Values are never null.** A data path is present or absent.

## 4. Definitions and versions

- A definition is JSON, stored in the database, published through the API. Publishing needs no deployment.
- A published version is immutable. A request stays on the version it started on. A start names the version whose start form was shown. Any published version can be started, so a publish while someone is filling in the form rejects nothing. A start that names no version uses the highest.
- The published definition format and its CEL environment are a long-lived contract: the engine must run a version for as long as a request on it is open. Publish writes every default explicitly; the CEL library and the form-schema validator are fixed per definition format; operations are versioned (`createIssue@1`) and an op version never changes.

The definition files in `workflows/` are written in a short notation for people. The concrete JSON of a published definition (format 1) and of each event payload is designed outside this package, field for field as spec sections 2 and 5 and `integrations.md` section 7.3 name them (`open-questions.md`, section 3).

## 5. People and permissions

- **Who may act** is decided when they act, from a live membership lookup, and recorded as evidence.
- **Who is being asked** is recorded when the wait opens, as user and group references that are not expanded. A reference's ID is the directory's immutable object ID. The list may be empty: the wait still opens, the request waits and is stuck with `nobody-to-ask`, and the default rule `n_stopped` tells the workflow admins (`integrations.md` sections 11.5 and 12.1). So does a task that nobody can answer: who can answer is the people asked directly plus the recorded members of the groups asked, minus the Requester where the Requester may not answer, as the definition's `nobodyToAsk` block states it. A failed membership read contributes nobody from its groups; a person asked directly still counts. A person who may not answer a task is not told about it.
- **Action items** for a person are the open person waits marked as obligations whose assignees name them or a group they belong to now.
- **Viewing:** every signed-in user can see every request.
- **Admins** of a request are the holders of an existing platform-admin entitlement and that workflow's admins, a per-workflow setting outside the published definition (`integrations.md`, section 6). An admin turn records who acted and their reason.

## 6. Testing

The test cases are the engine's first tests and its acceptance criteria.

| Test | Source | Checks |
|---|---|---|
| Workflow cases | `workflows/change-request-demo/test-cases.yaml` | For each input: the exact events appended, in order, or the refusal; the notification rules matched. Connectors are faked from the fixtures. |
| Replay-only cases | `kernel/replay-only.yaml` | `evolve` folds stored histories that `decide` does not write today. |
| Rebuild | any workflow case | Rebuilding a request's read-table rows from its events gives identical rows. |
| Catalogue snapshot | every declared entry | An entry's shape has not changed under its ID (`integrations.md` section 8.6). |

The cases inject call results as inputs, so they do not cover the parts below. Each needs its own tests:

- the call job: a duplicate result, a call whose wait closed before it was sent, a write whose wait closed after an `unknown` answer (kept, sent again), and a read in the same state (dropped);
- the stuck state and the 50-firing limit;
- the action-item query;
- each publish check, with a definition that fails it;
- the real connectors.

Integration cases drive every inbound event through the real hook with real signatures, against the in-memory mock systems. They include: a bad signature (401, nothing processed); a timestamp 301 s old or 301 s ahead (401); the same event twice (`duplicate`); a paused binding (`paused`, nothing kept); a person who sends `requester`, at the start or on a sent-back start form (refused, `invalid-data`); a ticket's reporter refused on their own request's approval after a connection start (`may`); a data-source answer with a forged label (the source's label is recorded) and with an unknown item (`choice-unknown`); the directory down when a person acts (`membership-unavailable`), and on a wait already closed (`wait-not-open`); a task with nobody to ask (published as stuck); a person start and a choices call. Each turn's outbound events are asserted by `id`, order, `time` and payload.

Cases that test concurrency (two deliveries of one event at once) run on real Postgres with two connections; PGlite serves one connection and cannot interleave transactions. Jobs and signature checks read the time from an injected clock that the test host advances.

## 7. Development host

The dev host is the server itself, on PGlite, with the in-memory mock connectors, a seeded directory and the development sign-in. One command starts it, and it serves both APIs on one port.
===\nengine/spec/integrations.md\n===
# Workflow engine: integrations

What the engine touches outside itself, against `kernel/kernel-spec.md` v2.20. Sections 1 to 6 say how the engine uses what already exists in the application it is built into: the directory, Jira, email and Slack, forms, sign-in. Sections 7 to 14 give the exact shapes of every integration in the first build: connections and their catalogue, a request started by an outside event, calls, act-time lookups, notifications, outbound events and alerts. Each door is built in its thinnest working form. The details that need the existing codebase are in `open-questions.md`, section 2.

## 1. Connectors

A connector is code: the engine's adapter to one kind of outside system. A connection is a configured instance of a connector (address, credentials, defaults), written in the deployment's configuration; its ID is recorded, the connector never is. A workflow reaches a connection through a call wait (`kernel/kernel-spec.md`, section 2): the call's connection, operation and arguments are recorded when the wait opens, a job sends it, and the result is recorded when it arrives. Replay never calls out.

Every connector must:

- **Never report "don't know" as failed.** A timeout or an unclear answer keeps the call pending; the job runs again. `failed` means the system clearly refused.
- **Declare its operations** in the catalogue (section 8), each named with a version (`createIssue@1`), with its fields. An op version's shapes never change; a change is a new op version.
- **Return one of four answers:** ok with data, failed with `{code, message}`, unknown, or, for an operation of sort await only, accepted with the outside job's reference. Unknown and accepted are never recorded; an accepted call is not sent again; its result is asked for by key and job reference.
- **Honour the idempotency key**, as the kernel spec says. For an await operation: start at most one job per key; for a key whose job failed, start a new one; name the job in every answer.

The Jira connector is a deliberate exception to the idempotency rule (section 3).

## 2. User directory

Used in these places:

| Use | How | Recorded |
|---|---|---|
| Who is in a group, for a workflow | A read call to the directory connection, `membersOf@1 { groups }` with group references, returning `{ groups: [ { id, members } ] }`, `id` a group reference and `members` user references (section 8.7). The membership read of a task that may ask a group, and a `members` step or an "is in group" test inside a condition, are such reads (section 11.5). "People in [group]" under who is asked asks the group itself and makes no read of its own. | As the call's result. |
| May this person act | A live lookup of the actor's group memberships (`groupsOf { user }`) when they act, outside any call wait. | As `evidence` on `WaitCompleted`. |
| Choices that are a group's members | The data source `groupMembers@1`, listed live when the form is shown and looked up by stored value when the person acts (section 11). | The answer, and the lookup in `evidence`. |
| Action items | A live lookup of the viewer's groups when the list is read. | Not recorded; it is a read. |

If the membership lookup cannot be made when a person acts, the act is refused with `membership-unavailable` and nothing changes; the person may try again, and a log line is written (section 14). The lookup is made before the request is locked (section 11.1).

The notifier also asks the directory for a group's members when it sends to a group. A people picker on a form also searches the directory. That is a page concern, not the engine's.

The order of `members` is whatever the directory returns. A workflow that takes the first member accepts that.

User and group IDs are the directory's immutable object IDs, never an email or a name. A reference is `{ type, id }`.

## 3. Jira

One operation, `jira.createIssue@1`, a write call. Result `{ key, url }`.

- **A plain create, with no duplicate check.** The connector does not look for an earlier issue before creating one. This knowingly breaks the idempotency rule above.
  - A retry after a clear failure is safe.
  - If Jira created the issue but the result was lost, the job's next try creates a second issue. That is accepted as rare; an admin closes the extra by hand. If the first result arrives late, its key is in history as a late result.
  - A later re-entry of the stage after a successful create creates a second issue, whatever the key.
  - Later fix if needed: a label holding the request ID, searched before creating.
- **A failed create faults the request.** An admin retries (clears the fault and re-enters the stage) or closes the request.
- **The description is an argument like any other:** text the workflow builds from its values.
- **Field mapping is a placeholder.** The demo passes project, summary, assignee and description. `assignee` is a user reference; the connector maps it to a Jira account.

## 4. Email and Slack

The notifier sends through the application's existing email and Slack service. A notification rule names its message (a key of the platform's words, or the author's text and values as parts) and its recipients (section 12). It sends to users and to the members of groups and skips any other reference. A crash while a turn's notifications are sent can send some twice; that is accepted.

A notification is never a call wait and never in a request's history. A workflow cannot wait on one.

## 5. Forms

The engine never renders a form. It touches form data in one place: the data given with a person wait's outcome. Starting a request is acting on the start wait, so the start form is the same case. The engine validates the data against the outcome's schema, runs the outcome's checks, and records it.

- The schema format is JSON Schema. The validator and its settings (no coercion, no removal of unknown fields) are fixed per definition format.
- A published definition pins the schema versions it uses (`definitions.schemas`).
- A form never submits null: an optional answer left empty is absent. A date is `YYYY-MM-DD`. A number is always read in CEL as a `double`.
- Conditional questions, conditional required and choices that come from an expression are outcome checks (`kernel/kernel-spec.md`, section 2). A page may ask which checks fail as a preview; the act-time check is authoritative.
- Whoever owns forms supplies the schema, an immutable version of it, and a renderer. The engine must keep working if a separate application takes over forms.
- A form causes no workflow effect before it is submitted.

A question's choices may come from a data source, the directory's members of a group included: the page asks for them by question, and the engine looks the answer up again when the person acts, as the outcome's `lookups` in the published definition say (section 11).

## 6. Sign-in and admins

- Any signed-in user may start a request, subject to the start wait's `may` and checks. A connection may start one through a live trigger binding (section 9); it is then the starter. The start wait's assignees are not checked at start.
- The engine does not sign anyone in. The application supplies the signed-in user with each API call; the engine records them as `by: { type: user, id }`, with the directory's immutable object ID.
- An admin turn on a request may be submitted by a holder of the application's existing platform-admin entitlement, or by one of that request's workflow admins. The engine checks this when the turn is submitted.
- The workflow admins are a per-workflow setting (users and groups, `workflow_settings.stuck_requests_go_to`, "Stuck requests go to"), kept outside the published definition and not versioned. It defaults to the workflow's authors. The stuck message (`n_stopped`, section 12.1) goes to them. Every change to a workflow's settings, a binding's pause included, is recorded with who and when (`settings_log`).
- The first build offers workflow admins two actions on a request: Retry (clear the fault, if any, and re-enter the stage), offered only for a request stuck with `action-failed` or `nobody-to-ask` (section 11.5), and Close, offered for any open request. For door 1 they may also pause and resume a binding, and list and run again refused starts (section 9.10).
- An admin may act on any request they administer, including their own. Accountability is the recorded name and reason.
- Connections and the engine itself act as `{ type: connection, id }` (the connection ID) and `{ type: system, id: engine }`.

## The exact shapes (sections 7 to 14)

The engine reaches outside systems through seven doors. Nothing enters a request's history any other way.

| # | Door | Direction | What it is in the engine | Section |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Start | In | The start input: a person submits the start form, or an outside system's event is mapped onto it by a trigger binding. | 9 |
| 2 | Act | In | A person completes a person wait. | 11 |
| 3 | Call | Out, result back in | A call wait: read, write, or await (ask an outside system to do something and ask about it until it reports the result). The request and the result are both recorded. | 10 |
| 4 | Membership | In | A live directory lookup when a person acts, recorded as evidence. | 11 |
| 5 | Choices | In | Data for a question's choices, read when the form is shown and looked up again when the person acts. | 11 |
| 6 | Notification | Out | The notifier applies notification rules to committed events. Not in history; nothing can wait on it. | 12 |
| 7 | Event out | Out | The publisher turns committed history into public events and posts them to the configured addresses. Not in history; nothing can wait on it. | 13 |

An outside event can start a request (door 1). It cannot reach a running request any other way. "Wait for system X" is an await call: the engine asks, so it can also check on it. Pages also read live data that is recorded nowhere (people search, choices while a form is open, names for display); nothing they return enters history except through door 2 or door 5. "Try it" below is the editor's test run of a draft, which uses each entry's samples instead of the connection.

Conventions:

- **Fixed** marks a shape that is kept forever or held by an outside party. A Fixed JSON body may gain fields; no field is removed, renamed or retyped. A Fixed enum may gain values.
- `{base}` is where the host mounts the engine's API. `{hooks}` is the engine's public base URL for outside systems. Where both are mounted in the existing application, and how the hooks are reachable over TLS: unknown: depends on the existing application.
- Codes (refusal reasons, causes, error codes, log line kinds) are kebab-case. Type discriminators are lowerCamelCase.
- "Workflow admins" are `workflow_settings.stuck_requests_go_to`, or the workflow's `authors` when it is null or empty. "Platform admins" are holders of the existing platform-admin entitlement.
- Jobs read the time from an injected clock. The test host advances it. `decide` and `evolve` have no clock.

Shared types:

```ts
type Json = string | number | boolean | Json[] | { [key: string]: Json };   // never null in data
type JsonObject = { [key: string]: Json };
type Cel = string;                                  // CEL source text, profile cel-1
interface By { type: "user" | "connection" | "system" | (string & {}); id: string }
interface Ref { type: "user" | "group" | (string & {}); id: string }   // the directory's immutable object ID
// A person or group anywhere in a request's data (answers, saved results, the Requester, values told
// to other systems) is a Ref, never a bare ID string. Connectors map an outside system's own terms to it.
interface StatusRef { id: string; label: string }
interface Location { item: string; part?: string }  // a place in the authored workflow: an item ID and a part
```

## 7. Names and IDs

### 7.1 Connection ID (Fixed)

| Rule | Value |
|---|---|
| Pattern | `^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{1,39}$` |
| Reserved, refused at start-up | `engine`, `system`, `platform` |
| Chosen by | The platform admin who writes the connection in the configuration |
| Changes | Never renamed, never reused. |
| Recorded in | `by.id` with `by.type: "connection"`; a call wait's `connection`; `RequestStarted.trigger.connection`; catalogue IDs; the inbound hook URL |

### 7.2 Catalogue ID (Fixed)

```
<connection>.<name>@<version>
name    = ^[a-z][A-Za-z0-9]{0,63}$          lowerCamelCase: createIssue, membersOf, ticketCreated
version = ^[1-9][0-9]{0,8}$
full    = ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{1,39}\.[a-z][A-Za-z0-9]{0,63}@[1-9][0-9]{0,8}$
```

The published definition and events never store the full ID. They store the connection and `<name>@<version>` in separate fields: a call wait's `connection` and `op`; a binding's and a trigger's `connection` and `event`. An ID never names a second shape (section 8.6).

### 7.3 Event fields that integrations write (Fixed, `v: 1`)

Spec section 5 lists every payload. The integration parts:

```ts
// RequestStarted
  by: By;                              // { type: "user" } for a person; { type: "connection" } for a binding
  trigger: EventTrigger | null;        // null when a person started the request

interface EventTrigger {
  kind: "event";                       // an open enum
  id: string;          // the binding's ID in the triggers block of the request's version (the authored sw_ ID)
  connection: string;  // the connection ID; equals by.id
  event: string;       // the catalogue trigger, "<name>@<version>": "ticketCreated@1"
  eventId: string;     // the sender's ID for this occurrence, 1 to 255 characters
}

// WaitOpened of a call
  connection: string; op: string;      // "createIssue@1"
  effect: "read" | "write" | (string & {});
  args: JsonObject;                    // an argument whose expression returned optional.none() is absent
  idempotencyKey: string;

// WaitCompleted
  by: By;                              // a call: { type: "connection", id: <connection ID> }
  evidence: Evidence | null;           // null for a call

interface Evidence {
  memberOf: string[];                  // assignee group IDs the actor belongs to; [] at a start
  checks: { id: string; reads: Read[] }[];   // each check that ran, in order
  lookups: LookupFound[];              // one per data-source answer looked up, in the outcome's lookups order; [] when none
}
interface LookupFound {
  property: string;                    // the outcome's data property: the question ID
  connection: string;
  source: string;                      // "<name>@<version>" of the data source
  inputs: JsonObject;                  // the inputs as evaluated for this act
  stored: string | number;             // what was looked up
  label: string | null;                // what was found: the item's labelField value; null for answer "person" (section 11.2)
}

type Read =                            // on TransitionFired.reads and on each check in evidence
  | { path: (string | number)[]; value: Json }
  | { path: (string | number)[]; absent: true };
```

### 7.4 Other names

| Name | Form | Kept by |
|---|---|---|
| Binding ID | The authored `StartsWhen.id` (`sw_...`) | `RequestStarted.trigger.id`, `inbound_log`, `workflow_settings.paused_bindings` |
| Thing told | The authored `ThingTold.id` (`told_...`) | `request.told@1` payloads |
| Platform outbound rule ID | `$request.started`, `$request.statusChanged`, `$request.stuck`, `$request.unstuck`, `$request.ended` | Outbound event `id` |
| Declared outbound rule ID | The authored action ID (`act_...`) | Same |
| Data key, path segment, schema property, catalogue field ID, told value name | Never starts with `$`. Field IDs and value names match `^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_]{0,63}$`. | History, payloads |
| Start answer `requester` | The one compiler-owned top-level key whose value a connection may supply as a start answer. Its value is a user `Ref`. | History |
| Membership read of a task | `<task ID>__members`, a call wait the compiler declares beside the task in the task's own engine stage (section 11.5) | History (`WaitOpened`, `WaitCompleted`) |
| Nobody-to-ask rule | `<full element ID of the person wait>__nobody`, in the `nobodyToAsk` block (section 11.5): `st_fix_deployment__tasks.tk_fix_deployment__nobody` | Published definition |
| Derived idempotency key | `<request ID>/<element ID>@<activation>#<seq>` (spec section 2, Call): readable text naming the request and the wait instance | History (`WaitOpened.idempotencyKey`) |
| "Once" key | `'once.' + request.id + '.' + '<action ID>'`, the explicit `idempotencyKey` of an action whose "when the stage is entered again" is "once" (section 10.1) | History (`WaitOpened.idempotencyKey`) |
| Stuck reason | `action-failed`, `nobody-to-ask`, `nothing-fits`, `error` | `request.stuck@1`, `request.unstuck@1`, the request view and lists |

## 8. Catalogue and connections

### 8.1 Field

A catalogue field. `kind` is one of the authored format's value kinds (`ValueKind`).

```ts
type ValueKind =                    // the authored format's value kinds
  | "text" | "longText" | "number" | "yesNo" | "date" | "choice" | "multipleChoice" | "person" | "group"
  | "choiceFromList" | "choiceFromConnection" | "people" | "list" | "fieldGroup";

interface Field {
  id: string;                 // ^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_]{0,63}$; unique among its siblings
  label: string;
  kind: Exclude<ValueKind, "choiceFromList">;   // a list kept with a workflow cannot come from outside
  required: boolean;          // false: the key may be absent; it is never null
  choices?: { value: string; label: string }[];  // exactly for choice and multipleChoice; values unique
  itemKind?: ValueKind;       // list only: the kind of each item; exactly one of itemKind and fields
  fields?: Field[];           // list of objects, or fieldGroup
  addressOf?: string;         // display only: this field is the web address of the sibling field it names
}
```

### 8.2 Entries (Fixed for every field the shape covers, section 8.6)

```ts
type CatalogueEntry = Operation | DataSource | Trigger | EventSink;

interface EntryBase {
  id: string;                          // "<connection>.<name>@<version>"
  connection: string;
  name: string;
  version: number;
  kind: "operation" | "dataSource" | "trigger" | "eventSink";
  label: string;
  description: string | null;
  supersededBy: string | null;         // a newer entry ID; published workflows keep running on this one
  status: "ready" | "disabled";        // always "ready" in the first build
}

interface Operation extends EntryBase {
  kind: "operation";
  sort: "read" | "write" | "await";    // read: "Look up"; write: "Do"; await: "Wait for"
  input: Field[];
  result: Field[];
  failureCodes: { code: string; label: string }[];   // code: ^[a-z][a-z0-9]*(-[a-z0-9]+)*$, unique
  onRepeat: "once" | "again" | null;   // the default for "when the stage is entered again": write and await; null for read
  timeoutSeconds: number;              // one send or one status question; default 30
  expectedWithinSeconds: number;       // a call with no result after this writes call-overdue log lines; default 900 for read and write; required for await
  await: null | {                      // non-null exactly when sort is "await"
    callback: boolean;                 // not used in the first build: the engine polls
    pollSeconds: number;               // required: every await op answers a status question; at least 10
  };
  sample: {
    input: JsonObject;                 // fits input
    result: JsonObject;                // fits result
    failure: { code: string; message: string } | null;   // code is one of failureCodes
  };
}

interface DataSource extends EntryBase {
  kind: "dataSource";
  input: Field[];                      // arguments, e.g. a filter or a parent choice
  item: Field[];                       // one item; a question names its stored and label fields
  searchable: boolean;                 // list accepts a search text
  cacheSeconds: number;                // list results only; default 60; 0 = never cached
  timeoutSeconds: number;              // one list or get; default 10
  sample: { input: JsonObject; items: JsonObject[] };
}

interface Trigger extends EntryBase {
  kind: "trigger";
  event: Field[];                      // what a binding reads as sent.<field>; a person field holds a user Ref
  sample: { event: JsonObject };
}

interface EventSink extends EntryBase {
  kind: "eventSink";                   // display only: shows the editor which systems receive outbound events
}
```

A connector declares entries without `id`, `connection` and `status`; start-up fills them and writes every defaulted field explicitly, so the catalogue served has no defaults.

### 8.3 JSON Schema derived from `Field[]`

`input`, `result`, `item` and `event` are each an object of fields. Profile `jsonschema-1` (dialect 2020-12, no coercion, no defaults applied). The same mapping types call arguments, results, items, trigger events and form data, so the editor, the type checker and the validator cannot disagree.

| Kind | JSON Schema |
|---|---|
| Object of fields | `{"type":"object","additionalProperties":false,"required":[<ids of required fields>],"properties":{<id>: <schema of the field>}}` |
| `text`, `longText` | `{"type":"string"}` |
| `number` | `{"type":"number"}`. Read in CEL as `double`; an integer must lie within +/-(2^53 - 1). |
| `yesNo` | `{"type":"boolean"}` |
| `date` | `{"type":"string","format":"date"}` |
| `choice` | `{"type":"string","enum":[<choices values>]}` |
| `multipleChoice` | `{"type":"array","items":{"type":"string","enum":[<choices values>]},"uniqueItems":true}` |
| `person` | `{"type":"object","additionalProperties":false,"required":["type","id"],"properties":{"type":{"const":"user"},"id":{"type":"string","format":"directory-object-id"}}}`: a user `Ref` |
| `group` | The same with `{"const":"group"}`: a group `Ref` |
| `people` | `{"type":"array","items":<the person schema>,"uniqueItems":true}` |
| `choiceFromConnection` | `{"type":"object","additionalProperties":false,"required":["stored","label"],"properties":{"stored":{"type":["string","number"]},"label":{"type":"string"}}}` |
| `list` | `{"type":"array","items":<schema of itemKind, or object of fields>}` |
| `fieldGroup` | Object of `fields` |
| `choiceFromList` | Not allowed in a catalogue field. |

Property names come from field IDs, so none starts with `$`. A connector answer whose data does not fit, including one that holds a key starting with `$`, is never recorded (sections 10.2, 10.3).

### 8.4 Start-up checks

Connections and their entries are read from the deployment's configuration at server start-up, the only time they are applied, and held in memory. Any failing check stops start-up.

- Field IDs match their pattern and are unique per level; `choices`, `itemKind` and `fields` appear exactly where section 8.1 says.
- `sort: "await"` has a non-null `await`; any other sort has `await: null`. `onRepeat` is null exactly for `read`.
- `failureCodes` codes are kebab-case and unique.
- Every sample validates against its derived schema; `sample.failure.code` is a failure code.
- `expectedWithinSeconds` is at least `timeoutSeconds`.
- The connector implements what its entries need (section 8.5): `call` for every operation, `status` as well for an await operation, `list` and `get` for a data source, `verify` and `parse` for a trigger.
- The connection named by the platform setting `directoryConnection` declares `membersOf@1` and `groupMembers@1` with the shapes in section 8.7.
- The platform setting `notifyConnection` names a configured connection.

### 8.5 Connector interface (code; cheap except where it states an outside promise)

```ts
interface Connector {
  name: string;                                   // the code's identity, e.g. "jira-cloud"; never recorded
  config: Field[];                                // non-secret settings in the configuration
  secrets: string[];                              // slot names: "apiToken", "inbound", ...
  entries(config: JsonObject): EntryDeclaration[];

  // door 3: every operation
  call?(ctx: Ctx, req: CallRequest): Promise<CallAnswer>;
  // door 3: every await operation (required for sort "await")
  status?(ctx: Ctx, req: StatusRequest): Promise<StatusAnswer>;
  // door 5: every data source (both required)
  list?(ctx: Ctx, req: ListRequest): Promise<ListAnswer>;
  get?(ctx: Ctx, req: GetRequest): Promise<GetAnswer>;
  // door 1: every connection with a trigger entry (both required)
  verify?(ctx: Ctx, req: RawRequest): Promise<VerifyAnswer>;
  parse?(ctx: Ctx, req: RawRequest): Promise<ParseAnswer>;
}
type EntryDeclaration = Omit<CatalogueEntry, "id" | "connection" | "status">;   // defaulted fields may be omitted

interface Ctx {
  connection: string;
  config: JsonObject;
  secret(slot: string): string;                       // from the configuration's environment
  http: HttpClient;                                   // bound to the entry's timeoutSeconds
  directory: { findUser(q: { email?: string; externalId?: string }): Promise<"unavailable" | string | null> };
  now(): Date;                                        // the injected clock
}

interface CallRequest {
  op: string;                    // "<name>@<version>"
  args: JsonObject;              // as recorded in WaitOpened
  key: string;                   // the recorded idempotency key
}
type CallAnswer =
  | { answer: "ok"; data: JsonObject; jobRef?: string }             // jobRef required for an await op
  | { answer: "failed"; code: string; message: string; jobRef?: string }   // jobRef required for an await op
  | { answer: "unknown"; detail: string }                            // timeout, 5xx, unclear: never recorded
  | { answer: "accepted"; jobRef: string };                          // await ops only; the job runs on

interface StatusRequest { op: string; key: string; jobRef: string }
type StatusAnswer =
  | { answer: "ok"; data: JsonObject; jobRef: string }
  | { answer: "failed"; code: string; message: string; jobRef: string }
  | { answer: "running"; jobRef: string }
  | { answer: "unknown"; detail: string };

interface ListRequest { source: string; inputs: JsonObject; search: string | null; cursor: string | null; limit: number }
type ListAnswer =
  | { answer: "ok"; items: JsonObject[]; next: string | null }       // next: an opaque cursor
  | { answer: "unavailable"; detail: string };

interface GetRequest { source: string; inputs: JsonObject; field: string; value: string | number }
type GetAnswer =
  | { answer: "found"; item: JsonObject }    // an item that list(inputs) would return, whose field equals value
  | { answer: "notFound" }
  | { answer: "unavailable"; detail: string };

interface RawRequest { method: string; headers: { [lowerCaseName: string]: string }; body: Uint8Array }   // body at most 256 KiB
type VerifyAnswer = { answer: "ok" } | { answer: "refused"; code: "bad-signature" | "stale" | "unsigned" };
type ParseAnswer =
  | { answer: "events"; eventId: string; events: { [nameAtVersion: string]: JsonObject } }   // one per trigger version served
  | { answer: "ignored"; eventId: string | null; detail: string }   // an event kind the connector does not map
  | { answer: "unparsable"; detail: string }
  | { answer: "unavailable"; detail: string };                      // the directory could not resolve a person now
```

Promises every connector makes (outside promises, Fixed):

| Kind | Promise |
|---|---|
| Every | Data it returns fits the entry's schema. A timeout or "don't know" is `unknown`, never `failed`. It never logs a secret. |
| read | No outside effect. |
| write | Honour the key: for a key that succeeded, return that result and do nothing else; for a key that failed, act again. The demo's Jira create is the one documented exception (section 3). |
| await | Start at most one job per key. For a key whose job succeeded, answer that result; for a key whose job failed, or with no known job, start a new job under the same key. Every `ok`, `failed`, `accepted` and `running` names the job (`jobRef`, 1 to 255 characters). `status(key, jobRef)` answers about that job only. |
| dataSource | No outside effect. `get` finds an item only if `list` with the same inputs would return it. Stored values are stable identifiers. |
| trigger | `verify` before `parse`. Verifying is the connector's job: it checks the sending system's own scheme. Where that scheme carries a signed timestamp, one more than 300 s from `ctx.now()`, before or after, is refused (`stale`). `eventId` is the same on every redelivery of one occurrence and unique per occurrence within the connection; a longer ID is replaced by `"sha256:" + hex(SHA-256(id))`. A person field holds `{type: "user", id}` with the ID found with `ctx.directory.findUser`, or is absent when none is found; the directory being down is `unavailable`. |
| dataSource of the directory | `groupMembers@1` items are the users who are members of the group now. |

### 8.6 An entry's shape never changes under its ID

The shape of an entry is, for an operation, `{kind, sort, input, result, failureCodes}`; for a data source, `{kind, input, item, searchable}`; for a trigger, `{kind, event}`; for an event sink, `{kind}`; each with every `label` removed at any depth. A snapshot test over every declared entry fails the build when a shape changes under an existing ID. Every other part of an entry (labels, `description`, `supersededBy`, `onRepeat`, the timings, `await`, `cacheSeconds`, `sample`) may change under one ID. `onRepeat` changes only later publishes, because publish writes the key choice explicitly.

### 8.7 Connections and who sets one up

A platform admin, never an author:

1. An engineer writes or reuses a connector and registers it in the server's connector registry; production and the dev host register different sets, and platform code names none of them.
2. A platform admin writes the connection in the deployment's configuration (ID, connector, label, `config`, `status`) and its secrets in the environment the configuration names. The server reads them at start-up only and keeps them in memory; there is no table, no save path and no screen. Status values: `notSetUp` (listed to authors, unusable), `ready`, `disabled`.
3. Authors see `ready` and `notSetUp` connections and every entry in the catalogue. Every author may use every ready entry in the first build.

The directory is a connection like any other; a platform setting names it (`directoryConnection`). Its connector also implements `groupsOf(user)`, `membersOf(groups)`, `search` and `lookup` for the engine's own lookups and for pages; the existing application's directory API: unknown: depends on the existing application. It must declare two entries, with these shapes, because the compiler emits them:

| Entry | Kind | Input | Output | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `membersOf@1` | operation, read | `groups`: list of `group` | `groups`: list of `{id: group, name?: text, members: people}`; `name` is the group's name as the directory lists it | A recorded read: the membership read of a task that may ask a group (section 11.5); a `members` step or an "is in group" test inside a condition (section 11.2) |
| `groupMembers@1` | dataSource, searchable | `group`: `group`, required | item `{id: text, name: text, email?: text}` | Choices that come from the directory (`from: "directory"`): read live when the form is shown and looked up by `id` at act time (section 11.3) |

Notify goes through a connection a second platform setting names (`notifyConnection`). The notifier uses it through the message-service adapter; a workflow never names it. The existing application's message service: unknown: depends on the existing application.

Event sinks: the configuration lists the addresses outbound events are posted to (section 13.4). An `eventSink` entry only shows the editor which systems receive them.

### 8.8 The catalogue served to the editor

`GET {base}/catalogue` returns:

```ts
interface Catalogue {
  version: string;                  // "cat1." + base64url(SHA-256(JCS({ connections, entries, directoryConnection, notifyConnection })))
  connections: { id: string; label: string; description: string | null; status: "ready" | "notSetUp" | "disabled" }[];
  entries: CatalogueEntry[];        // every entry of every connection, defaults written
  directoryConnection: string;      // the platform setting (section 8.7); `compile` is pure and learns it here
  notifyConnection: string;         // the platform setting (section 8.7): the connection that carries Notify
}
```

Both settings are always present. The version covers them, so changing either gives a new version. It is worked out at start-up.

A check result names the catalogue `version` it used. Publish: an entry of a `notSetUp` connection is a To do (`catalogue.connectionNotSetUp`); of a `disabled` one, Worth knowing (`catalogue.connectionDisabled`). Finding codes pass only between the core and the editor and keep the editor's spelling.

## 9. Door 1: a request started by an outside event

### 9.1 The `triggers` block (Fixed)

An optional top-level key of the published definition, beside `notifications`. `decide` never reads it.

```ts
interface PublishedDefinition {
  // ... format 1 fields ...
  triggers?: TriggerBinding[];      // declared order = the authored startsWhen order; absent when empty
}

interface TriggerBinding {
  id: string;                       // the authored StartsWhen ID
  connection: string;
  event: string;                    // "<name>@<version>" of a trigger entry of that connection
  when: Cel;                        // boolean; from onlyWhen; "true" when there is none
  outcome: string;                  // the start wait's outcome: the button the binding presses
  data: { [property: string]: Cel };  // the start outcome's data; from answers, and requester as the key "requester"
}
```

- `data` keys are property names of the outcome's schema. An expression may return an optional; `optional.none()` leaves the key absent.
- The mapping of a question that has a "Show when" is wrapped in it: `(<the Show when, each answer it reads replaced by that answer's mapping>) ? <mapping> : optional.none()`. A question hidden by what was sent therefore arrives empty, as a hidden question must.
- The authored `requester` (a `sentField` of kind person) compiles to `data.requester`. A binding with no `requester` writes no such key.
- The origin map gains `trigger:<binding ID>`, pointing at the authored `StartsWhen`.

### 9.2 The binding's CEL environment

| Name | Type | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| `sent` | The trigger entry's event fields, typed by section 8.3 | What the other system sent, for this binding's `event` version, people already resolved |
| Each constant | As declared | The definition's `constants`, where the compiler writes the workflow's lists |

Nothing else: no `data`, `request`, `actor`, `waits`, no clock, no I/O. The mapping is a pure function of what was sent, so Try it, a redelivery and a run again compute the same input. It runs before the turn, outside `decide`: a mapping error refuses the start and never faults a request.

### 9.3 Which bindings are live; pausing one

- Live: the bindings of each workflow's highest published version, read when the event is processed. A publish that removes a binding stops it. An earlier version's bindings are never live.
- The start runs on the version whose binding matched: mapping, schema, `may` and checks all come from it.
- A workflow admin pauses or resumes a binding without publishing: `workflow_settings.paused_bindings` holds binding IDs, and each pause and resume is a `settings_log` row with who and when. Not versioned; effective for the next event. An event a paused binding would take is refused: the answer is `paused`, decided before the mapping runs, and later bindings of that workflow are not tried. It is a refused start like any other, with reason `paused`: its `inbound_log` row keeps it, it is listed with the refused starts, and "run again" starts its request once the binding is resumed. The outside system need not send it again.
- The paused-deliveries list is always empty, and a resume runs nothing again: `rerun` and `gone` are 0.
- A platform admin disables a whole connection in configuration (`status: disabled`, applied at start-up); the hook then answers 503 so the sender keeps its events and retries.

### 9.4 The starter and the Requester

- The starter is the connection: `by: {type: "connection", id}` in `RequestStarted.by`, the start wait's `WaitCompleted.by`, `request.by` and `actor` in the start turn, and `requests.started_by`.
- The Requester a binding names is the start answer `requester`: a user `Ref`, `{type: "user", id}`. Only a connection may supply it. The compiler adds, to every outcome of the start wait whose schema has `requester`, the check

  ```
  id:      <start task ID>__requester
  when:    actor.type == 'connection' || !has(input.requester)
  message: ""          (compiler-added; the editor words it by code and location)
  ```

  A person who sends `requester`, at the start or when the request is sent back to the start form, is refused with `invalid-data` (`unknown-question`, location the start task): the check is how the compiler enforces it, and a refusal names no compiled check.
- The compiler emits, on every transition that leaves the start stage after the start wait completes, the Set `requester = waits.<start>.data.?requester.or(data.?requester)`. A resubmission by a person therefore keeps the value; a person's start sets nothing.
- The authored `{request: "requester"}` compiles to the optional `REQ` = `data.?requester.or(request.by.type == 'user' ? optional.of(request.by) : optional.none())`, a user `Ref`. For a connection start with no Requester it is empty, so `ifEmptyUse` applies.
- The Requester rule is the compiler's. A task with `requesterCanAnswer: false` compiles to the wait's `may`: `actor != REQ.orValue({'type': '', 'id': ''})`, which compares the actor with the Requester. This is what stops a ticket's reporter from answering their own request after a connection start.
- `requester` is no authored value: authored value IDs start with `v_`, and every other top-level data key belongs to the compiler.

### 9.5 A reference that is not a person

- The compiler builds `whoIsAsked` and notification recipients only from user and group references.
- Kernel rule (spec section 2): a resolved assignee whose `type` is not `user` or `group` is dropped when the person wait opens and is not recorded. A hand-written `assignees: [request.by]` after a connection start opens the wait with nobody; the request is stuck with `nobody-to-ask` (section 11.5), the stuck message goes to the workflow admins, and the request waits.
- The notifier skips such recipients (section 12.3).

### 9.6 The inbound endpoint (Fixed)

`POST {hooks}/hooks/v1/events/{connection}`, one URL per connection.

Verifying an inbound request is the connector's job: a real system signs its own way, and its connector's `verify` checks that scheme. The platform's own scheme is Standard Webhooks, which every mock uses:

| Header | Content |
|---|---|
| `webhook-id` | The sender's message ID, stable across retries. It is the `eventId`. |
| `webhook-timestamp` | Unix seconds. Refused when more than 300 s from the engine's clock, in the past or in the future. |
| `webhook-signature` | Space-separated `v1,<base64 HMAC-SHA256(secret, id + "." + timestamp + "." + body)>`; any one valid signature passes. The secret is the connection's `inbound` slot, `whsec_` + base64 of at least 24 bytes; the HMAC key is those decoded bytes, as Standard Webhooks says. |
| `content-type` | `application/json` |

Body of the platform's scheme: `{"type": "<trigger name>", "data": {...}}`. A connector for one system (each mock included) maps `data` from that system's terms to the trigger's event fields, a person to a user `Ref`. The engine validates the result (section 9.7, step 5). The real Helpdesk's scheme, and whether it carries a signed timestamp: unknown: depends on the existing application. A scheme without one leaves replay protection to the dedupe alone: an old event that never started a request can be replayed into a newer binding.

Limits: a body over 256 KiB (262144 bytes) is refused unread, by `Content-Length` or by stopping the read at the limit.

### 9.7 Processing, step by step

Before any transaction:

1. Body over the limit: `413 too-large`.
2. No such connection, or its connector has no trigger entry: `404 unknown-connection`.
3. The connection is `notSetUp` or `disabled`: `503 connection-unavailable`, `Retry-After: 300`.
4. `verify` refuses: `401 unauthenticated`.
5. `parse`: `unparsable` is `400 unparsable`; `unavailable` is `503 unavailable`, `Retry-After: 60`; `ignored` is `200` with `results: []`. For `events`, each event is validated against its trigger version's schema; a failure is `400 event-invalid`.

An answer from steps 1 to 5 writes one `inbound_log` row with no workflow and the answer's `error` as its code, without the body.

Then, for every candidate workflow (every workflow whose highest published version has a binding on this connection whose `event` is one of the parsed `<name>@<version>` keys), in workflow ID order:

1. An `inbound_log` row with result `started` exists for `(connection, eventId, workflow)`: `duplicate`, with that row's request.
2. Take that version's bindings on this connection with a parsed event, in declared order, and evaluate each `when` over its `sent`. An error: `refused`, `mapping-error`. The first that is true is the binding. None: `notMatched`.
3. The binding is paused: `paused`.
4. Evaluate each `data` expression. An error: `refused`, `mapping-error`.
5. One transaction, the start turn (`kernel/data-model.md` section 1): insert the `inbound_log` row with result `started`, then start the request on that version with `by` the connection, `input: {outcome, data}` and `trigger: {kind: "event", id, connection, event, eventId}`. The start wait's `may`, schema, data-source lookups (section 11.3) and checks apply; its assignees are not checked and no membership lookup is made. Commit: `started`. A start whose firings fault is `started`: the request exists, faulted.
6. A conflict on the unique index of started rows (a concurrent delivery won): roll back; `duplicate`, with the winner's request.
7. A final refusal (`mapping-error`, `may`, `invalid-data`, `choice-unknown`, `check`, `rule-error`): roll back; result `refused`.
8. `source-unavailable`, or any other error inside this workflow's start (an exception, a lost store connection, a lock not obtained): roll back; result `unavailable`. Other workflows of the event are processed as usual.

Every result except `started` is written as its own `inbound_log` row after its transaction, with the parsed event in `sent` and, for `refused`, the problems. A `refused` result also writes a `start-refused` log line. If any workflow's result is `unavailable`, the answer is `503 unavailable`, `Retry-After: 60`; the sender's retry finds the workflows that started as `duplicate`. Otherwise `200` with the answer.

One start is one transaction; an event that starts several workflows makes several. A crash leaves the sender without an answer, and the sender's retry is processed afresh: the unique index on started rows makes that safe. Nothing runs an event again unless the sender sends it again or an admin runs a refused start again (section 9.10).

### 9.8 The answer (Fixed)

```ts
interface InboundAnswer {                    // 200, content-type application/json
  eventId: string | null;                    // null only for an ignored delivery without an ID
  results: InboundResult[];                  // one per candidate workflow, in workflow ID order; [] when none
}

type InboundResult =
  | { workflow: string; version: number; result: "started";   binding: string; requestId: string; readableId: number }
  | { workflow: string; version: number; result: "duplicate"; binding: string; requestId: string; readableId: number }
  | { workflow: string; version: number; result: "notMatched" }
  | { workflow: string; version: number; result: "paused";    binding: string }
  | { workflow: string; version: number; result: "refused";   binding: string; problems: Problem[] };

interface Problem {
  code: "mapping-error" | "may" | "invalid-data" | "choice-unknown" | "check" | "rule-error" | (string & {});
  where: Location | null;                    // authored location: the binding part, the question, or the button
  params: JsonObject;                        // invalid-data: { rule }; check: { button }; mapping-error and rule-error: { error }, the expression error kind; otherwise {}
}

interface HookError { error: string }        // every non-200 answer
```

`workflow` is the server's workflow ID. For `duplicate`, `version` and `binding` are those that started the request. No CEL error text and no check message leaves the platform.

| HTTP | `error` | When | The sender should |
|---|---|---|---|
| 200 | | Processed, whatever happened per workflow | Not retry |
| 400 | `unparsable`, `event-invalid` | The body cannot be read, or fails the trigger's schema | Not retry; fix the sender |
| 401 | `unauthenticated` | Signature, timestamp or scheme refused | Fix configuration |
| 404 | `unknown-connection` | | Fix configuration |
| 413 | `too-large` | Over 256 KiB | Not retry |
| 503 | `connection-unavailable`, `unavailable` | The connection is not ready or disabled; the store, the directory or a data source cannot be reached; an unexpected error inside a workflow's start | Retry after `Retry-After` |

### 9.9 `RequestStarted.trigger`

As in section 7.3. Every `EventTrigger` field is always written. `null` for a person's start. `evolve` stores it as recorded and never branches on it; `trigger.kind` is an open enum. It is not in CEL: a condition that must tell a connection start from a person start reads `request.by.type == 'connection'`. The raw event is not in history; history holds the mapped input.

### 9.10 Refused starts, and running one again

A refused start is an `inbound_log` row with result `refused`. The workflow admins of its workflow and platform admins list those of the last 30 days that no later row runs again (`retry_of`):

```ts
listRefusedStarts(args: { workflow?: string }): RefusedStart[];   // newest first; others get not-admin
type RefusedStartId = string;   // opaque; names one inbound_log row
interface RefusedStart {
  id: RefusedStartId;
  workflow: string;
  startsWhen: string;      // the binding's ID
  at: string;              // RFC 3339
  code: string;            // a Problem code (section 9.8)
  params: JsonObject;
  location?: Location;     // the authored location, when there is one
}
retryRefusedStart(id: RefusedStartId): RetriedStart;   // POST {base}/refused-starts/{id}/retry
type RetriedStart =
  | { result: "started"; requestId: string; readableId: string; binding: string; version: number }
  | { result: "duplicate"; requestId: string; readableId: string }
  | { result: "notMatched" }
  | { result: "paused"; binding: string }
  | { result: "refused"; binding: string; refusals: Refusal[] };   // Refusal: a code, an authored location and params, as Problem
```

`retryRefusedStart` reads the row's `sent` and runs the per-workflow steps of section 9.7 for that workflow only, on the bindings of the workflow's live version at that moment, so the usual fix is to publish and then run it again. It writes its own `inbound_log` row (`by` the admin, `retry_of` the refused row). The unique index on started rows means it can never start a second request for a workflow (`duplicate`). A start refused again is listed again.

### 9.11 Publish checks for bindings

The names below are rule names, not finding codes. The core reports each under one of its own finding codes, which keep the editor's spelling: for example `binding-answer-missing` as `startsWhen.neededNotFilled`, `binding-trigger-missing` as `catalogue.unknownEntry`, and `connection-not-set-up` as `catalogue.connectionNotSetUp`.

| Name | Severity | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `binding-trigger-missing` | To do | `connection` and `event` name a trigger entry in the catalogue. |
| `binding-button-missing` | To do | `outcome` is an outcome of the start wait (the authored format already makes an absent button with several buttons a To do). |
| `binding-when-not-boolean` | To do | `when` type-checks to `bool`. |
| `binding-sent-maybe-absent` | To do | `when` and every `data` expression read a sent field that is not `required` only through `has()` or optional syntax, as spec section 6 requires of data paths. Otherwise every event without that field is refused with `mapping-error`. |
| `binding-answer-invalid` | To do | Every `data` key is a property of the outcome's schema, and its expression's type fits it. |
| `binding-answer-missing` | To do | Every property the outcome's schema requires, and every question in the bound button's effective needed set (`neededToPress` plus `neededForEveryButton`), whether or not it has a `showWhen`, is mapped by an expression that cannot be absent apart from the compiler's `showWhen` wrapping (section 9.1). |
| `binding-requester-invalid` | To do | `requester` is a `sentField` of kind `person`. |
| `connection-not-set-up` | To do | The connection is `notSetUp`. |

### 9.12 Tables

`inbound_log`, `workflow_settings.paused_bindings` and `settings_log`: `kernel/data-model.md`.

## 10. Door 3: calls

### 10.1 What the kernel sees

- An await is a write call: the compiler writes `effect: "write"` for `sort: write` and `sort: await`, and `"read"` for `sort: read`. The recorded `op` names the catalogue entry, and an op version never changes, so history always says it was an await.
- "When the stage is entered again" comes from the authored `ifStageEntersAgain`, or else the entry's `onRepeat`. `again` compiles to `keyScope: activation`: the derived key (section 7.4), new on every entry. `once` compiles to the explicit `idempotencyKey: 'once.' + request.id + '.' + '<action ID>'`, so every entry of the stage sends the same key. A read always has `keyScope: activation`. Publish writes the choice explicitly.
- Recorded: `WaitOpened` when the stage is entered; `WaitCompleted` or `CallResultLate` when the result is recorded. "Accepted", the job reference and polls are working state.

### 10.2 One job per call

The turn that opens a call wait inserts its `pending_calls` row and one `call` job, in the turn's transaction. The job, each time it runs:

1. Reads its row. No row: done. A row with `wait_closed` that was never sent (`attempts = 0`), or whose call is a read: the row is deleted, nothing is recorded, done.
2. With no `job_ref`: increments `attempts` and calls `call(op, args, key)`. With a `job_ref` (an await whose job is running): calls `status(op, key, job_ref)`.
3. `ok` or `failed`, valid (data fits `result`; `code` is a failure code; an await op names its job, and the job the row holds when it has one): a result turn (section 10.3). Done.
4. `accepted` from an await op: sets `job_ref`; `running`: nothing. The job runs again after `pollSeconds`.
5. `unknown`, an answer that does not fit (logged `result-invalid`), an answer naming another job than the row's (logged `job-mismatch`), or the connection not `ready`: `last_error` is set and the job runs again after 10 s, 30 s, 1 min, 5 min, then every 15 min, with the same key. Never recorded.

There is no limit on tries. A job that dies while running (a crash) is taken again by the next worker once its lock is stale, and sends again with the same key. Each try past the operation's `expectedWithinSeconds` writes one `call-overdue` log line. There is no callback endpoint: an await is only polled.

### 10.3 A result is tied to its job and to its wait

1. **To its wait.** A result is recorded for the wait of the row whose job got it. No other row is touched.
2. **To its job.** For an await op the row's `job_ref` is set from `accepted`, or from the `jobRef` of an immediate `ok` or `failed`, and is never overwritten. A status answer counts only if it names that job. So a stale result of a failed job never completes the wait of the job that replaced it.
3. **The result turn.** One input, one transaction, under the request's lock. The request's events are folded.
   - If the wait already has a `WaitCompleted` or a `CallResultLate` in history, the result is a duplicate: it is dropped and the row is deleted.
   - Else, if the wait is open: `WaitCompleted {wait, outcome: "ok" | "failed", data, by: {type: "connection", id}, evidence: null}`. A `failed` result's `data` is `{code, message}`.
   - Else (cancelled, skipped, or the request closed): `CallResultLate {wait, outcome, data}`.
   - The row is deleted.
4. Whether a wait has a result, or is open, is read from history, never from `pending_calls`.

### 10.4 Leaving the stage; retry and close

- Leaving the stage (an arrow, a send-back), a retry or a close tells the outside system nothing. The wait is closed in history; the turn sets `wait_closed` on its row. A write or await that was sent at least once keeps its job, which sends again or asks again with the same key until a clear answer, recorded as `CallResultLate`, which conditions never read; each such try writes a `call-outcome-unknown` log line. A read, and a call never sent, are dropped when the job next runs: nothing is recorded.
- The first build offers workflow admins and platform admins two actions:

| Action | Admin turn | What happens to calls |
|---|---|---|
| Retry | Offered only for a request stuck with `action-failed` or `nobody-to-ask` (section 11.5): clear the fault, if any, and re-enter the stage where the request stopped. `action-failed`: the action is tried again. `nobody-to-ask`: the group is read again and the stage's tasks are asked again. | The old waits are closed, their rows get `wait_closed`. The re-entered stage opens new call waits. Under "once" the key is the same: the connector returns the earlier result, joins the running job, or, if that job failed, starts a new one. Under "again" the key is new and a new job starts; an old one still running runs on detached. |
| Close | For any open request, stuck or not | Every open wait is cancelled; rows get `wait_closed`; outstanding results of sent writes and awaits are recorded late; reads, and calls never sent, are dropped. |

- Retry on a request that is not stuck is refused with `not-stuck` (409); on one stuck with `nothing-fits` or `error`, with `not-retryable` (409). Neither writes anything to history. For `nothing-fits` and `error` only Close is offered: both would repeat the same result, and after an error the request sits where its turn began, so a retry could repeat an outside action that had already succeeded. A call that is merely slow is waited for, or the request is closed.

## 11. Doors 4 and 5 at act time; who can be asked; the stuck state

### 11.1 Membership

- When a person acts on a wait whose recorded assignees include a group, the engine asks the directory connection `groupsOf(actor)` within 5 s. The lookups made when a person acts (this one and the data-source lookups of section 11.3) happen before the request is locked, after an unlocked check that the wait is open; the wait is checked again under the lock. No outside call is made while a request is locked.
- The directory cannot be reached, answers unclearly, or its connection is not ready: the act is refused with `membership-unavailable` ("try again"). An act on a wait that is not open answers `wait-not-open` even while the directory is down, because the unlocked check comes first. Nothing is written to history or to `attempts_log`. The runtime API answers it as HTTP 503. A `directory-unavailable` log line is written.
- `evidence.memberOf` lists the assignee groups the actor belongs to, in the order of the recorded assignees.
- The start turn makes no membership lookup. The action-item list and the notifier keep their existing behaviour on failure (a partial list with `groupsUnavailable`; a notifier job that runs again).

### 11.2 The question-scoped choices call

Directory choices are a data source like any other: a question whose choices come from the directory (`from: "directory"`, the members of a group) compiles to a lookup on the directory connection's `groupMembers@1` with input `group` from `peopleIn`. Its list is read live when the form is shown and its answer is checked by a lookup when the person acts, on the start form too. A `members` step and an "is in group" test inside a condition still compile to a recorded `membersOf@1` read: a separate read call in its own engine stage, placed just before the step that uses it, so it sees a group saved earlier in the same section.

An outcome of the published definition carries `lookups`, one per answer that names an item of a data source. The choices call and the act-time check read only this, never the authored form:

```ts
interface Outcome {               // published definition, person wait
  id: string; schema: string; checks: Check[];
  lookups: Lookup[];              // [] when none; in form order
}
interface Lookup {
  property: string;               // the outcome's data property: the question ID
  connection: string;
  source: string;                 // "<name>@<version>" of a dataSource entry
  inputs: { [name: string]: Cel };// over input, data, request (not request.id) and the constants; an expression may give an optional, and optional.none() leaves that input out
  storedField: string;            // the item field compared with the answer
  labelField: string;             // the item field shown as the label
  answer: "item" | "person";      // item: the answer is {stored, label}; person: the answer is a user Ref (directory choices)
}
```
